explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The finding of two contrast-filled lumens separated by a thin intimal flap (the "double-barrel" appearance) is a classic sign of Aortic Dissection.

  • In an aortic dissection, a tear occurs in the inner layer (intima) of the aortic wall. High-pressure blood enters this tear and peels the layers of the aorta apart, creating a false lumen alongside the true lumen.
  • On a CT angiogram, the contrast flows through both channels, and the remaining strip of tissue between them is seen as the intimal flap.



Reference:
  1. https://www.journalofcardiologycases.com/article/S1878-5409(21)00089-X/pdf
  2. https://radiopaedia.org/articles/aortic-dissection
question: A CT angiogram shows an aorta with two contrast-filled lumens separated by an intimal flap, giving a double-barrel appearance. This finding is most characteristic of which condition?

correctAnswer: C. Emergency surgical repair of the ascending aorta
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The CT image shows an intimal flap within the ascending aorta, consistent with Stanford type A aortic dissection.

  • Stanford type A aortic dissection is a surgical emergency due to the high risk of rupture, tamponade, and coronary involvement.
  • Immediate operative repair is required.

Aortic dissection - Management:

  • Initial management (all cases):
    • ICU care, arterial line
    • Anti-impulse therapy
      • β-blockers first (esmolol/labetalol)
      • Target: HR 60–80 bpm, SBP 100–110 mmHg
      • Add a vasodilator only after β-blockade
    • IV opioids for pain
  • Ascending dissection (Stanford A):
    • Emergency surgery (absolute indication)
  • Descending dissection (Stanford B):
    • Medical management preferred
    • Surgery/TEVAR only if complicated (rupture, malperfusion, expansion, persistent pain)
  • Chronic dissection:
    • Lifelong β-blockers
    • Strict BP control
    • Regular CT/MRA surveillance



Reference:

Schwartz Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Pages 882, 884

options.text: Emergency surgical repair of the ascending aorta

question: A 55-year-old man presents with sudden onset of severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back, associated with hypertension and diaphoresis. CT angiography of the chest is shown above. What is the most appropriate management for this condition?

correctAnswer: C. Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm measuring 5.8 cm
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • For an asymptomatic ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm (ATAA), the threshold for elective surgical repair in an otherwise healthy patient is typically > 5.5 cm.

Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm (TAA) - Indications for Repair:

  • Ascending aorta: ≥ 5.5 cm
  • Descending thoracic aorta: ≥ 6.0 cm
  • Rapid growth: > 0.5 cm/year
  • In case of associated conditions:
    • Marfan syndrome: Ascending aorta ≥ 5.0 cm
    • Loeys–Dietz syndrome: Ascending aorta 4.4–4.6 cm
    • Descending TAA (Marfan / Loeys–Dietz): < 6.0 cm
    • Women planning pregnancy: Consider repair at ≥4.0 cm
  • Rupture or acute dissection


Reference:

Schwartz Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Page 860.

options.text: Descending thoracic aortic aneurysm measuring 5.8 cm
Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm measuring 5.8 cm
Thoracic aneurysm with a 0.4 cm increase in size last year

question: A 62-year-old asymptomatic man is found to have an ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm on a CT scan during routine evaluation. Which of the following is an indication for operative repair?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Popliteal artery aneurysms should be repaired if symptomatic or if asymptomatic but >20 mm in diameter, due to the high risk of thrombosis and distal embolisation.

Indications for repair in a popliteal aneurysm:

  • All symptomatic popliteal aneurysms
  • Asymptomatic aneurysm >20 mm
  • Smaller aneurysms with intraluminal thrombus (risk of embolisation)

Surgeries: Two techniques for surgical repair may be used:

  1. Exclusion bypass: Medial approach to the above- and below-knee popliteal arteries, ligation of the aneurysm and restoration of flow to the foot with a bypass graft using saphenous vein.
  2. Inlay repair: Posterior approach.


Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1023
question: A 66-year-old man is found to have a popliteal artery aneurysm detected on duplex ultrasonography during evaluation for knee swelling. He is asymptomatic and has palpable distal pulses. Which of the following is an indication for repair of a popliteal artery aneurysm?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image shows an infected arterial aneurysm (mycotic aneurysm), typically resulting from bacterial infection of the arterial wall.

  • The most common organism that causes a mycotic (infected) aneurysm is Staphylococcus aureus, which occurs due to microbial invasion of the vessel wall
  • Common causes: Bacteremia, septic emboli (endocarditis), direct spread
  • Most common organism: Staphylococcus aureus
    • Others: Salmonella, Gram-negative bacilli
  • Common sites: Aorta, intracranial, peripheral arteries
  • Clinical features: Fever, pain, rapidly enlarging pulsatile mass, sepsis
  • Imaging: Contrast CT / MRI (saccular aneurysm, perivascular inflammation)
  • Management:
    • Prolonged IV antibiotics
    • Surgical or endovascular repair (usually required)


Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560736/
question: A 58-year-old man with infective endocarditis presents with fever and a painful, pulsatile abdominal mass. Angiographic imaging of the affected artery is shown above. Which organism most commonly causes this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The popliteal artery is the most common site of peripheral arterial aneurysms, accounting for approximately 70% of all peripheral aneurysms.

  • They commonly occur in elderly men and are frequently bilateral, with a significant association with abdominal aortic aneurysm.

  • Pulsatile swelling behind the knee

  • Complications:

    • Acute limb ischaemia due to thrombosis

    • Distal embolisation causing digital or foot ischaemia

  • Rupture is rare



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1023
question: An elderly man with a long history of smoking and atherosclerosis presents with a slowly enlarging, painless swelling behind his knee. On examination, the mass is pulsatile and expansile. A peripheral arterial aneurysm is suspected. Which of the following arteries is the most common site for a peripheral aneurysm?

correctAnswer: C. Asymptomatic AAA measuring 5.0 cm in diameter
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Surgical repair of AAA is generally recommended when the diameter is ≥5.5 cm in men (≥5.0 cm in women) or if other high-risk features are present. An asymptomatic 5.0 cm AAA in a man does not yet meet the size threshold for surgery.

Aspect

Details

Surveillance
  • Small AAAs (3.0–3.9 cm): Monitor every 2–3 years using ultrasound.
  • Medium AAAs (4.0–5.4 cm): Monitor every 6–12 months with ultrasound.
  • Large AAAs (≥5.5 cm): Surgical intervention recommended; if not, frequent imaging and clinical review.

Medical Management

Risk Factor Modification:

  • Smoking Cessation
  • Blood Pressure Control
  • Cholesterol Management: Statins recommended.

Surgical Intervention

Indications for Surgery:

  • Aneurysm Diameter ≥ 5.5 cm (High risk of rupture)
  • Rapid Growth: >0.5 cm increase in six months. (Option B)
  • Symptomatic AAAs: Consider surgery. (Option A)
  • Ruptured AAA (Option D)

Surgical Options:

  • Open Surgical Repair: Using a Dacron graft, which is durable and has a higher morbidity.
  • Endovascular Aneurysm Repair (EVAR): Less invasive, requires long-term surveillance for complications.



Reference:

Sabiston’s Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Pages 1747-1751

options.text: Asymptomatic AAA measuring 5.0 cm in diameter

question: A 68-year-old man is incidentally found to have an infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm on ultrasound during routine evaluation. Which of the following is not an indication for surgical repair of AAA?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Based on the image, the most likely diagnosis is a Cirsoid aneurysm.

A cirsoid aneurysm is a high-flow arteriovenous fistula/malformation of the scalp that is not connected to intracranial vessels.

  • Clinical features:
    • Pulsatile scalp mass
    • Visible dilated veins
    • Thrill and audible bruit
    • May cause pain, headache, tinnitus, or haemorrhage in some patients.
  • Management:
    • Surgical ligation/resection
    • Embolisation (percutaneous or endovascular)
    • Combined therapy yields good cosmetic and functional results.

Hemangioma (Option A): These are benign vascular tumours of infancy that usually regress (shrink) by age 10. They are not pulsatile and do not have a bruit. A lifelong, growing, "worm-like" mass in a young adult does not fit this profile.

Arteriovenous Fistula (AVF) (Option C): While a cirsoid aneurysm is functionally a type of AVF, "Arteriovenous Fistula" is a general descriptive term. Cirsoid Aneurysm is the specific clinical diagnosis used for this particular high-flow, plexiform malformation of the scalp.

Potts Puffy Tumour (Option D) is a non-vascular complication of frontal sinusitis (osteomyelitis of the frontal bone). It presents as a doughy, non-pulsatile forehead swelling accompanied by fever and headache, rather than a pulsatile mass with a bruit.



Reference:

https://radiopaedia.org/articles/cirsoid-aneurysm
question: What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The aortic isthmus is the most common site due to sudden deceleration forces.
  • The aortic isthmus is part of the descending aorta, just distal to the left subclavian artery.
  • Fixed by the ligamentum arteriosum, making it vulnerable to shearing injury


Reference:
  1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2454
  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK555980/
question: A 28-year-old man sustains a high-speed motor vehicle accident. CT angiography shows a traumatic aortic aneurysm. What is the most common site of a traumatic aortic aneurysm?

correctAnswer: C. Aggressive fluid resuscitation to normalise blood pressure
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In the management of a suspected ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA), aggressive fluid resuscitation to normalise blood pressure (Option C) is not useful.
  • While it seems counterintuitive, trying to bring the blood pressure back to "normal" levels (normotension) in a patient with an active internal bleed is dangerous.

Ruptured AAA:

  • 80% retroperitoneal, 20% intraperitoneal (Option A)
  • Classic triad:
    • Abdominal/back pain
    • Hypotension
    • Pulsatile mass
  • Mortality:
    • Operative mortality: 50%
    • Overall, 80–90% mortality
  • CT scan confirms rupture & EVAR suitability (Option B)
  • Management:
    • Immediate resuscitation (oxygen, intravenous replacement therapy, central line)
    • Urinary catheter, cross-match blood
    • Maintain systolic pressure, but not >100 mmHg
    • EVAR is preferred if anatomy allows
    • Treatment: Urgent surgery, not prolonged resuscitation (Option D)


Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1021,1022.

options.text: Most ruptures occur in the retroperitoneal space
A CT scan is useful to confirm rupture and assess EVAR suitability
Aggressive fluid resuscitation to normalise blood pressure
Ruptured AAA is a surgical emergency

question: A 70-year-old man presents with sudden severe abdominal pain, hypotension, and a pulsatile abdominal mass. A ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is suspected. Which of the following statements is false?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most common symptom of occlusive peripheral vascular disease (PVD) is Intermittent claudication.

  • Caused by anaerobic muscle metabolism due to inadequate arterial blood flow.
  • Characterised by cramp-like muscle pain that is:
    • Brought on by walking
    • Not present with the first step (unlike osteoarthritis)
    • Relieved by rest (standing or sitting) within ≤5 minutes

Rest pain (Option A): Occurs in more severe, advanced disease, not as common initially.

Non-healing foot ulcer (Option C): A late manifestation of critical limb ischemia.

Gangrene (Option D): An end-stage presentation, uncommon as an initial symptom.



Reference:
  1. Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 998.
  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430745/
question: A middle-aged smoker reports calf pain brought on by walking and relieved by rest. What is the most common symptom of occlusive peripheral vascular disease?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Leriche syndrome is due to aortoiliac occlusive disease at the aortic bifurcation (bilateral buttock/thigh claudication, erectile dysfunction, weak femoral pulses). The definitive surgical management in a fit patient is aortobifemoral bypass grafting, which restores blood flow to both iliac systems.

Femoro-popliteal bypass grafting (Option A): Treats infrainguinal disease, not aortic bifurcation occlusion.

Iliofemoral bypass grafting (Option C): Used for unilateral iliac disease, not bilateral aortoiliac occlusion.

Aortofemoral bypass grafting (Option D): Not the standard term for bilateral disease; the correct operation is aortobifemoral bypass.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 998,1000.
question: What is the most appropriate surgical management of Leriche syndrome?

correctAnswer: C. It is commonly associated with old age
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Buerger’s disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) typically affects young male smokers, not the elderly.

Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger’s disease) is an occlusive inflammatory disease of small- and medium-sized arteries and veins of the limbs. (Option B)

  • Associations:
    • Strongly linked to smoking & common in young men
    • Associated with thrombophlebitis and Raynaud phenomenon (Option D)
  • Pathology: Inflammatory changes in vessel walls → thrombosis.
  • Management:
    • Complete smoking cessation (arrests progression, does not reverse disease) (Option A)
    • Established occlusions are managed like atherosclerotic disease
    • Amputation may be required in advanced cases


Reference:
  1. Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1024.
  2. Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Pages 974, 975.

options.text: Smoking cessation does not reverse progression
Both arteries and veins are involved
It is commonly associated with old age

question: A 35-year-old heavy smoker is suspected of having Buerger’s disease. Which statement about this condition is false?

correctAnswer: C. Primary Raynaud is more severe than secondary
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Primary Raynaud phenomenon is usually benign, milder, and not associated with tissue loss.

  • Raynaud phenomenon is characterised by episodic reduction in blood flow, typically in the fingers, triggered by cold exposure or stress. (Option A)

  • Clinical Features:

    • Pallor (white): Due to reduced blood flow. (Option B)

    • Cyanosis (blue): Due to deoxygenation of blood, Pain +

    • Rubor (red): Blood flow returns, often with swelling and tingling.

    • Cold Sensitivity: Cold, numb fingers.

  • Types:

    • Primary Raynaud Phenomenon (Raynaud Disease):

      • Occurs without an underlying disease.

      • More common and has a better prognosis.

    • Secondary Raynaud Phenomenon (Raynaud Syndrome):

      • Occurs due to an underlying condition (e.g., scleroderma, lupus).

      • Often more severe.

  • Management:

    • Lifestyle Modifications: Avoid cold exposure, stress reduction, and smoking cessation.

    • Medications: Calcium channel blockers (e.g., nifedipine) (Option D), alpha-blockers (e.g., prazosin), and other vasodilators.

    • Avoidance of Triggers: Avoid cold, beta-blockers, and caffeine.

    • Advanced Treatments: Surgical sympathectomy for severe cases.



Reference:

Ganong’s Review of Medical Physiology, 26th Edition, Page 260.

options.text: It is triggered by cold exposure or emotional stress
Pallor occurs due to vasospasm of digital arteries
Primary Raynaud is more severe than secondary
Calcium channel blockers are used in the management

question: A 26-year-old woman presents with episodic colour changes in her fingers precipitated by cold exposure. Her fingers turn white, then blue, followed by redness on rewarming. She has no systemic illness. Which of the following statements about this condition is false?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis is Paget-Schroetter syndrome (also known as "effort thrombosis"), and the structure affected is the Axillary vein.

Thrombosis of the axillary vein is often triggered by excessive exercise in patients with an anatomically abnormal thoracic outlet.

  • Risk Factors: Cervical rib, excessive muscle bulk (e.g., weightlifters).

  • Clinical Features: Swelling and pain of the affected arm.

  • Management:

    • Early stage: Catheter-directed thrombolysis via an arm vein.

    • Post-thrombolysis: Imaging to assess venous compression during arm elevation.

    • Definitive treatment: Thoracic outlet decompression-resection of the cervical or first rib if compression is confirmed.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1047,1048.
question: A 25-year-old male weightlifter presents with sudden swelling, pain, and heaviness of his right arm after an intense workout. Imaging reveals thrombosis in a vessel compressed at the thoracic outlet. Which structure is most likely affected?

correctAnswer: A. First part of the subclavian artery
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This clinical scenario describes Subclavian Steal Syndrome, where stenosis occurs proximal to the origin of the vertebral artery (first part of the subclavian artery). During exertion of the affected arm, blood is “stolen” from the vertebral artery to supply the arm, causing dizziness, syncope, or vertebrobasilar symptoms.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1008

options.text: First part of the subclavian artery
The second part of the subclavian artery
The third part of the subclavian artery

question: A 62-year-old man experiences dizziness and syncope during left arm exertion. On examination, his left arm BP is lower than the right. Which artery is affected in the most probable condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has diabetic foot gangrene, which develops due to the combined effects of peripheral neuropathy, peripheral arterial disease (ischemia), and infection.

  • Immunosuppression plays a major role in the development and progression of diabetic foot infections by impairing host defence mechanisms and wound healing.

Pathogenesis of diabetic foot:

  • Ischemia (Option A): Peripheral arterial disease, particularly involving the infrapopliteal arteries, reduces tissue perfusion, leading to poor wound healing and tissue necrosis.
  • Peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy:
    • Sensory neuropathy (Option C) is the earliest and most common manifestation, resulting in loss of protective sensation and repeated unnoticed trauma.
    • Motor neuropathy causes intrinsic muscle wasting, foot deformities, abnormal plantar pressure, and callosity formation (Option D), predisposing to ulceration.
  • Immunosuppression: Chronic hyperglycemia impairs neutrophil chemotaxis, phagocytosis, intracellular bacterial killing, and cell-mediated immunity, increasing susceptibility to infection and delaying wound healing.

Management includes optimal glycemic control, pressure off-loading, wound debridement, culture-directed antibiotics when infection is present, assessment for revascularisation (angioplasty or bypass surgery), and amputation for non-salvageable limbs.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1009, 1010.

options.text: Motor neuropathy causes callosities in the sole

question: A 58-year-old man with long-standing diabetes mellitus presents with black discoloration and necrosis of the toes, as shown in the image. He reports long-standing numbness of both feet and a markedly reduced ability to perceive pain. Which of the following statements regarding the underlying condition is false?

correctAnswer: C. Poor proximal blood supply hastens the separation of gangrenous tissue
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image demonstrates gangrene of the foot, characterized by tissue necrosis due to severe ischemia with or without infection. Poor proximal blood supply slows or prevents the formation of a clear demarcation and separation of gangrenous tissue, increasing the risk of spread.

Gangrene:

  • Death of tissue, black from haemoglobin breakdown, usually in the distal limbs due to arterial obstruction.
  • Types:
    • Dry: From gradual arterial occlusion; tissue desiccates; neat separation along a zone of demarcation. (Option A)

  • Wet: Infection and putrefaction; may show crepitus; surgical emergency. (Option B)

  • Demarcation forms via granulation tissue.
  • Poor circulation delays separation; gangrene may spread or form skip lesions.
  • Management:
    • Revascularisation to improve circulation for conservative debridement. (Option D)
    • Major amputation if sepsis, non-functional limb, or circulation cannot be restored.


Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1008,1009.

options.text: Dry gangrene occurs from arterial obstruction with a clear demarcation.
Wet gangrene is a surgical emergency due to infection
Poor proximal blood supply hastens the separation of gangrenous tissue

question: A patient presents with black discolouration and necrosis of the foot with surrounding tissue destruction, as shown in the image above. Which of the following statements regarding gangrene is false?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has classic features of atheromatous embolisation: acute kidney injury after an invasive procedure, blue toes/livedo reticularis, and eosinophilia. The temporal relationship with angiography is a key clue.

  • Definition: Embolisation of cholesterol crystals from atherosclerotic plaques into small arteries.
  • Triggers: Spontaneous or after angiography, vascular surgery, anticoagulation/thrombolysis.
  • Pathology: Cholesterol crystals → small-vessel occlusion → inflammation & fibrosis.
  • Common organs: Kidney (most common), skin (livedo reticularis, blue toe), GI tract, CNS/retina.
  • Clinical clue: Acute/subacute renal failure + peripheral embolic signs after a procedure.
  • Diagnosis: Clinical suspicion; biopsy shows cholesterol clefts.
  • Management: Supportive care, risk-factor control, statins; avoid further anticoagulation if possible.

Acute tubular necrosis (Option A): Usually presents with renal failure but without peripheral embolic signs.

Septic emboli (Option C): Would show systemic infection signs (fever, positive cultures).

Deep vein thrombosis (Option D): Causes limb swelling, pain, and sometimes pulmonary embolism, not livedo reticularis or renal failure.



Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3184670/
question: A 72-year-old man with severe atherosclerosis undergoes coronary angiography. One week later, he develops acute kidney injury and painful discolouration of the toes, as shown in the image. Examination also reveals livedo reticularis, and laboratory tests show eosinophilia and elevated serum creatinine. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The autologous great saphenous vein provides the highest long-term patency rates for femoropopliteal bypass and is the conduit of choice, especially for below-knee bypasses.

Femoropopliteal bypass:

  • Best conduit: Autologous great saphenous vein (GSV)
  • Alternatives: Lesser saphenous (Option C) / arm veins (Option A)
  • If no vein: PTFE graft (lower patency) (Option B)
  • Vein collar (Miller cuff / St Mary’s boot) may improve outcomes


Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1005.
question: A 62-year-old man with lifestyle-limiting claudication due to long-segment superficial femoral artery occlusion is planned for a femoropopliteal bypass. Which of the following is the best graft for this procedure to achieve optimal long-term patency?

correctAnswer: C. Angioplasty has no role in patients with tissue loss
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Angioplasty is indicated not only for claudication but also for rest pain and tissue necrosis.

Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA) treats arterial occlusive disease by balloon dilatation of a stenosed or occluded artery.

  • Indications:
    • Intermittent claudication
    • Rest pain
    • Tissue loss/necrosis
  • Best results: Iliac and femoropopliteal arteries (Option A)
    • Below-knee vessels: less successful but improving
  • Subintimal angioplasty: guidewire crosses lesion in subintimal plane to create a new lumen for long occlusions (Option B)
  • Stenting:
    • Used when balloon angioplasty fails due to elastic recoil (Option D)
    • Types:
      • Balloon-expandable stents
      • Self-expanding (nitinol) stents


Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1003,1004.

options.text: It is effective in treating iliac and femoropopliteal arterial lesions
Subintimal angioplasty is useful for long arterial occlusions
Angioplasty has no role in patients with tissue loss
Stenting may be required if there is elastic recoil after balloon dilatation

question: A 62-year-old man with intermittent claudication due to femoropopliteal arterial disease is planned for percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA). Which of the following statements regarding angioplasty is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Duplex Doppler ultrasound (DUS) is the primary non-invasive investigation used to confirm PAD, localise disease, and assess severity. It is as accurate as angiography in experienced hands and is safe and cost-effective.

Disadvantages:

  • The aortoiliac segment can be difficult to visualise because of bowel gas or obesity.
  • Heavily calcified vessels can reduce DUS accuracy in assessing stenosis severity.

CT angiography (Option A): Used when DUS is inadequate or for pre-intervention planning.

MR angiography (Option B): Advanced imaging; not first line.

DSA (Option C): Invasive; reserved when endovascular intervention is planned.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1001,1002
question: A 60-year-old chronic smoker presents with calf pain on walking that is relieved by rest. Peripheral pulses are diminished. There is no rest pain or tissue loss. What is the most appropriate first-line investigation to confirm the presence, severity, and anatomical level of disease?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI), formerly known as critical limb ischemia, represents the most advanced stage of peripheral vascular disease. It is defined by a lack of blood flow that threatens the viability of the limb. It is characterised by

  • Rest pain: Persistent, aching pain in the foot or toes that persists even when the patient is at rest. It often worsens at night when the legs are elevated.
  • Ulceration: Ischemic sores or wounds, typically on the feet or toes, that fail to heal due to inadequate blood supply.
  • Gangrene: Tissue death (necrosis) resulting from a total lack of blood flow to the affected area.


Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 999
question:
Which of the following findings are characteristic of chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI)?

  1. Intermittent claudication
  2. Rest pain
  3. Ulceration
  4. Gangrene

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The above features point towards Leriche syndrome. It is caused by chronic occlusion of the distal abdominal aorta and/or aortoiliac bifurcation, leading to buttock/thigh claudication and erectile dysfunction.

Site of Obstruction

Clinical Findings

Aortoiliac
  • Claudication in the buttocks, thighs, and calves
  • Femoral and distal pulses absent in both limbs
  • Bruit over the aortoiliac region
  • Impotence (Leriche syndrome)

Iliac

(Option A)
  • Unilateral claudication in the thigh & calf, sometimes in the buttocks
  • Bruit over the iliac region
  • Unilateral absence of femoral and distal pulses

Femoropopliteal

(Option B)
  • Unilateral claudication in the calf
  • Femoral pulse palpable with absent unilateral distal pulses

Distal
  • Femoral and popliteal pulses palpable
  • Ankle pulses absent
  • Claudication in the calf and foot

Common femoral artery (Option D): Rarely isolated; obstruction here does not produce the classic Leriche triad.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1000
question: A 55-year-old man presents with claudication of buttock and thighs and erectile dysfunction. He has a history of smoking and intermittent claudication in his calves. What is the most likely site of arterial obstruction in this patient with Leriche syndrome?

According to the CEAP classification, what is the clinical stage of the disease in this case?

In the Tessari technique, the typical ratio of sclerosant to air is 1:3. This ratio is used to create a stable foam with a larger surface area, which improves contact with the vein walls during sclerotherapy.

Sclerotherapy
  • A sclerosing agent, typically sodium tetradecyl sulphate, is injected into the affected vein.
  • This agent damages the vein lining, causing it to collapse and eventually be absorbed by the body.
  • To enhance the effectiveness of the sclerosant, it is mixed with air to create a foam.
  • This foam allows for greater contact with the vein wall and displaces blood that could inactivate the sclerosant

Indications: Telangiectasias, reticular veins, and small, nonaxial varicose veins (<6 mm) visible in chronic venous disease; suitable for patients with persistent symptoms despite medical management.

Indications and Contraindications

Foam Preparation
  • Two syringes: one with sclerosant, one with air/gas (CO2)
  • Connected via multi-way stopcock.
  • Sclerosant to air ratio is usually 1:3 or 1:4
  • Repeated plunger action to create foam
  • STS: Synthetic sodium salt with anesthetic properties
  • Polidocanol: Synthetic polyethylene glycol, also an anesthetic.
  • Effective for telangiectasias, reticular veins
  • HTS: 23% hypertonic saline, osmotic agent
  • Candidates: Asymptomatic patients and those with controlled recent or recurrent venous bleeding may undergo sclerotherapy without additional diagnostics.
  • Contraindications: Avoid sclerotherapy during acute venous thrombosis or pregnancy.

  • Vessel Size: Suitable for veins up to 6 mm in diameter, including small, nonaxial varicose veins, reticular veins, and telangiectasias.

Injection Technique
  • Downstream injection from larger to smaller veins.
  • Controlled foam volume to displace blood.

Advantages
  • Minimally invasive, enhanced efficacy, safety profile.
  • Reduced volume requirement due to foam.
  • STS: Rapid clearance in blood, effective for larger veins.
  • Polidocanol: Decreased risk of thrombosis, suitable for smaller veins.

Duplex imaging is the preferred modality for assessing venous insufficiency. A significant finding in duplex imaging is a perforator vein with a diameter greater than 3.5 mm and a reflux time of 500 milliseconds or longer, which indicates significant perforator reflux. This finding helps guide the management of varicose veins and associated symptoms.

  • The duplex scan should NOT be performed with the patient in a supine position (Option A) to evaluate reflux.
  • In the supine position, valves may remain open without any flow, leading to an erroneous assessment.
  • The correct method is to perform the scan with the patient standing or in a markedly trunk-elevated position to assess valve function and reflux accurately.
  • A reflux time of 500 milliseconds or longer (Option B) is considered clinically significant, not <500 milliseconds. This threshold helps differentiate normal venous function from pathological reflux, which can contribute to varicose vein formation and chronic venous insufficiency.
  • The duplex scan is not primarily used to locate perforating veins (Option D). Instead, it is used to assess venous reflux in both superficial and deep veins, identifying incompetent valves and evaluating the overall function of the venous system.
  • While perforator veins can be visualized, the scan’s main purpose is to determine the presence and extent of reflux.

The Brodie-Trendelenburg test/ Trendelenburg I test is done to determine the patency of the saphenofemoral junction and hence shows a saphenofemoral incompetence if filling from above is seen.

Procedure:

Perforator incompetence (Option B) is determined by the Trendelenburg test II, which is similar to test I in that the patient is asked to stand up after the same steps. However, here, the tourniquet is not released, and the filling of blood from below signifies perforator incompetence.

Presence of DVT (Option D) is determined by Perthe’s test, in which the patient is asked to walk around or exercise with an elastic bandage wrapped around the legs. The development of severe cramp-like pain in the calf determines DVT.

  • DVT typically propagates proximally, from the calf veins through the popliteal vein and into the femoral vein.
  • The common femoral vein is the next major deep vein in the anatomical sequence above the popliteal vein.

Anatomy of Deep Veins in Lower Limb:

  • Foot and ankle: Deep veins accompany the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries.

  • Thigh: The popliteal vein becomes the femoral vein as it passes through the adductor canal. The great saphenous vein (a superficial vein), and the deep femoral vein drain into the femoral vein in the femoral triangle when it becomes known as the common femoral vein.
  • Pelvis: The common femoral vein becomes the external iliac vein (Option D), which joins with the internal iliac vein to form the common iliac vein.
  • Abdomen: The left and right common iliac veins join to form the inferior vena cava which goes on to the right atrium.


The great saphenous vein (Option A) is a superficial vein, not part of the deep venous system. DVT primarily affects the deep veins and is less likely to involve superficial veins.

Risk factors for varicose veins:

Classification based on cause:

  • Primary varicose veins: These occur due to intrinsic venous wall or valvular weakness without any identifiable underlying cause.
  • Secondary varicose veins: These develop due to an underlying condition, such as:
    • Deep venous thrombosis (post-thrombotic syndrome)
    • Arteriovenous fistula
    • Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome
    • May-Thurner syndrome

question: A 50-year-old woman presents with visible, dilated veins on both legs. She has a history of two pregnancies and works as a retail clerk. On examination, the dilated veins are most prominent along the posterior aspect of her calves. Which of the following describes the classification of her varicose veins based on the involved venous system?

correctAnswer: D. Medial knee, approximately 10 cm below the knee joint line
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The Boyd perforator vein, also known as the upper paratibial perforator, is typically located on the medial aspect of the leg, approximately 10 cm below the knee joint line. This perforator connects the great saphenous vein or its tributaries to the deep veins of the leg, specifically the posterior tibial veins.

Superficial veins:

  • Great Saphenous Vein (GSV): Originates from the medial marginal vein of the foot, ascends along the medial aspect of the leg and thigh, and drains into the common femoral vein at the saphenofemoral junction.
  • Small Saphenous Vein (SSV): Begins at the lateral aspect of the foot, ascends posteriorly along the calf, and typically drains into the popliteal vein at the saphenopopliteal junction which then becomes the femoral vein.

Perforator veins:

Perforators connect the superficial and deep venous systems, allowing blood to flow from superficial to deep veins. Key perforators include:

  • Ankle perforators:
    • Cockett perforators (posterior tibial perforators): Three perforators located along the medial ankle and distal calf.
    • May and Kusters perforators
  • Calf perforators:
    • Boyd perforator: Located approximately 10 cm below the knee joint on the medial aspect of the leg, connects the great saphenous and superficial femoral veins.
  • Sherman perforator: Located in the mid-calf region.
  • Thigh perforators:
    • Dodd perforator: Located in the middle third of the medial thigh.
    • Hunterian perforator: Located in the upper thigh, connecting the GSV to the femoral vein.
  • Lateral perforators:
    • Lateral calf perforators: Less clinically significant, connecting the lateral venous system to deep veins.

The medial ankle, posterior to the medial malleolus, describes the Cockett perforators (Option A), a group of three perforators located in the distal third of the leg.

The medial calf, approximately 10 cm above the medial malleolus, is more consistent with the position of the middle Cockett perforator (Option B), not the Boyd perforator.

The lateral calf, at the junction of the middle and lower thirds location (Option C), does not correspond to any major named perforator vein. The lateral aspect of the calf contains smaller, less clinically significant perforators.

Post-thrombotic syndrome:

Post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS), also called postphlebitic syndrome and venous stress disorder is a medical condition that may occur as a long-term complication of deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

    • Lipodermatosclerosis
    • Leg ulcer

question: A patient came with complaints of discoloration of his left leg as shown in the image. He has a history of deep vein thrombosis and has been inconsistent on medication. What is the possible diagnosis here?

correctAnswer: C. Place a retrievable IVC filter
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In this case, the patient has an acute DVT with a high risk of progression to pulmonary embolism. However, he also has significant contraindications to anticoagulation: Thrombocytopenia (platelet count 40,000/μL) and Coagulopathy (INR 1.8).
  • These factors make anticoagulation extremely high-risk.
  • In such scenarios, where there is an acute proximal DVT and a contraindication to anticoagulation, placement of an IVC filter is indicated.
  • The choice of a retrievable filter allows for potential removal once the contraindications to anticoagulation resolve. Reassessment in 3 months is appropriate to evaluate if the filter can be safely removed and anticoagulation initiated.

Start anticoagulation with LMWH (Option A) is incorrect due to the high bleeding risk associated with the patient's active GI bleeding, thrombocytopenia, and coagulopathy.

Place a permanent IVC filter (Option B): While an IVC filter is indicated, a permanent filter is not the best choice. Retrievable filters are preferred when possible, as they allow for removal once anticoagulation becomes feasible, reducing long-term complications associated with permanent filters.

Start anticoagulation with UFH (Option D): Even anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin carries a significant risk of exacerbating the patient's bleeding complications.

question: A 45-year-old man with metastatic colorectal cancer is diagnosed with an acute DVT of the left leg. He had an episode of upper GI bleed 2 days ago. His lab results show a platelet count of 40,000/μL and an INR of 1.8. Which of the following is the most appropriate management strategy for preventing pulmonary embolism in this patient?

correctAnswer: B. LMWH followed by oral anticoagulant
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Treatment of DVT:

Anticoagulation: For initial management of acute DVT without contraindications to anticoagulation, the current recommended approach is to start with LMWH and transition to an oral anticoagulant.

This approach has several advantages:

  • LMWH provides rapid anticoagulation without the need for monitoring.
  • Oral anticoagulants have shown non-inferiority or superiority to warfarin in large clinical trials. They have a better safety profile and do not require regular INR monitoring.
  • This regimen allows for outpatient management in many cases, reducing hospitalization rates.

Investigation of DVT:

Venous Doppler with Duplex scanning

Non-invasive; detects thrombus by impaired blood flow and inability to compress veins.

  • Presence of echogenic material completely filling the lumen of vein
  • Absence of compressibility
  • Absence of blood flow

Venogram

Accurate for detecting and locating thrombus and differentiating occlusive and non-occlusive thrombus but less commonly used due to invasiveness.

Impedance Plethysmography

Measures changes in venous volume and flow using a cuff. Less useful for calf DVT and previous thrombosis.

Fibrin and Fibrinogen Assays

Measures fibrin degradation products, including D-dimer.

D-dimer has a high negative predictive value.

Radioactive Fibrinogen Study

Uses radiolabeled fibrinogen to detect thrombus. Less commonly used.

Magnetic Resonance Venous Imaging (MRVI)

Non-invasive; Useful for imaging iliac veins and IVC.

Management of DVT :

Initial Anticoagulation
  • Subcutaneous LMWH: Rapidly anticoagulate confirmed DVT cases.
  • Intravenous Unfractionated Heparin: For patients with significant renal impairment.
  • Fondaparinux or Bivalirudin: Alternatives for those with heparin sensitivity or heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

Transition to Oral Anticoagulation
  • Duration: At least 3 months or longer based on risk factors or recurrence.
  • Novel anticoagulants (NOACs): Rivaroxaban, Apixaban (factor Xa inhibitors), Dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor).
  • Vitamin K Antagonists: Warfarin (alternative to NOACs).

Monitoring Anticoagulation
  • Heparin: Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT).
  • Warfarin: INR maintained between 2.0 to 3.0.

For Patients with contraindications to Anticoagulation

Temporary IVC Filter (Option D): Consider if bleeding risk prevents anticoagulation or to prevent pulmonary embolism. It does not treat the existing thrombus and is associated with long-term complications.

Endovascular Surgery
  • Thrombus removal, lysis, and stenting.
  • Beneficial in selected patients, especially those with iliofemoral thrombosis, to reduce risk of chronic post-thrombotic syndrome.

Unfractionated heparin followed by warfarin (Option A) was the traditional approach, but it has largely been superseded by LMWH and DOACs due to the need for hospitalization, frequent aPTT monitoring for unfractionated heparin, and long-term INR monitoring for warfarin.

Catheter-directed thrombolysis (Option C) is generally reserved for massive iliofemoral DVT with severe symptoms or limb-threatening situations. It carries a higher risk of bleeding and is not first-line therapy for most DVT cases.

question: A 45-year-old man with a history of colorectal cancer underwent surgery 3 weeks ago and is now presenting with complaints of left leg swelling and pain for 3 days. His left calf is 4 cm larger than the right. Using Wells' criteria for DVT, what is his pre-test probability score and risk category?

correctAnswer: D. Localized tenderness along the course of the deep veins
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Localized tenderness along the course of the deep veins is one of the most specific clinical signs of DVT. This symptom occurs due to a thrombus within the deep veins, which triggers pain when pressure is applied along the affected vein.

Clinical Feature

Significance

1. Localized tenderness

Specific for DVT; indicates inflammation along the vein.

2. Asymmetrical calf swelling

Common but not specific to DVT.

3. Erythema and warmth

Suggestive of inflammation or thrombosis.

4. Pain in the affected limb

Can occur with or without movement; can indicate venous obstruction.

5. Dilated superficial veins

May indicate compensatory circulation due to deep venous obstruction.

6. Homans' sign

Non-specific; Passive forceful dorsiflexion of the foot with extended knee will cause tenderness in the calf.

7. Mose’s sign

Painful response to gentle squeezing of the lower calf from side-to-side.

8. Neuhof's Sign

Thickening and deep tenderness in the calf muscles upon palpation.

9. Phlegmasia Alba Dolens

DVT of the femoral vein causes painful congestion and edema of the leg with lymphangitis, which further increases edema (white leg).

10. Phlegmasia Caerulea Dolens

Extensive DVT in iliac and pelvic veins leading to a blue leg with possible venous gangrene or infarction.

Pratt's sign: Applying pressure to the calf muscle; if it feels tense and causes pain, it may indicate acute deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

Calf pain on dorsiflexion of the foot (Option A): Homans' sign is the pain or Resistance of the calf muscles to forcible dorsiflexion of the foot. It has been traditionally associated with DVT but is not specific and should not be routinely elicited due to its lack of reliability.

Asymmetrical calf swelling (Option B) is a common feature of DVT but is not specific. It can be present in other conditions, such as lymphedema or muscular injuries.

Pain that worsens with leg elevation (Option C) is more indicative of arterial insufficiency. In DVT, the pain may worsen with dependency due to increased venous pressure.

question: A 25-year-old male athlete develops sudden pain and swelling of his dominant arm after strenuous overhead activity. He has no catheter, malignancy, or thrombophilia. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Based on the clinical presentation, the most likely diagnosis is Trousseau syndrome- a paraneoplastic hypercoagulable state characterised by migratory thrombophlebitis (recurrent inflammation and thrombosis of different venous segments).

  • The hallmark of this case is migratory superficial thrombophlebitis - characterised by recurrent, tender, erythematous "cords" (clotted surface veins) that appear, resolve, and then reappear at different sites.
  • Strongly linked with underlying malignancy, especially adenocarcinomas (pancreatic, gastric, lung).

Buerger disease (Option A) is seen in young male smokers; it causes segmental inflammatory thrombosis of small - medium arteries and veins, not migratory superficial thrombophlebitis, and is not associated with malignancy.

Polyarteritis nodosa (Option B) is a medium-vessel necrotising vasculitis causing systemic symptoms, hypertension, renal and GI involvement; it does not cause migratory thrombophlebitis.

Acute deep vein thrombosis (Option D) presents as a single-site deep venous thrombosis with limb swelling and pain; not migratory and lacks the recurrent, superficial pattern seen in Trousseau syndrome.

question: A 40-year-old patient with long-standing varicose veins due to saphenofemoral junction incompetence is planned for surgical management. What is done in the Trendelenburg operation for varicose veins?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Sodium tetradecyl sulfate (STS) is the most commonly used sclerosant worldwide.

  • Sclerosing agent (e.g., sodium tetradecyl sulphate) damages the vein lining → vein collapses → absorbed by the body.
  • Foam technique: Sclerosant mixed with air/CO₂ → better vein wall contact, displaces blood.

Indications:

  • Telangiectasias, reticular veins, small nonaxial varicose veins (<6 mm)
  • Persistent symptoms despite medical management

Foam Preparation (Tessari Technique):

  • Two syringes: one sclerosant, one air/CO₂
  • Sclerosant: air ratio 1:3 or 1:4
  • Other common sclerosants:
    • STS (Option A): Synthetic sodium salt, anaesthetic properties, rapid clearance
    • Polidocanol (Option C): PEG, lower thrombosis risk, suitable for small veins

question: A 38-year-old woman with symptomatic lower-limb varicose veins and spider veins is planned for sclerotherapy as an outpatient procedure. Which is the most commonly used sclerosant agent in sclerotherapy?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Virchow’s triad includes venous stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability. Increased blood viscosity may contribute to thrombosis, but is not a formal component of the triad.

  • Venous stasis (Option A):
    • Immobility (e.g., prolonged bed rest, long-distance travel)
    • Paralysis
    • Venous obstruction (e.g., pelvic tumours)
    • Increasing age
  • Hypercoagulability (Option C):
    • Genetic thrombophilias (e.g., factor V Leiden mutation, protein C or S deficiency)
    • Acquired conditions (e.g., malignancy, pregnancy, oral contraceptives)
    • Antiphospholipid syndrome
  • Vessel wall injury/Endothelial injury (Option B):

    • Surgery

Venography (Option B): An invasive test requiring contrast; rarely used today and reserved for complex or recurrent cases, not first-line.

question: A 60-year-old patient undergoes major abdominal surgery and is at high risk for venous thromboembolism. Which of the following is the most effective method to prevent deep vein thrombosis in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The presentation of sudden pallor, swelling, and pain in a tense, cool limb with palpable pulses & milk leg in the image is suggestive of Phlegmasia Alba Dolens, which is caused by massive DVT leading to venous obstruction. This indicates venous pressures that are so high they are impeding tissue perfusion.

  • Phelgamsia cerulea dolens: It is characterised by progressive lower extremity oedema distal to the thigh, tight shiny skin, cyanosis (inadequate blood oxygenation)

Arterial thrombosis (Option A): While this causes a cool, pale limb, the swelling in arterial occlusion is usually minimal compared to the gross oedema seen here. Also, pulses would be absent.

Lymphedema (Option C) is a chronic, gradual condition, not a "sudden" presentation of pallor and pain.

Cellulitis (Option D) presents with warmth, redness (rubor), and fever, rather than a cool, pale limb.

question: A 55-year-old woman presents with sudden pallor, swelling, and pain in the left leg. The leg is tense, cool, and pulses are palpable. There is no cyanosis & findings are shown in the image below. What is the probable cause of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image depicts Homan’s sign- calf pain or resistance on forced dorsiflexion of the foot while the knee is extended, suggestive of DVT.

  • Procedure: The clinician performs passive dorsiflexion of the patient's foot
  • Positive Result: The sign is considered positive if the patient experiences pain in the calf or popliteal region.
  • Clinical Significance: Traditionally used as a clinical indicator for Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT), it is neither sensitive nor specific and should not be relied upon for diagnosis.

Trendelenburg sign (Option A) is used to assess the strength of the hip abductor muscles (Gluteus medius and minimus) by observing the pelvis when the patient stands on one leg.

Moses’s sign (Option B) is elicited by squeezing the calf muscles transversely; pain suggests DVT (similarly unreliable).

Phalen’s sign (Option D) is a provocative test for Carpal Tunnel Syndrome, where the patient holds their wrists in complete flexion for 60 seconds to see if tingling occurs.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1044.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Venous ulcers are primarily a complication of venous insufficiency, not lymphedema.

Complications of Lymphedema:

  • Recurrent Cellulitis/Erysipelas (Option A): Protein-rich fluid acts as a medium for bacterial growth, leading to frequent skin infections.
  • Lymphangitis: Repeated inflammation further destroys remaining lymphatic channels.
  • Dermatophytosis: Fungal infections like tinea pedis occur due to impaired local immunity.
  • Progressive Fibrosis (Option C): Chronic inflammation causes tissue to harden and become non-pitting.
  • Skin Remodelling: Results in hyperkeratosis, acanthosis (thickening), and wart-like papillomatosis.
  • Lymphostatic Elephantiasis: The terminal stage involving extreme limb deformity and deep skin folds.
  • Stewart-Treves Syndrome (Option B): A rare, highly lethal angiosarcoma arising in long-standing lymphedema (typically >10 years).

question: Direct contrast lymphangiography is planned in a patient with a suspected lymphatic abnormality. Which of the following statements regarding this procedure is true?

correctAnswer: C. It is associated with mutations in the FLT4 (VEGFR-3) gene
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The scenario describes Milroy's disease. A genetic primary lymphedema presenting with congenital or early-onset lower-limb swelling due to impaired lymphatic drainage.

  • Swelling: Present at birth or soon after, usually bilateral lower-limb lymphedema (often feet), may be asymmetric.
  • Gene: Pathogenic variants in FLT4 (VEGFR-3), affecting lymphatic vessel development.
  • Autosomal dominant (Option B) with variable expression and reduced penetrance.
  • Other signs: Prominent veins below knees, upslanting toenails, hydrocele in males, papillomatosis.

Filarial infection (Option A): This is the most common cause of secondary lymphedema worldwide, but it is an acquired parasitic infection, not a congenital genetic condition present from birth.

Spontaneous resolution (Option D): Lymphedema is a progressive and usually irreversible condition. Without management, it typically worsens through stages of fibrosis rather than resolving.

  3. Pyrexia (Fever) and Productive Cough: Indicative of pulmonary suppuration (infection).

Investigations:

  • Rigid Bronchoscopy: The gold standard for both diagnosis and removal of foreign bodies. It allows direct visualization and retrieval. It reaches up to the third-generation bronchioles and requires general anaesthesia, with ventilation facilitated by multiple holes in the scope.
  • Flexible Bronchoscopy (Option D) is primarily used for diagnostics and deep lung biopsies, performed under local anaesthesia. While it can remove foreign bodies, rigid bronchoscopy is more effective, especially for larger objects and in pediatric cases.

Complications:

  • Lung Collapse (Atelectasis)
  • Pneumonia
  • Respiratory Failure
  • Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)
  • Bleeding
  • Infection
  • Perforation
  • Bronchospasm

Chest X-ray (Option A) and CT Scan (Option B) are primarily diagnostic tools rather than therapeutic ones.

Pancoast Tumor

Also known as Superior Sulcus Tumor, is a rare peripheral lung carcinoma originating from the apex of the lung, accounting for 5% of lung cancers.

  • Invades the brachial plexus, sympathetic chain, upper ribs, and vertebrae.
  • Symptoms: Intractable upper chest and arm pain, arm weakness.

Treatment:

  • Radiotherapy
  • Chemotherapy: Methotrexate.

CT scan (Option C) provides detailed imaging of the lung mass, including its relationship to the ribs, vertebrae, and surrounding structures, however, MRI would provide additional critical information regarding soft tissue and nerve involvement, which is why it might be considered more appropriate in this specific context.

    • Done only after late teens- when no further growth of chest wall will happen.
  • Non-Surgical Options:
    • External Bracing (Option B): Used for younger patients whose chest wall growth is not completed yet, to correct deformity before growth slows.

question: A 48 y/o female presents with fluctuating muscle weakness, difficulty speaking, and drooping eyelids that worsen with physical activity. Imaging reveals a mass in the anterior mediastinum. Which of the following is the most likely paraneoplastic syndrome associated with her condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A contrast-enhanced CT scan is the next best step for evaluating a thymoma. It provides detailed imaging, assessing the tumour's relationship with surrounding structures and helping to determine the extent of the disease.

  • Clinical features
    • Mostly asymptomatic (small tumor), incidentally detected.
    • It may compress the trachea (dyspnea), esophagus (dysphagia), recurrent laryngeal nerve (dysphonia or hoarseness of voice), and superior vena cava (superior vena cava syndrome).

  • Investigations:
    • CT scan: Investigation of choice
      • Determine the extent of the disease.

  • Histology (definitive diagnosis)
    • Noninvasive thymomas: Medullary-type epithelial cells (elongated or spindle-shaped) or a mixture of medullary- and cortical-type epithelial cells (admixture of polygonal cortical-type epithelial cells and a denser infiltrate of thymocytes).

  • Invasive thymoma: Cytologically benign but locally invasive. The epithelial cells are with abundant cytoplasm and rounded vesicular nuclei, mixed with numerous thymocytes.

  • Cytokeratin (marker to distinguish thymoma from lymphoma, thymomas are positive for cytokeratin)

Serum markers (Option A) are not typically used to evaluate an anterior mediastinal mass suspected to be a thymoma. They are generally used to differentiate between seminimatous & non-seminimatous germ cell tumours based on the AFP levels.

Chest X-ray with a lateral view (Option B): While a lateral chest X-ray can help localize the mass within the mediastinum, it is not as informative as a CT scan. A lateral view could provide some additional information, but a CT scan is superior in detailing the characteristics and extent of the mass.

Pulmonary function tests (Option D) are important in assessing lung function, particularly before surgery, but they do not provide specific information about the thymoma itself. They are useful in surgical planning rather than in the initial evaluation.

question: A 55 y/o male presents with a persistent cough and dyspnea on exertion. A chest x-ray reveals an anterior mediastinal mass with tracheal deviation. What is the next best step in evaluating this patient for a potential thymoma?

explanationHtml:
• Complete surgical resection of the tumour is the most appropriate treatment plan for a Stage III thymoma with invasion into nearby structures.
  • Surgical resection may include removing and reconstructing the involved structures, such as the pericardium and superior vena cava.
  • For optimising patient care, a multidisciplinary approach with chemotherapy, neoadjuvant chemotherapy, radiotherapy and immunotherapy is usually undertaken after resection and reconstruction to prevent disease recurrence.

The Masaoka-Koga system is based on surgical findings and describes the extent of tumour spread. It categorizes thymomas into stages I-IV, with higher stages indicating more extensive disease.

Masaoka-Koga Staging System

Stage I

The tumour is completely encapsulated, meaning it is confined within the thymus gland and has not spread beyond its capsule.

Stage II

The tumour has spread beyond the capsule of the thymus.

Microscopic or macroscopic invasion into the surrounding fatty tissue or mediastinal pleura.

Stage III

The tumour has spread to adjacent organs in the chest, such as the pericardium, the lungs, or the great vessels (aorta, vena cava, pulmonary artery).

Stage IV

The tumour has spread to distant sites in the body.

  • Stage IVa: Spread to the pericardium or pleura
  • Stage IVb: Spread to distant organs through the bloodstream or lymphatic system.


Radiation therapy alone (Option B) is generally not sufficient for a Stage III thymoma, especially one that has invaded surrounding structures. It is typically used as an adjunctive treatment after surgery or as palliative therapy in inoperable cases.

Observation and periodic follow-up imaging (Option C) is not an appropriate treatment strategy for a Stage III thymoma. This approach might be suitable for small, asymptomatic, and non-invasive thymomas, but not for advanced-stage tumors.

Chemotherapy as a primary treatment without surgery (Option D): While chemotherapy can be used as a primary treatment for patients who are not candidates for surgery, this patient has no contraindications to surgery and would benefit from the curative option of surgical resection following chemotherapy.

question: A 63 y/o female is diagnosed with a Stage III thymoma and presents with symptoms of myasthenia gravis. The tumour appears to have invaded the superior vena cava and pericardium. What is the most appropriate treatment plan for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient’s history of pulmonary tuberculosis, along with imaging findings showing fibrosis and compression of the SVC and oesophagus, strongly suggest chronic fibrous mediastinitis.

  • Chronic fibrous mediastinitis is a rare disorder characterized by extensive fibrotic tissue formation in the mediastinum.
  • This fibrosis can compress vital mediastinal structures such as the SVC, oesophagus, trachea, and pulmonary arteries, leading to symptoms like shortness of breath, facial swelling, and dysphagia.
  • The condition often follows a history of granulomatous infections such as tuberculosis or histoplasmosis, which provoke a chronic inflammatory response in the mediastinum.

Superior vena cava syndrome (Option A): This is a condition where the SVC is obstructed, leading to symptoms like facial swelling and difficulty swallowing but there is no associated mediastinal fibrosis. It is not the primary diagnosis.

Pulmonary embolism (Option B): This condition causes sudden shortness of breath and chest pain but does not typically cause facial swelling or difficulty swallowing. There is also no associated mediastinal fibrosis.

Thymoma (Option D) is a tumour that occurs in the anterior mediastinum. It can cause compression of mediastinal structures but is less likely to be associated with a history of granulomatous infection and extensive fibrosis.



Reference:

Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Pg.736

SSP is common in older adults with underlying lung diseases such as COPD. The patient's symptoms of severe shortness of breath, chest pain, and a history of COPD are classic for SSP.


Aspect

Primary Spontaneous

Pneumothorax (PSP)

Secondary Spontaneous

Pneumothorax (SSP)

About
  • Occurs without underlying lung disease. (Option A)
  • Typically affects young individuals (under 35 years)
  • It arises from the rupture of small blebs or cysts on the lung surface, leading to air entering the pleural space.

.
  • Occurs in individuals with existing lung pathology.
  • More common in older adults (typically over 45 years).
  • Recurrence rates are higher compared to PSP, with up to 80% of patients experiencing additional episodes

Risk Factors
  • Male sex
  • Tall and thin body type
  • Smoking
  • Family history of pneumothorax
  • Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
  • Cystic fibrosis
  • Tuberculosis
  • Lung cancer
  • Other lung diseases (e.g., asthma, sarcoidosis)

Clinical Features
  • Sudden onset of chest pain
  • Mild to moderate dyspnea
  • Rarely life-threatening
  • Severe dyspnea
  • Hypoxemia and hypercapnia
  • Chest pain
  • Potential for acute respiratory failure

Investigations
  • Chest X-ray
  • CT scan may be used for confirmation in some cases
  • Chest X-ray
  • CT scan for differential diagnosis, especially in emphysema cases

Treatment
  • Observation for small, asymptomatic cases.
  • Needle aspiration for larger cases.
  • Chest tube placement if aspiration fails.
  • Surgical options (VATS, pleurodesis) for recurrent cases.
  • Hospital admission for monitoring.
  • Chest tube placement for large or symptomatic cases.
  • Surgical intervention based on underlying disease.



Chest X-ray of Pneumothorax

CT of Pneumothorax

Chylothorax (Option C):

Chylothorax is caused by the accumulation of chyle (a milky fluid rich in triglycerides, chylomicrons, and white blood cells) in the pleural space due to disruption of the thoracic duct. It is associated with dyspnea and cough, but the pleural fluid is typically milky or clear. This patient’s presentation of sudden chest pain and respiratory distress with a history of COPD is more indicative of SSP rather than chylothorax.

Hemothorax (Option D):

Hemothorax refers to the presence of blood in the pleural cavity, often caused by trauma, surgery, tumours, or spontaneous bleeding. It presents with chest pain, signs of shock, and dullness on percussion. The patient’s history and the absence of trauma or surgery make SSP a more likely diagnosis in this case. Hemothorax would also typically present with signs of bleeding and shock, which are not described here.

question: A 72-year-old male with COPD presents with sudden severe shortness of breath and right-sided chest pain. On examination, he is cyanotic, in respiratory distress, and has diminished breath sounds on the right side. A CXR shows a large air collection in the right pleural space. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Apply a sterile occlusive dressing over the wound, taped on three sides
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient’s history of trauma to the chest leading to an open wound of 4cm and clinical findings of absent breath sounds are characteristic of open pneumothorax.

Applying a sterile occlusive dressing, taped on three sides, helps to seal the wound and prevent air from being drawn into the pleural space with each breath, which can help stabilize the patient and prevent progression to a tension pneumothorax.

OPEN PNEUMOTHORAX

Pathophysiology
  • Large defect in the chest wall (>3 cm).
  • Intrathoracic pressure = Atmospheric pressure.
  • If the size of the defect > 2/3rds of the trachea’s diameter, the air is drawn through the wound rather than the trachea, leading to air accumulation in the hemithorax, hypoventilation, and hypoxia.

Initial Management
  • Seal the Defect with a sterile occlusive plastic dressing (e.g., OPSITE™) taped on three sides to create a flutter valve.
  • Chest Tube Placement: Insert a chest tube as soon as possible at a site distant from the injury.

Potential Complications

Tension Pneumothorax if the defect creates a one-way valve effect.

Perform needle thoracocentesis in the 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line (Option A): Needle thoracocentesis is used for tension pneumothorax, not open pneumothorax.

Insert a chest tube immediately at the site of the injury (Option B): While chest tube placement is crucial for managing pneumothorax and pleural effusion, it should be performed at a site remote from the injury. The immediate priority for an open pneumothorax is to seal the defect first to prevent further complications.

Obtain a chest X-ray to assess the injury and confirm the diagnosis (Option D):

Although a chest X-ray is helpful for diagnosis, the management of an open pneumothorax should not be delayed for imaging. Immediate sealing of the wound is critical to stabilize the patient and prevent further complications.

question: A 30-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a stabbing injury to the chest, having respiratory distress, 4 cm wound on the right side. On examination, his breath sounds are decreased on the right side, and he shows signs of hypoxia. His vital signs are stable. What is the most appropriate first step in managing this patient?

correctAnswer: B. Perform an immediate needle thoracocentesis in the 5th intercostal space, in anterior axillary line
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient presents with low blood pressure, distended jugular veins, and signs of tension pneumothorax, including severe respiratory distress, tracheal deviation, and hyper-resonance. This life-threatening condition requires immediate needle thoracocentesis to relieve the pressure. Once stable, a chest tube should be inserted.

TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX

Pathophysiology
  • D/t ‘one-way valve’ air leaks from the lung or chest wall.
  • Air is sucked into the thoracic cavity without any escape, collapsing and compressing the affected lung.
  • The mediastinum shifts to the opposite side, reducing venous return and compressing the opposite lung, leading to decreased cardiac output and function. This can result in sudden death.

Causes
  • Penetrating Chest Trauma.
  • Blunt Chest Trauma with parenchymal lung injury and persistent air leak.
  • Iatrogenic Lung Injury (e.g., central venepuncture)
  • Mechanical Positive-Pressure Ventilation.

Clinical Features
  • Tachypnea and Tachycardia
  • Hyper-resonance and Decreased/Absent Breath Sounds
  • Resonant Percussion with severe mediastinal/tracheal shift
  • Cyanosis and Hypotension
  • Chest Pain
  • Distended Neck Veins

Emergency Management
  • Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and treatment should never be delayed by waiting for radiological confirmation.
  • Immediate Thoracocentesis (needle): Wide bore needle (typically a 20- or 22-gauge) in the 5nd intercostal space in the safety triangle.
  • Decompression should be performed in the "safe triangle."
  • Safe Triangle Boundaries:
    • Posterior: Latissimus dorsi
    • Anterior: Lateral border of the pectoralis major
    • Inferior: A line drawn perpendicularly from the nipple to the back, just anterior to the mid-axillary line.
  • In critical situations, a finger thoracostomy can be done in the same location.
  • Nasal Oxygen for support.
  • Intercostal Tube Placement (ICT) once stable and confirmed by chest X-ray.

Additional Care

  • Antibiotics and analgesics for treatment.
  • Ventilator Support with IPPV in severe cases.


Order an urgent chest X-ray to confirm the diagnosis (Option A): While a chest X-ray can confirm the diagnosis of tension pneumothorax, it should not delay immediate treatment. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and requires urgent intervention without waiting for imaging confirmation.


Insert a chest tube into the 5th intercostal space in the anterior axillary line (Option C): Chest tube insertion is an important step after initial decompression but is not the first intervention. Needle thoracocentesis is performed first to immediately relieve the pressure.


Perform a finger thoracostomy in the safe triangle (Option D): A finger thoracostomy may be performed in extreme situations where other methods are not feasible or in a pre-hospital setting, but needle thoracocentesis is typically the preferred method in an emergency department setting.

question: A 25-year-old male, after a motor vehicle accident, presents with severe respiratory distress, decreased breath sounds on the right, hyper-resonance, and tracheal deviation to the left. His BP is 85/55 mmHg, and jugular veins are distended. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Given the significant blood in the pleural cavity (hemothorax) and the patient’s hemodynamic instability, ICT placement is necessary to evacuate the blood, relieve pressure on the lung, and stabilize the patient before considering further surgical intervention if needed.

HEMOTHORAX

Definition

The presence of blood in the pleural cavity, causes irritation, pain, and potential shock.

Causes
  • Trauma (e.g., rib fractures)
  • Postoperative complications (e.g., lung, cardiac, esophageal surgeries)
  • Tumours (lung, mediastinum, pleura)
  • Leaking aneurysms

Clinical Features
  • Chest pain and tenderness
  • Dyspnea
  • Dullness on percussion
  • Diminished breath sounds
  • Signs of shock

Investigations
  • Chest X-ray
  • Aspiration (pleural tap)
  • Chest CT scan

Treatment
  • Intercostal chest tube (ICT) placement in the mid-axillary line in the 5th intercostal space.
  • Antibiotics and bronchodilators
  • Thoracotomy if persistent or large blood loss
    • Criteria for Thoracotomy:
      • >1.5 L blood lost in last 1 hour (or)
      • >200cc/hour over next 2-4 hours

Complications
  • Infection and empyema
  • Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)

Observation and follow-up with chest X-ray (Option A): Observation is inappropriate in this case due to the large blood volume in the pleural cavity and the patient’s hemodynamic instability. Immediate intervention is required to address the underlying issue.

Administration of antibiotics and bronchodilators only (Option B): While antibiotics and bronchodilators may be necessary adjuncts to prevent infection and improve lung function, they are not sufficient for the initial management of a large hemothorax.

Thoracotomy with evacuation and lung decortication (Option C): Thoracotomy is usually reserved for cases where there is initial chest tube output of 1500 ml of blood or persistent bleeding (over 200-300 mL/hr) or clotted hemothorax that cannot be managed with chest tube drainage alone. Although this might be considered later, the initial step should be ICT placement.

Filarial infection is the most common cause of chyluria, as it can obstruct intestinal lymphatics, leading to lymph leakage into the urine.

Chyluria

  • Passage of milky white chylous urine, aggravated after fatty meals.
  • Causes:
    • Most Common: Filarial infections (2% of cases).
    • Other Causes: Tumors, tuberculosis, malaria, and ascariasis infestation.
  • Mechanism: Obstruction of intestinal lymphatic vessels leads to high lymphatic pressure, causing lymph to enter the renal lymphatics, or rupture of intestinal lymphatics into the renal pelvis/ureter, forming a lympho-urinary fistula.
  • Clinical Features:

  • Diagnostic Tools: Urine study, culture, intravenous urogram (IVU), lymphangiography, and abdominal ultrasound.
  • Management:
    • Dietary changes (low-fat, protein-rich diet).
    • Antibiotics and diethylcarbamazine (DEC).
    • Increase oral fluid intake.
    • Surgical options include ligation of dilated lymphatics or sclerosing lymph vessels.

Renal stone disease (Option A): While renal stones can cause urinary symptoms, they do not typically lead to chyluria or milky white urine.

Tuberculosis (Option C): Although tuberculosis can cause urinary symptoms, it is not the most common cause of chyluria compared to filarial infections & also the history is not pointing towards TB.

question: A 35 y/o male presents with milky urine and abdominal pain after a fatty meal. He reports weight loss and frequent urinary infections. Urinalysis shows chyluria. What is the most likely underlying cause of chyluria in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The X-ray shows a lung abscess. Aspiration is the most common cause of lung abscesses, particularly in the apical lower lobe, and is frequently associated with anaerobic bacteria from the oral cavity.

Lung Abscess Localized suppuration in the lung is characterized by tissue necrosis

Aetiology:

  • Infectious: Pneumonia due to Streptococcus, Pneumococcus, Haemophilus, Staphylococcus, anaerobic bacteria, etc.
  • Chronic upper respiratory infections (e.g., sinusitis, tonsillitis, dental infections).
  • Mechanical: Bronchial obstruction due to tumours or foreign bodies.
  • Other Causes: Septicaemia and aspiration, commonly lead to lung abscess in the apical lower lobe.

Sites of Infection:

  • Apical Lower Lobe: Most frequently involved in aspiration-related lung abscesses.
  • Posterior Segments: Can be affected due to gravity when aspiration occurs.
  • Upper Lobes: May be involved in cases of tuberculosis or certain types of pneumonia.

Routes of Infection:

  • Aspiration: Inhalation of oropharyngeal or gastrointestinal secretions, often leading to anaerobic infections from the oral cavity.
  • Hematogenous Spread: From e.g., endocarditis or septicemia
  • Direct Extension: Localized infections in adjacent structures (e.g., pneumonia, empyema) can extend into lung tissue.

Hematogenous spread from endocarditis (Option B): While it can cause lung abscesses, it is less common than aspiration in the context of anaerobic infections and would typically present with multiple abscesses rather than a localized opacity.

Direct extension from pneumonia (Option C) can cause lung abscesses, but in this case, the specific presence of anaerobic bacteria and the apical location suggest aspiration as the more likely cause.

Bronchial obstruction due to lung cancer (Option D) is a possible cause of infection and abscess formation, but the presence of anaerobic bacteria and the patient's age make aspiration a more plausible cause, especially in the context of a localized opacity in the lung.

question: A 60 y/o male presents with fever, cough, and foul-smelling sputum. A chest X-ray reveals a localized opacity in the apical lower lobe. Sputum culture shows the presence of anaerobic bacteria. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The high protein and LDH ratios, along with the elevated LDH level, are consistent with a pleural effusion due to exudative cause. Lung cancer is a common cause of exudative pleural effusions, which meet Light’s criteria for exudates.

Transudative effusions result from an imbalance in hydrostatic or oncotic pressure, leading to protein-poor, clear or straw-coloured fluid.

Exudative effusions stem from inflammation or increased capillary permeability, producing protein-rich, often turbid, bloody, or purulent fluid.

Light's criteria for exudative effusions

Pleural fluid protein to serum protein ratio

> 0.5

Pleural fluid LDH to serum LDH ratio

> 0.6

Pleural fluid LDH level

> 2/3 of the upper limit of normal for serum LDH



Causes of Pleural Effusion

Transudative

Exudative
  • Congestive heart failure
  • Cirrhosis
  • Nephrotic syndrome
  • Superior vena cava obstruction
  • Pulmonary embolism
  • Sarcoidosis
  • Hypoalbuminemia
  • Fluid retention/overload
  • Lobar collapse
  • Meigs syndrome
  • Malignant:
    • Lung cancer
    • Lymphoma
    • Mesothelioma
    • Metastatic cancers
  • Infectious:
    • Bacterial pneumonia/empyema
    • Tuberculosis
    • Fungal infections
    • Viral infections
    • Parasitic infections
  • Collagen Vascular Disease-related:
    • Rheumatoid arthritis
    • Wegener granulomatosis
    • Systemic lupus erythematosus
    • Churg-Strauss syndrome
  • Abdominal/Gastrointestinal disease-related:
    • Esophageal perforation
    • Subphrenic abscess
    • Pancreatitis/pancreatic pseudocyst
    • Meigs syndrome
  • Other Causes:
    • Pulmonary embolism with infarction
    • Coronary artery bypass grafting
    • Radiation/trauma
    • Dressler syndrome
    • Asbestosis
    • After lung transplantation
    • After bone marrow transplantation
    • Drug-induced
    • Uremia

Congestive heart failure (Option A): Typically associated with transudative effusions, which are low in protein and LDH. This patient's pleural fluid analysis suggests an exudative effusion, making this option less likely.

Nephrotic syndrome (Option C): Usually causes transudative effusions due to low protein levels. This effusion has a higher protein content, making this option unlikely.

Cirrhosis (Option D): Also commonly leads to transudative effusions due to low oncotic pressure from hypoalbuminemia. The characteristics of this effusion align more with an exudative process.



Reference:
  1. Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st edition, Pg.1629
