question: What is the sign of the gallbladder seen in this USG?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The MRCP (Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography) image reveals dilation of the common bile duct (CBD) along with filling defects, representing gallstones within the duct.

  • Filling defects on MRCP indicate an obstruction in the bile ducts, commonly caused by gallstones (choledocholithiasis) or other blockages. These defects appear as areas where the bile duct does not fill properly or has reduced signal intensity.
  • Symptoms of choledocholithiasis typically include jaundice, abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting.
  • Treatment often involves endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with sphincterotomy and stone extraction.

Incorrect Options:

Stricture (Option A): A bile duct stricture appears as narrowing or constriction of the bile duct caused by inflammation, scarring, or tumours obstructing the duct. While it can mimic choledocholithiasis on imaging, it does not show the characteristic filling defects seen in choledocholithiasis.

Cholecystitis (Option C) is the inflammation of the gallbladder, usually due to gallstones blocking the cystic duct. MRCP typically shows gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, and gallstones in the gallbladder but not changes in the bile ducts, so it wouldn't cause CBD dilation or filling defects.

Cholangiocarcinoma (Option D) is a malignant tumour of the bile duct epithelium. On MRCP, it can cause bile duct dilation and strictures and may also show intraductal masses or nodules. However, the pattern of obstruction caused by a tumour differs from the filling defects seen with choledocholithiasis, as these defects are caused by gallstones, not a mass.



Reference:

Sabiston’s Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page 1501.
question: Which condition is most likely based on the image findings?

However, it typically doesn't lead to blackish discoloration of the perineal skin. Hypotension may occur in severe cases due to systemic inflammation and fluid shifts, but the perineal discoloration is not a common feature of acute pancreatitis.

Option C - Chronic Pancreatitis: Chronic pancreatitis is a long-standing inflammation of the pancreas, often due to alcohol abuse or other underlying factors. It leads to persistent abdominal pain, digestive issues, and potentially complications over time. However, it is unlikely to cause the rapid onset of perineal skin discoloration and hypotension as seen in the given presentation.

Option D - Traumatic Fat Necrosis: Traumatic fat necrosis can occur as a result of physical trauma to fatty tissues, leading to localized inflammation and tissue damage. While it can cause skin discoloration, it typically presents as a localized issue rather than involving the perineal skin. It's also less likely to cause the severe systemic symptoms, including hypotension, seen in this case.

question: A 45-year-old male presents with abdominal pain in the emergency room. . On examination, there is blackish discoloration involving the periumbilical skin. What is the most likely diagnosis for this presentation?

explanationHtml:
Correct option B - Pringle's maneuver

  • Pringle's maneuver involves temporarily clamping the hepatoduodenal ligament, which contains the portal vein, hepatic artery, and common bile duct.
  • This maneuver is used to control bleeding from the liver by temporarily interrupting blood flow to the liver.
  • It is a common technique used during liver surgery or to manage traumatic liver bleeding.

Incorrect options:

Option A - Kocher maneuver:

  • Kocher maneuver is a surgical technique used during cholecystectomy to mobilize the duodenum and improve access to the gallbladder.
  • It is not relevant to controlling liver bleeding.

Option C - Cattell-Braasch maneuver:

  • Cattell-Braasch maneuver is a mobilization surgical technique that allows good access to the retroperitoneal structures.
  • The inferior vena cava, abdominal aorta below the superior mesenteric artery, and retroperitoneal organs of the right side are exposed when it is completed.

Option D - Mattox maneuver:

  • Mattox maneuver, also known as a left medial visceral rotation, is a surgical step to explore and handle Zone 1 and 2 retroperitoneal injuries (aorta, left iliac and pelvic vessels).
  • It starts with incising the parietal peritoneum at the white line of Toldt from the sigmoid colon to the splenic flexure.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient most likely has acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI), classically presenting with severe abdominal pain out of proportion to examination findings, especially in patients with atrial fibrillation.

Statement 1 is True:

  • “Pain out of proportion to examination findings” is a classic early feature of acute mesenteric ischemia.
  • Severe visceral ischemic pain occurs early
  • Peritoneal signs are initially absent
  • Abdomen may remain soft with minimal tenderness

Statement 2 is False:

    • Superior mesenteric artery (SMA) occlusion

Explanation:

Cecal volvulus occurs due to the twisting of a mobile cecum and ascending colon around its mesentery, causing closed-loop intestinal obstruction.

  • Previous abdominal surgery is an important predisposing factor and is present in approximately 30-70% of cases. Common associated procedures include:
    • Appendectomy
    • Cesarean section
    • Gynecologic surgery
    • Colonic surgery
  • Mechanism:
    • Postoperative adhesions and peritoneal bands create fixed points.
    • These promote abnormal cecal mobility and facilitate volvulus formation.
  • Clinical features:
    • Abdominal pain
    • Distension
    • Vomiting
    • Features of intestinal obstruction
  • Cecal volvulus commonly occurs in patients with a congenitally mobile cecum.
  • It may rapidly progress to ischemia, gangrene, and perforation.

High-fibre diet (Option B) & Lactulose abuse (Option C): These are classic risk factors for sigmoid volvulus, not cecal volvulus. A high-fibre diet and chronic laxative use lead to chronic constipation, faecal overloading, and an elongated, heavy, redundant sigmoid colon that easily twists under its own weight.

Female sex (Option D): While pregnancy and prior obstetric surgeries (cesarean sections) can predispose to cecal volvulus, female sex itself is not a risk factor.

question: A 55-year-old patient presents to the emergency department with abdominal pain, distension, and vomiting suggestive of intestinal obstruction. Imaging confirms a diagnosis of cecal volvulus. Which of the following risk factors accounts for 30-70% of cases of cecal volvulus?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This patient presents with the classic triad of Courvoisier's Law (Courvoisier's sign):

  1. Painless progressive jaundice (obstructive)
  2. Palpable, non-tender gallbladder
  3. Constitutional symptoms (weight loss, pruritus)

Courvoisier's Law

  • Courvoisier's law states that in a jaundiced patient, a palpable gallbladder is unlikely to be due to gallstones and usually suggests malignant biliary obstruction.
  • Mechanism:
  • A tumour in the pancreatic head gradually obstructs the distal common bile duct.
  • Progressive obstruction causes distension of a healthy gallbladder.

Clinical Presentation of Carcinoma Head of Pancreas:

  • Elderly patient with painless progressive jaundice,
  • Significant weight loss (cachexia from malignancy),
  • Pruritus (bile salt deposition),
  • Pale stools,
  • Dark urine, and
  • Smooth, distended gallbladder.
  • The obstruction is gradual and distal in the bile duct.

Choledocholithiasis (Option B): Gallstones cause a tender gallbladder (if palpable) and rarely cause a painless, distended gallbladder. CBD stones typically cause acute cholecystitis with a fibrotic, shrunken gallbladder that is not palpable

Cholangiocarcinoma (Option C): While this is a malignancy causing obstructive jaundice, it frequently originates higher up in the biliary tree (such as a Klatskin tumor at the hepatic duct confluence). Obstructions at this high level leave the gallbladder collapsed and empty, making it non-palpable.


Gallbladder carcinoma (Option D): This tumour typically presents as a hard, irregular, and often tender mass in the right upper quadrant, rather than a smooth, distended, non-tender gallbladder full of backed-up bile.



Reference:

Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Pages 1139, 1554
question: A 60-year-old patient presents with pruritus, weight loss and obstructive jaundice. On examination, a palpable, non-tender gallbladder is noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient has RUQ pain, fever with chills and rigours, anorexia, raised liver enzymes, and is HIV-positive with a history of drug abuse, a classic clinical setting for a pyogenic liver abscess.
  • The CT image shows a hypodense hepatic lesion, consistent with an abscess (often with internal debris or gas).

Pyogenic Liver Abscess:

  • Aetiology:
    • Biliary sepsis (35%) - most common
    • Portal vein sepsis (appendicitis, diverticulitis)
    • Hepatic artery spread (pneumonia, UTI, endocarditis)
  • Pathology:
    • Right lobe (75%), usually solitary
    • Common in diabetics, elderly
  • Clinical features:
    • RUQ pain
    • High fever with rigours
    • Toxicity ± jaundice
  • Diagnosis:
    • USG / Contrast CT (IOC)
    • Blood culture
    • USG-guided aspiration
  • Treatment:
    • IV antibiotics (3rd-gen cephalosporin + metronidazole)
    • USG-guided percutaneous drainage - treatment of choice
    • Open drainage if failure / >5 cm
  • Complications:
    • Septicaemia, liver failure
    • Klebsiella → endophthalmitis

Hepatocellular carcinoma (Option B): Typically presents with chronic symptoms (weight loss, jaundice, cirrhosis background) and is usually afebrile.

Hydatid cyst (Option C): Classically painless, slow-growing, and not associated with fever with rigors or sepsis.

Liver metastases (Option D): Usually present with multiple chronic lesions and systemic malignancy features, not acute infective symptoms.



Reference:

SRB’s Manual of Surgery, 6th Edition, Pages 593, 594
question: A patient with a history of drug abuse presents with right upper quadrant pain, fever with chills and rigours, and anorexia. The patient is HIV positive and has elevated liver enzymes. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient's chronic abdominal pain, weight loss, steatorrhea, and CT findings of pancreatic calcifications with a dilated irregular pancreatic duct are characteristic of chronic pancreatitis.
  • Normal CA 19-9 makes pancreatic malignancy less likely, although it does not completely exclude it.
  • The initial treatment is primarily medical, including:
    • Pancreatic enzyme supplementation for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.
    • Nutritional support.
    • Analgesics for pain control.
    • Insulin if diabetes develops.
  • Therefore, pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy is the most appropriate initial management.

Whipple surgery (Option B): Primarily indicated for resectable pancreatic head malignancy or selected inflammatory masses, not as initial treatment for chronic pancreatitis.

ERCP and stenting (Option C): Reserved for symptomatic pancreatic duct obstruction, strictures, or stones, not routine initial management.

Total pancreatectomy (Option D): Considered only as a last resort for intractable pain after failure of medical and other surgical/endoscopic treatments, owing to its significant morbidity.



Reference:

Bailey and Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1279

Surgical Management of DCIS:

  • Breast-Conserving Surgery (BCS) + Radiotherapy (RT).
  • Axillary management: Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB); axillary dissection only if SLN positive.
  • Total Mastectomy Indications:
    • Positive margins after wide local excision
    • Multicentric tumours (≥2 primaries)
    • Radiation contraindicated (e.g., collagen vascular disease)
    • Tumour-to-breast size ratio unsuitable for BCS
    • Diffuse microcalcifications
    • Strong family history
    • DCIS during pregnancy
  • Skin-Sparing Mastectomy (SSM): Ideal for mastectomy candidates; allows immediate reconstruction (TRAM or latissimus dorsi flap).

Adjuvant therapy:

  • Radiotherapy: Reduces local recurrence after BCS.
  • Hormone therapy (Tamoxifen): Prevents local recurrence and development of new primary breast carcinoma in ER-positive patients.

Mastectomy (Option B): Not required; indicated only for positive margins, multicentric disease, or contraindications to radiotherapy.

Breast-conserving therapy/re-excision (Option C): Only needed if margins are <2 mm or positive.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This patient has early TURP syndrome due to absorption of hypotonic irrigation fluid, causing acute dilutional hyponatremia and fluid overload.
  • Initial management is to reduce intravascular volume and free water.
  • IV furosemide promotes diuresis and prevents progression of cerebral edema.

TURP Syndrome (Dilutional hyponatremia):

Pathophysiology: Fluid is absorbed intravascularly due to high volumes of hypotonic irrigation fluid used during the resection, causing dilutional hyponatremia and various neurologic symptoms.

Risk factors:

  • Size of prostate > 75g
  • Duration of surgery > 90 minutes
  • Pre-existing hyponatremia
  • Renal failure

Clinical features:

  • Confusion, agitation, nervousness, nausea, hemolysis, visual disturbances, coma, and shock.

Treatment:

  • Drug of choice- IV furosemide.
  • Mild to moderate cases: IV furosemide and normal saline
  • Severe or symptomatic patients: IV 3% Saline
  • Fluid restriction: Useful after initial stabilisation and correction of severe hyponatremia to prevent further fluid overload.

3% Hypertonic saline (Option A): Reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatremia (seizures, coma), not the initial step in mild-moderate symptoms.

Check serum electrolytes (Option B): Important, but do not delay treatment when TURP syndrome is clinically evident.

Intubate and ventilate (Option D): Only if severe respiratory or CNS compromise.

question: A 70-year-old man undergoing TURP procedure under spinal anaesthesia develops confusion and irritability. What is the initial management?

correctAnswer: B. Convert to an open procedure with T-tube drainage
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A lateral/partial CBD injury recognised on the table should be managed immediately.
  • Conversion to open surgery allows proper assessment and safe repair.
  • Primary repair over a T-tube ensures biliary drainage and reduces stricture risk.

Bile duct injury - Management:

  • Intraoperative (On-table) Management: (During laparoscopic/open cholecystectomy)
    • Convert to open surgery: Long subcostal / bucket-handle incision
    • Intraoperative cholangiogram mandatory
    • Based on Type of Injury:
      • Partial CBD injury <30% circumference
        • Primary repair + T-tube
      • Extensive injury >30%, cautery injury, or complete transection
        • Roux-en-Y choledochojejunostomy
      • Isolated hepatic duct injury
        • <3 mm → Ligation
        • >3 mm → Reimplantation or Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy
    • If definitive repair is not feasible:
      • Place the drain, close the abdomen
      • Refer to the higher centre
  • Delayed (Late-recognised) Injury:
    • Wait ~6 weeks for inflammation to subside
    • After assessment:
      • Roux-en-Y choledochojejunostomy or
      • Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy

Continue the laparoscopic procedure and place a drain (Option A): Drain-only management does not address the CBD defect, leading to persistent bile leak, bile peritonitis, and a high risk of late biliary stricture.

Ligate the duct proximal to the injury (Option C): Ligation causes complete biliary obstruction, resulting in obstructive jaundice, cholangitis, and secondary biliary cirrhosis.

Close the abdomen and refer for ERCP (Option D): ERCP is useful for postoperative bile leaks (e.g., cystic duct stump), but is not appropriate for a recognised intraoperative CBD injury, which requires immediate surgical repair.



Reference:

SRB’s Manual of Surgery, 6th Edition, Page 658.

Definition

Spontaneous full-thickness tear of the esophagus, usually due to sudden increase in intraesophageal pressure against a closed glottis (forceful vomiting)

Plummer-Vinson Syndrome is characterized by a cervical esophageal web, iron deficiency anemia, and dysphagia, fitting the patient’s symptoms.

Plummer Vinson Syndrome

Overview
  • A rare condition affecting middle-aged women.
  • Characterized by a triad of:
    • Cervical esophageal web
    • Iron deficiency anemia
    • Dysphagia.

Causes
  • Iron/nutritional deficiencies
  • Genetic factors
  • Autoimmune conditions

Risks
  • Increased risk of post-cricoid and cervical esophageal cancer

Treatment
  • Iron supplements
  • Dietary modifications,
  • Endoscopic dilatation if necessary


Achalasia (Option A): Achalasia is due to failure of LES relaxation and presents with progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids. It shows bird-beak appearance on barium swallow, not an esophageal web. It is not associated with iron deficiency anemia or cervical webs.

Barrett’s Esophagus (Option B): Barrett’s esophagus is a complication of chronic GERD, characterized by intestinal metaplasia of the lower esophagus. It presents with heartburn and reflux symptoms, not cervical dysphagia. It does not cause esophageal webs or iron deficiency anemia.


Esophageal Carcinoma (Option D): Typically presents with progressive dysphagia (first solids, then liquids), weight loss, and anorexia. It is seen in older patients, not classically associated with esophageal webs. Although Plummer–Vinson syndrome is a risk factor for carcinoma, the given presentation is of the syndrome itself, not malignancy.

Explanation:

  • Esophagectomy is the primary treatment for locally advanced esophageal cancer where the tumor has invaded the muscularis propria.

Carcinoma Esophagus- Management

Staging
  • Accurate staging is essential for treatment planning.

Early-Stage Disease
  • Endoscopic Mucosal Resection (EMR): Removes superficial cancers (T1a) and early cancers with minimal submucosal invasion (T1b). (Option A ruled out)
  • Endoscopic Submucosal Dissection (ESD): Removes larger lesions with en bloc resection. (Option B ruled out)
  • Radiofrequency Ablation (RFA): Treats early Barrett's esophagus-associated cancers. Uses heat to destroy cancer cells. No surgical specimen for pathological assessment. (Option D ruled out)

Locally Advanced Disease
  • Esophagectomy: Primary treatment for locally advanced cancer. Removes esophagus and reconstructs the digestive tract using the stomach, jejunum, or colon. Surgical approaches: transhiatal, transthoracic, minimally invasive (MIE). (Option C)
  • Multimodality Therapy: Combines chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and surgery.
  • Neoadjuvant Chemoradiation: Shrinks the tumor before surgery. CROSS trial showed survival benefit for neoadjuvant chemoradiation followed by surgery.

Palliative Treatment
  • Endoscopic Stenting: Maintains esophageal patency, helps with swallowing difficulties.
  • Chemotherapy: Slows cancer progression, shrinks the tumor.
  • Radiotherapy: Shrinks tumors, controls bleeding.
  • Brachytherapy: Internal radiation therapy targeting the tumor.

It is characterized by the progressive degeneration of ganglion cells in the esophageal wall. This leads to a loss of peristalsis in the lower esophagus and failure of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) to relax during swallowing

Clinical Features
  • Dysphagia: May initially affect liquids more than solids.
  • Regurgitation
  • Halitosis
  • Chest Pain
  • Weight Loss

Investigations:

Esophageal Manometry

Gold Standard: This is the definitive diagnostic test for achalasia. It measures the pressure and pattern of muscle contractions in the esophagus.

  • Elevated resting LES pressure (typically > 45 mmHg).
  • Incomplete LES relaxation.
  • Absence of peristalsis in the esophageal body.
  • Periodic contractions with normal amplitude or high amplitude contractions (type I and II achalasia).

Barium Swallow (Esophagram)

Dilated esophagus with a narrowing at the LES (Bird beak appearance).

Upper GI Endoscopy (Option A)

Normal mucosa, but may show a dilated esophagus with possible food debris. It is important to rule out other causes of dysphagia, such as tumors.

Toupet fundoplication is a 270° partial posterior fundoplication in which the gastric fundus is wrapped around the posterior aspect of the distal esophagus.

  • Fundoplication is an anti-reflux procedure in which the gastric fundus is wrapped around the distal esophagus to reinforce the lower esophageal sphincter and prevent gastroesophageal reflux.

Nissen fundoplication (Option A) involves a 360° complete wrap of the gastric fundus around the distal esophagus and is the preferred procedure for patients with normal esophageal motility.

  • Empirical high-dose PPI therapy (Option D) is reasonable as first-line treatment in typical cases.
  • If PPI non-responsive: proceed with advanced tests → endoscopy, multichannel intraluminal impedance/pH monitoring, esophageal manometry.
  • Adjunctive management: speech & language therapy, antidepressants, and cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) for persistent cases.

question: Which of the following is considered the gold standard investigation for diagnosing esophageal perforation?

correctAnswer: A. Crepitus in neck and difficulty breathing after nasogastric tube insertion
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Cervical esophageal perforations (suggested by neck crepitus, often after NG tube or foreign body trauma) are usually small, localized, and less septic. These can often be managed conservatively with:

  • Nil by mouth (NPO)
  • IV fluids
  • Broad-spectrum antibiotics
  • Close monitoring and nutritional support

Surgical intervention is indicated in esophageal perforation when:

  • There is significant sepsis and drainage cannot be achieved by other means (e.g., interventional radiology).
  • Effective closure of the perforation is not possible otherwise (i.e., endoscopic or conservative approaches fail).
  • The perforation is large.
  • The perforation is in the intrathoracic esophagus.
  • The pleura is breached.
  • There is a large septic load.
  • The presentation is delayed, making primary closure unlikely to succeed.

Sudden severe chest pain and dyspnea following multiple episodes of forceful vomiting (Option B): Boerhaave’s syndrome → usually needs aggressive management, often surgical or endoscopic.

Septic shock with pyothorax and mediastinitis due to lower thoracic esophageal perforation (Option C): Mediastinitis with septic shock → requires surgery plus drainage.

Epigastric pain radiating to the shoulder with pneumoperitoneum on X-ray (Option D): Abdominal esophageal perforation with peritonitis → surgical exploration is indicated.



Reference:

Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page. 1128

Definition

Full-thickness tear of the lower third of the esophagus due to forceful vomiting against a closed glottis

Sudden increase in intraesophageal pressure during vomiting or retching

Sudden severe chest pain, upper abdominal pain, subcutaneous emphysema, shock

Mediastinitis, pleural contamination, sepsis, shock

Most Common Site

Mid-esophagus at the level of the aortic arch (due to external compression slowing transit)

Upper esophagus (rare), lower esophagus (less common)

Antibiotics (doxycycline, tetracycline), NSAIDs, bisphosphonates, potassium chloride, iron tablets

Sudden-onset retrosternal pain, odynophagia, dysphagia

Ulcers, erosions, sometimes strictures in severe or repeated cases

Definition

Chronic, immune/antigen-mediated esophageal disease with eosinophilic infiltration

Common Associations

Atopic disorders: asthma, allergic rhinitis, eczema, food allergies

Symptoms

Intermittent dysphagia, food impaction, chest pain, heartburn refractory to PPIs

Concentric rings (“trachealization”), strictures, narrow-caliber esophagus

Multiple rings, linear furrows, white exudates or plaques

GERD (Option D): Can cause heartburn and reflux, but typically not multiple concentric rings or food impaction refractory to PPIs.

Midoesophageal diverticulum

Type

True diverticulum (traction)

Size

Usually small

Pathophysiology

Traction from chronic mediastinal inflammation, fibrosis, or lymphadenopathy (e.g., granulomatous diseases)

Complications

Rarely may fistulate into the airway in uncontrolled pulmonary tuberculosis

Often asymptomatic; may present if large or complicated

Investigation

High-resolution manometry (HRM) may be indicated in symptomatic patients to exclude pulsion diverticulum due to motility disorders (e.g., hypercontractile esophagus)

Treatment

Asymptomatic: no treatment; symptomatic: treat underlying cause, consider HRM-guided management

Zenker’s diverticulum (Option A): False diverticulum; involves only mucosa and submucosa.

Epiphrenic diverticulum (Option C): False diverticulum caused by motility disorders; only mucosa and submucosa herniate.

Traction diverticulum secondary to granulomatous disease (Option D): Rare, may be true but most mid-esophageal diverticula (Rokitansky) are the classic examples.

question: A 67-year-old man presents with regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, and intermittent dysphagia. A barium swallow shows a posterior outpouching above the upper esophageal sphincter, pointing to the left side. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is false?

Explanation:

Diffuse oesophageal spasm

Definition

Incoordinated contractions of the esophagus causing chest pain or dysphagia

Common Location

Distal 2/3 of the esophagus

Pathophysiology

Hypertrophy of circular muscle fibers with very high persistent pressure (400–500 mmHg)

Symptoms

Chest pain, dysphagia

Diagnostic Finding

High-pressure, uncoordinated contractions on manometry; corkscrew appearance on barium swallow

Treatment

Calcium channel blockers, vasodilators, endoscopic dilatation, extended esophageal myotomy up to the aortic arch (mainly for dysphagia)

Heller’s myotomy with fundoplication (Option B): Extended esophageal myotomy can be used for severe dysphagia, but is not first-line.

Proton pump inhibitors (Option C): Do not address the spasm itself.

Beta-blockers (Option D): Have no role in treating diffuse esophageal spasm.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Achalasia cardia is considered a precancerous condition, with a sevenfold increased risk of developing squamous cell carcinoma, reaching approximately 8% after 15 years.

Adenocarcinoma (Option A): Typically arises in Barrett’s esophagus due to chronic GERD, not in achalasia.

Small cell carcinoma (Option C): Rare and usually arises in the lung; not associated with achalasia.

Undifferentiated carcinoma (Option D): Extremely rare in the esophagus and not linked to achalasia.

question: Patients with long-standing achalasia cardia are at increased risk of developing which type of esophageal carcinoma?

explanationHtml:
• The scenario is of achalasia cardia. Heller’s cardiomyotomy with fundoplication is the most definitive and durable treatment for achalasia.

Management of achalasia cardia

Pharmacological Treatments

Calcium Channel Blockers

Reduce LES pressure.

Nitrates

Relax the LES.

5'-Phosphodiesterase Inhibitors

Increase cyclic GMP to lower LES pressure.

Botulinum Toxin (Botox) Injections

Temporarily paralyze LES muscles.

Non-Surgical Interventions

Bougie/Balloon Dilatation

Ruptures LES muscle fibers to reduce pressure.

Surgical Treatments

Laparoscopic Heller's Cardiomyotomy

(Most common)

Incision in LES muscle to reduce pressure.

It is often combined with a fundoplication.

Partial Fundoplication

Prevents reflux; options include Dor or Toupet fundoplication.

Endoscopic Treatments

Per-Oral Endoscopic Myotomy (POEM)

Newer Minimally invasive procedure involving dissection of LES muscle fibers.

Management of Chronic Cases

Megaesophagus

Severe cases may require esophagectomy (surgical removal of the esophagus).

Endoscopic pneumatic dilatation (Option A): Provides symptomatic relief by disrupting LES fibers but has a high recurrence rate, so not definitive.

Botulinum toxin injection at the lower esophageal sphincter (Option C): Minimally invasive option but temporary, usually reserved for poor surgical candidates.

Calcium channel blockers (Option D): Reduce LES pressure pharmacologically but are used only for symptom control, not definitive cure.



Reference:
  1. Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page. 1122-1125

question: A 42-year-old man presents with progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids for the past 1 year, along with regurgitation of undigested food. He has also experienced weight loss of 5 kg over 3 months. A barium swallow reveals a markedly dilated esophagus with smooth tapering at the gastroesophageal junction (bird-beak appearance). Which of the following is the most definitive treatment for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Loss of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus leads to absent peristalsis in the esophageal body, along with failure of lower esophageal sphincter relaxation.

Achalasia cardia

Definition

It is characterized by the progressive degeneration of ganglion cells in the esophageal wall. This leads to a loss of peristalsis in the lower esophagus and failure of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) to relax during swallowing

Clinical Features
  • Dysphagia: May initially affect liquids more than solids.
  • Regurgitation
  • Halitosis
  • Chest Pain
  • Weight Loss


GERD (Option B): Peristalsis is generally preserved; reflux occurs due to transient LES relaxation.

Diffuse esophageal spasm (Option C): Peristalsis is present but uncoordinated, producing a corkscrew pattern.

Esophageal carcinoma (Option D): Mechanical obstruction may cause dysphagia, but peristalsis is not primarily absent.

  2. Schwartz's Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Page. 1056, 1057

Achalasia Cardia investigations

Esophageal Manometry

Gold Standard: This is the definitive diagnostic test for achalasia. It measures the pressure and pattern of muscle contractions in the esophagus.

Barium Swallow (Esophagram)

Dilated esophagus with a narrowing at the lower esophageal sphincter (Bird beak appearance).

Endoscopy

Normal mucosa but may show dilated esophagus with possible food debris, It is important to rule out other causes of dysphagia such as tumors.

Esophageal carcinoma (Option B): Shows irregular, eccentric narrowing with shouldering, unlike the smooth tapering in this case.

Diffuse esophageal spasm (Option C): Produces a corkscrew or rosary-bead appearance on barium swallow, not bird-beak.

GERD (Option D): May cause reflux with distal stricture, but does not produce marked esophageal dilatation with bird-beak tapering.

A 40-year-old patient is brought to the emergency department with melena and dizziness. Her BP is 100/ 80 mmHg, and her pulse rate is 100 bpm. correctAnswer: B. Overexpression of transforming growth factor-α causing mucous cell proliferation and reduced acid secretion
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This patient has Ménétrier’s disease, a protein-losing hypertrophic gastropathy characterized by massive enlargement of gastric folds in the fundus and body with sparing of the antrum, along with foveolar hyperplasia and parietal cell atrophy.

  • Loss of protein through the gastric mucosa leads to hypoalbuminemia, edema, and ascites, while reduced parietal cell mass results in hypochlorhydria or achlorhydria.
  • The underlying mechanism is overexpression of transforming growth factor-α (TGF-α), which stimulates epithelial (mucous cell) proliferation and suppresses gastric acid secretion.
  • The condition is premalignant with increased risk of gastric carcinoma, and severe or refractory cases may require gastrectomy.

Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells leading to intrinsic factor deficiency (Option A): Seen in Type A gastritis, associated with pernicious anemia.

Increased gastrin secretion causing parietal cell hyperplasia and hyperchlorhydria (Option C): Seen in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, not in this condition.

Chronic Helicobacter pylori infection causing antral-predominant inflammation (Option D): Seen in Type B gastritis, not hypertrophic gastropathy.



Reference:

Sabiston’s principles of surgery, 21st Edition, Page 1235

explanationHtml:
Explanation :

Gastric volvulus is defined as rotation of the stomach around its fixed points-the cardia and pylorus.

  • In the organoaxial type, the stomach rotates along its longitudinal axis, making it the most common form.

  • It is frequently associated with diaphragmatic defects (Option B), especially paraoesophageal hernia, where the stomach (often along with the transverse colon) may herniate into the thoracic cavity.

  • The condition may be chronic with symptoms like difficulty in eating, or acute with ischemia, presenting with Borchardt triad (pain, retching, inability to pass NG tube).

  • Management is surgical (Option D), increasingly via a laparoscopic transabdominal approach, involving reduction of herniated contents, closure of the diaphragmatic defect (± mesh), and anterior gastropexy to fix the stomach.

Rotation occurs along the transverse (short) axis of the stomach (Option A) Describes mesenteroaxial volvulus, not organoaxial.

question: Which of the following statements best describes organoaxial gastric volvulus?

correctAnswer: B. Rapid entry of hyperosmolar chyme causing fluid shift into the intestinal lumen
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This is early dumping syndrome, commonly seen after procedures such as Billroth II or Roux-en-Y surgery.

  • It occurs immediately after meals (within 30-40 minutes) and is often more severe and precipitated by bulky or carbohydrate-rich meals.

  • The underlying mechanism is rapid emptying of hyperosmolar gastric contents into the small intestine, which draws fluid from the intravascular compartment into the intestinal lumen, leading to hypovolemia and increased intestinal motility.

  • This produces vasomotor symptoms (sweating, tachycardia, hypotension) and gastrointestinal symptoms (colicky pain, diarrhea).

  • Symptoms are often relieved by lying down.

In contrast, late dumping syndrome occurs 1-3 hours after meals due to excess insulin release following initial hyperglycemia, resulting in hypoglycemia with features like tremor and fainting. (Option A)

Increased gastric acid secretion due to vagal overactivity (Option C) Not related to dumping syndrome; seen in conditions like Cushing’s ulcer.

Delayed gastric emptying causing gastric distension (Option D) Opposite mechanism; dumping is due to rapid gastric emptying.



Reference:

SRB’s manual of surgery, 6th Edition, Page 830

Rapid entry of hyperosmolar chyme causing fluid shift into the intestinal lumen
Increased gastric acid secretion due to vagal overactivity
Delayed gastric emptying causing gastric distension

question: A patient develops sweating, tachycardia, colicky abdominal pain, and diarrhea within 30-40 minutes of meals following gastric surgery. Which of the following best explains the underlying mechanism?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has hollow viscus perforation with generalized peritonitis, evidenced by sudden severe pain, board-like rigidity, shock (tachycardia + hypotension), and free air under the diaphragm.

  • This is a life-threatening surgical emergency. Immediate management requires aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation to correct hypovolemia and stabilize circulation, followed by urgent exploratory laparotomy for source control (repair of perforation and peritoneal lavage).
  • Supportive measures such as nasogastric decompression, urinary catheterization, and broad-spectrum antibiotics are also initiated concurrently.

Ultrasound abdomen (1) Not required; diagnosis is already confirmed by X-ray and clinical findings, and it may delay urgent management.

Elective surgery (4) Inappropriate in an emergency setting.

Conservative management (5) Contraindicated in generalized peritonitis with hemodynamic instability; reserved only for stable, sealed perforations.



Reference:

Bailey & Love Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1088
question:
A 40-year-old man presents with sudden onset severe abdominal pain. On examination, he is tachycardic, hypotensive, and has board-like abdominal rigidity. An erect chest X-ray reveals the following finding. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

  1. Ultrasound abdomen
  2. Intravenous fluid resuscitation
  3. Exploratory laparotomy
  4. Elective surgery
  5. Conservative management

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Highly selective vagotomy (HSV), also called parietal cell vagotomy or superselective vagotomy, involves division of vagal fibers supplying the parietal cell mass (fundus and body) while preserving the nerve of Latarjet (Option C), which maintains antral pump and pyloric function; hence no drainage procedure is required.

  • The distal 6 cm of stomach proximal to the pylorus (Crow’s foot) is preserved to maintain gastric emptying.
  • Because only the acid-secreting area is denervated, acid reduction is the least among vagotomy procedures, making option B incorrect.
  • This limited acid reduction explains the higher recurrence rate (~10-15%) (Option A) compared to more extensive procedures.
  • However, preservation of normal gastric motility results in minimal postoperative complications (Option D) such as dumping syndrome and diarrhea.
  • HSV has low operative mortality and morbidity, but complications like lesser curvature ischemia can occur.


Reference:

question: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the image shown below?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image shows a highly selective vagotomy (HSV), also known as proximal gastric vagotomy or parietal cell vagotomy.

  • It demonstrates division of the vagal branches along the lesser curvature supplying the parietal cell mass (fundus and body) while preserving the terminal branches of the nerve of Latarjet (Crow's foot) near the distal 6-7 cm of the stomach proximal to the pylorus.
  • HSV denervates only the parietal cell mass, preserving the nerve of Latarjet and thereby maintaining antral contractions and pyloric function. As a result, a drainage procedure is usually not required. (Option C ruled out)
  • In truncal vagotomy, the main vagal trunks are divided at the lower esophagus, reducing maximal gastric acid output by approximately 50%.
  • Since HSV denervates only the acid-secreting proximal stomach, its acid-reducing effect is less than that of truncal vagotomy. (Option B)
  • Because acid suppression is less complete, HSV has the highest ulcer recurrence rate (approximately 10-15%) among vagotomy procedures. (Option A ruled out)
  • Preservation of normal gastric motility results in fewer postoperative complications, such as gastric stasis, dumping syndrome, post-vagotomy diarrhea, and bile reflux, compared with truncal vagotomy. (Option D ruled out)


Reference:

Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1161

Type IV gastric ulcers are proximal ulcers near the gastroesophageal junction and are difficult to manage surgically due to their location.

  • They are typically treated by more extensive resection, such as subtotal gastrectomy.
  • The Kelling-Madlener procedure involves antrectomy with excision of the proximal gastric ulcer, and is specifically used for Type IV gastric ulcers.
  • Variants like Csendes procedure or extended resections along the lesser curvature may also be used for these proximal lesions.
  • Although medical therapy with PPIs and mucosal protective agents is first-line in modern practice, surgery is indicated in complicated, refractory, or suspicious (malignant potential) ulcers.

Maki’s pylorus-preserving gastrectomy (Option A): Used in Type I gastric ulcer; preserves pylorus but has higher recurrence rates.

De Miguel’s antrectomy (Option B): Involves distal antrectomy with ulcer excision; used for distal gastric ulcers, not proximal Type IV ulcers.

Highly selective vagotomy with ulcer excision (Option D): Used in selected peptic ulcer disease; not appropriate for proximal Type IV gastric ulcers.

Explanation:

Curling’s ulcers are acute stress ulcers seen after severe burns (>35% TBSA) due to mucosal ischemia from hypovolemia and reduced splanchnic blood flow.

  • These ulcers most commonly involve the fundus and body of the stomach, while the antrum and pyloric region are typically spared.
  • They may present with hematemesis or upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Treatment is conservative:
    • IV ranitidine
    • IV pantoprazole 80 mg in 100 ml DNS-slow, later 40 mg IV maintenance.
  • This contrasts with Cushing’s ulcers, which occur in CNS injury due to increased vagal stimulation and acid hypersecretion.

Antrum (Option B): Typically spared in Curling’s ulcers; more commonly involved in H. pylori-related disease.

Lesser curvature (Option C): Common site for chronic peptic ulcers, not stress-related ulcers.

Pyloric canal (Option D): Not a typical site for Curling’s ulcers.

question: In patients with AIDS, which of the following organisms is a recognised cause of gastritis?

explanationHtml:
A positive urea breath test indicates infection with Helicobacter pylori, which plays a critical role in the development of chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, and gastric cancer.

  • This corresponds to Type B gastritis, which predominantly affects the antrum and commonly presents with dyspepsia.
  • It may progress to pangastritis, and chronic atrophic changes can lead to intestinal metaplasia and increased malignant potential.
  • PPIs alone do not eradicate the organism; treatment requires combination therapy with antibiotics and a PPI.

Type A gastritis (Option A) Autoimmune gastritis affecting the body and fundus, associated with parietal cell antibodies, leading to achlorhydria, vitamin B12 deficiency, pernicious anemia, and increased gastric cancer risk; antrum is typically spared.

Reflux gastritis (Option C) Caused by enterogastric (bile) reflux, often seen after gastric surgery; not associated with H. pylori, so urea breath test is negative.

Erosive gastritis (Option D) Caused by NSAIDs, alcohol, or stress, due to disruption of the mucosal barrier; not primarily related to H. pylori infection.

question: A 26-year-old male presents with persistent dyspepsia despite a 1-month course of PPIs. A urea breath test is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation :

In hypovolemic shock, there is reduced splanchnic blood flow due to systemic hypoperfusion, with blood preferentially shunted to vital organs such as the brain and heart.

  • As a result, ischemia occurs first in watershed areas of the colon, which have limited collateral circulation.
  • The splenic flexure (Griffith’s point) lies at the junction of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) and inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) territories and is therefore the most vulnerable site to ischemia in low-flow states.
  • The rectosigmoid junction (Sudeck’s point) (Option B) is another watershed area but is less commonly affected initially.

Terminal ileum (Option C): Typically affected in mesenteric arterial occlusion, not the earliest site in systemic hypoperfusion.

Stomach (Option D): Highly resistant to ischemia due to rich collateral blood supply.

question: In hypovolemic shock, which part of the gastrointestinal tract is most vulnerable to ischemia due to poor collateral blood supply?

correctAnswer: B. Assessment of airway, breathing, and circulation (ABCs) with intravenous access establishment
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The primary step in managing acute UGIB is to ensure the patient’s airway, breathing, and circulation (ABCs) are stable and establish intravenous access for fluid resuscitation.

Management of acute UGI bleed

Initial Stabilization and Resuscitation

Prioritise assessment of airway, breathing, and circulation (ABCs). Establish intravenous access with two large-bore catheters for fluid resuscitation.

Risk Stratification

Use the Glasgow-Blatchford Score (GBS) for early risk assessment.

Patients with a GBS of 0 are low-risk and may not need hospital admission.

Blood Transfusion Strategy

(Option D)

Adopt a restrictive transfusion strategy, aiming for a haemoglobin level of 70–90 g/L. Consider a more liberal transfusion approach only in cases of massive blood loss.

Pharmacotherapy

(Option C)

In suspected variceal bleeding, administer intravenous terlipressin to improve outcomes and reduce the need for additional interventions.

Role of Endoscopy (Option A)

Perform endoscopy urgently in unstable patients and within 24 hours for others.

Endoscopy serves to:

  • Identify the bleeding source.
  • Assess prognosis using criteria like the Forrest classification.

Treat with techniques such as:

  • Injection therapy: Adrenaline injection.
  • Thermal coagulation: Using heat probes or electrocoagulation.
  • Mechanical methods: Endoscopic clips to close bleeding sites.

Alternative Interventions

If endoscopy fails or bleeding recurs, consider interventional radiology or surgery.

Post-Endoscopy Management

High-risk patients should receive intravenous proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) for 72 hours, followed by twice-daily oral PPI for 11 days.

Address underlying conditions, including the eradication of H. pylori if present, to prevent rebleeding.

question: During a Billroth II procedure, the surgeon carefully dissects the pyloric region. Which of the following statements about this area's anatomy is most accurate?

correctAnswer: C. Erosion of mucosa due to pulsations from a large submucosal artery
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Dieulafoy’s lesion involves a large, tortuous artery in the submucosa that causes erosion of the overlying mucosa due to its pulsations, leading to bleeding.

Dieulafoy’s lesion
  • Dieulafoy's lesion is characterized by an abnormally large, tortuous artery that runs through the submucosa of the stomach without a primary ulcer.
  • Artery measures 1-3 mm and is typically found near the gastroesophageal junction along the lesser curvature.
  • The lesion develops as the pulsations of the large submucosal artery erode the superficial mucosa. (Option C)
  • The mucosal defect is usually small, measuring 2-5 mm, and is surrounded by normal-appearing gastric mucosa. Once the artery is exposed to gastric contents, further erosion and bleeding occur.

Erosion due to excessive acid secretion (Option A) describes peptic ulcer disease. PUD shows a true ulcer crater with inflamed surrounding mucosa, not a small isolated defect. Bleeding is usually less abrupt compared to massive arterial bleed of Dieulafoy’s lesion.


Rupture of varices due to portal hypertension (Option B); Endoscopy shows dilated veins, not a single mucosal defect with a visible artery. No mention of liver disease or portal hypertension, so ruled out.


Ulceration due to chronic NSAID use (Option D): NSAIDs cause gastric ulcers via prostaglandin inhibition. It leads to diffuse mucosal damage and ulcer formation, not a focal arterial lesion.



Reference:
  1. Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page 1235
  2. Bailey and Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1167

Gastric Outlet Obstruction (GOO) from Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD)
Pathogenesis

  • In adults, GOO is most commonly due to PUD (benign) or gastric cancer (malignant).

  • In infants- congenital pyloric stenosis.

  • H. pylori → Chronic active gastritis (most common worldwide)

  • ↑ Gastrin → Hyperacidity → Peptic ulcer disease

    • Antral-predominant → Duodenal ulcer

    • Corpus-predominant → Gastric ulcer

  • Chronic inflammation + fibrosis near pylorus → Gastric Outlet Obstruction (GOO)

  • Long-term infection → Gastric adenocarcinoma & MALT lymphoma → WHO Class I carcinogen

Diagnosis

  • Endoscopy: Directly visualizes the pylorus to evaluate stenosis and obtain biopsies to rule out cancer.
  • Assess for H. pylori infection. (Option D)
  • Contrast Radiology: Assesses pylorus narrowing and obstruction severity

  • Fluid and Electrolyte Correction: Intravenous fluids and electrolytes.
  • Nutritional Support: Dietary modifications, enteral or parenteral nutrition.

Addressing Underlying PUD:

  • Medical Therapy: H. pylori eradication therapy, Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs).
  • Endoscopic Dilation: Dilate narrowed tract area; stent placement (Option B).

Surgical Intervention:

  • Antrectomy with Reconstruction and Vagotomy: Removal of antrum, stomach reconnection, and vagus nerve cutting (Option A).
  • Vagotomy with Drainage Procedure: Jaboulay Gastroduodenostomy, Gastrojejunostomy, Pyloroplasty.

The symptoms of unproductive retching, epigastric pain & distention, and inability to pass a nasogastric tube align with Borchardt's triad, indicating acute gastric volvulus.

Gastric Volvulus:

  • Definition: Rotation/Torsion of the stomach around the axis between the cardia and pylorus.
  • Types:
    • Horizontal (organoaxial)- rotation occurs in the horizontal direction (most common)
    • Vertical (mesentroaxial)- rotation occurs along the vertical direction

  • Presentation:
    • Chronic: Difficulty eating.
    • Acute: Ischemia and risk of gastric infarction.
    • Diagnosis: Endoscopy may be challenging; contrast radiography is preferred.
  • Treatment:
    • Surgical intervention, often laparoscopic.
    • Reposition hernial sac if present; close diaphragm defect with mesh.
    • Anterior gastropexy to prevent future rotation.

Gastric Cancer (Option A) can also cause abdominal pain and distention, but it is less likely to present with the specific symptoms of unproductive retching and inability to pass a nasogastric tube characteristic of gastric volvulus.

Peptic ulcer disease (Option C) can also cause abdominal pain and vomiting, they do not typically present with the hallmark symptoms of Borchardt's triad, particularly the inability to pass a nasogastric tube.

Intestinal obstruction (Option D) can also cause abdominal distention and vomiting, but the specific combination of symptoms described, particularly the unproductive retching and failure of the nasogastric tube, is more indicative of gastric volvulus.

question: A 2-week-old infant presents with vomiting, dehydration, and poor feeding. An abdominal X-ray shows a "double bubble" sign. Which of the following statements correctly differentiates Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis from Duodenal Atresia?

correctAnswer: C. Postoperative intravenous fluids are administered until the infant can resume feeding, which usually occurs within 24 hours.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:
After surgery, intravenous fluids are given until the infant can begin feeding, typically within 24 hours.

Treatment of Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis (CHPS)

1. Fluid Resuscitation: To correct the hypokalemia, hypochloremia & metabolic alkalosis

  • 0.9% saline
  • 0.15%KCl
  • 5% glucose

2. Surgical Treatment:

  • Procedure: Ramstedt's pyloromyotomy
    • Can be performed laparoscopically or via incision in the supraumbilical or right upper quadrant.
    • Involves incision in the serosa of the pylorus while preserving the submucosa from the duodenum to the gastric antrum.
    • The incision must extend onto the stomach to prevent an early recurrence.

3. Postoperative Care:

  • Intravenous fluids are administered until the infant can resume feeding, typically within 24 hours.
  • Some vomiting may occur immediately after surgery but usually resolves quickly.
  • Persistent vomiting is more likely due to gastro-esophageal reflux rather than incomplete myotomy.

The incision during Ramstedt's pyloromyotomy should only involve the mucosal layer to avoid complications (Option A), The incision must involve the serosa of the pylorus while preserving the submucosa to prevent complications.

Infants with CHPS typically do not exhibit hunger after vomiting (Option B), Infants with CHPS often show hunger after vomiting, distinguishing it from vomiting caused by infections.

Persistent vomiting after surgery is primarily due to incomplete myotomy (Option D), Persistent vomiting is more likely due to gastroesophageal reflux rather than incomplete myotomy.

question: A 3-week-old infant is diagnosed with Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis after presenting with projectile vomiting and signs of dehydration. The surgical team plans to perform Ramstedt's pyloromyotomy. Which of the following statements about this condition and its management is true?

explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C) Hypokalemia

Explanations:

The given condition is congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Persistent vomiting causes a loss of gastric acid (HCl), leading to metabolic alkalosis and hypokalemia, which is a common electrolyte disturbance in infants with pyloric stenosis.

Diagnosis of Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis (CHPS)

1. Clinical Presentation:

  • Typical onset: 3 to 6 weeks of age
  • Symptoms:
    • Projectile, non-bilious vomiting
    • Visible gastric peristalsis
    • Palpable "olive-like" mass in the abdomen (hypertrophied pylorus), best felt from the left side
    • Dyselectrolytemias-
      • Hypochloremia
      • Hypokalemia due to persistent vomiting
      • Metabolic alkalosis (due to loss of H+).

2. Imaging Techniques:

  • Ultrasound (Gold Standard):
    • Characteristic "doughnut sign" indicating thickened pyloric muscle
    • Diagnostic criteria:
      • Pyloric muscle thickness ≥ 4 mm
      • Pyloric canal length > 14 mm
      • "Cervix sign" on long-axis view
      • "Target sign" on short-axis view
  • Barium Meal (Less Common):
    • Can assist in diagnosis but is less accurate than ultrasound
    • Signs suggestive of CHPS:
      • "String sign": Thin streak of contrast through narrowed pylorus
      • "Railroad track sign": Two thin lines of contrast indicating mild narrowing
      • "Double track sign": Similar to railroad track sign, indicating thickened muscle

Hyperkalemia (Option A) refers to elevated potassium levels, which are not typically associated with pyloric stenosis. Persistent vomiting usually leads to low potassium levels.

Hypernatremia (Option B), While dehydration can lead to elevated sodium levels, hypernatremia is not a characteristic finding specifically associated with pyloric stenosis.

Hypocalcemia (Option D) refers to low calcium levels, which is not typically associated with pyloric stenosis or vomiting and is not the expected electrolyte disturbance in this condition.



Reference:
  1. SRB’s Manual of Surgery, 6th Edition, Page 811, 812
  2. Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 280

correctAnswer: B. FLOT (fluorouracil, leucovorin, oxaliplatin, docetaxel) regimen
explanationHtml:
Explanation:
The FLOT regimen has been demonstrated to provide a significant survival advantage, with a median overall survival of 50 months as per the FLOT4 trial. This makes it the most effective neoadjuvant chemotherapy option for patients diagnosed with resectable gastric cancer, thus making this the correct answer.

Treatment of Stomach Cancer

  • Surgical Treatment:

    • Surgical resection is the only curative treatment for gastric cancer.
    • Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy:
      • Most surgical candidates receive neoadjuvant chemotherapy to improve survival.
      • The FLOT4 trial found that the FLOT (fluorouracil, leucovorin, oxaliplatin, docetaxel) regimen offers a significant survival advantage over the ECF (epirubicin, cisplatin, 5-fluorouracil) regimen (median overall survival: 50 months vs 35 months).

Types of Gastric Resection

  • Total Gastrectomy:
    • Involves the removal of the stomach, spleen, and pancreas.
    • Includes D2 lymphadenectomy.
    • Preferred for resectable gastric cancer.
  • Subtotal Gastrectomy:
    • May be performed if the tumour is located in the distal stomach.
    • Involves Roux-en-Y reconstruction.
  • Palliative Surgery:
    • Considered for symptom alleviation in inoperable or metastatic gastric cancer.

Non-Surgical Treatment

  • Palliative Chemotherapy or Radiotherapy: Offered to patients with advanced gastric cancer.

ECF (epirubicin, cisplatin, 5-fluorouracil) regimen (Option A) has been a standard chemotherapy protocol for gastric cancer; however, recent clinical trials, such as the FLOT4 trial, have shown that it offers a lower median overall survival (50 months vs 35 months) compared to the FLOT regimen.

Palliative chemotherapy (Option C) is typically offered to patients with advanced or metastatic gastric cancer, where the intent is not curative but to alleviate symptoms.

Total gastrectomy without prior chemotherapy (Option D), While total gastrectomy may be an appropriate surgical option for resectable gastric cancer, proceeding without prior neoadjuvant chemotherapy would not give the same results. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is recommended to enhance surgical outcomes and overall survival.



Reference:
  1. Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1174-1177

Carney’s Triad:

It is a rare syndrome characterized by the presence of three specific tumors: gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs), extra-adrenal paragangliomas, and pulmonary chondromas.

Tumor Type

Characteristics

Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors (GISTs)
  • Often found in the stomach and multifocal.

  • Benign tumors of cartilage.
  • Found in the lungs.


Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) (Option A) is characterized by skin changes, such as café-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, and an increased risk of various tumors, including malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors. While NF1 can be associated with GISTs.


Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) (Option C) is characterized by the development of hundreds to thousands of polyps in the colon and rectum, leading to a high risk of colorectal cancer. It is not associated with GISTs or paragangliomas.


Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (Option D) is characterized by intestinal polyps and mucocutaneous pigmentation, along with an increased risk of various cancers, including gastrointestinal cancers. However, it is not associated with GISTs or paragangliomas.

question: A 55-year-old woman presents with abdominal pain and a palpable epigastric mass. CT shows a well-defined stomach mass. Biopsy confirms a gastrointestinal stromal tumor, with CD117 and DOG1 positivity. Which statement is most accurate about this patient?

correctAnswer: C. Subtotal gastrectomy with D2 lymph node dissection
explanationHtml:
Explanation:
Subtotal gastrectomy is suitable for tumors in the antrum, and a D2 lymph node dissection involves removing the perigastric lymph nodes as well as nodes along the major arterial trunks. This extensive dissection is recommended in cases with lymph node involvement to ensure a more thorough removal of potentially cancerous nodes and to improve survival rates.

Primary Treatment of stomach cancer- Surgical Resection

  • Types of Surgical Resection:

    • Total Gastrectomy: Removes the entire stomach; used for proximal or middle stomach tumors.

    • Subtotal Gastrectomy: Removes a portion of the stomach; used for distal stomach tumors.

    • Lymph Node Dissection: D1 (perigastric nodes) or D2 (major arterial trunks) based on tumor location and stage.

    • Reconstruction: Roux-en-Y method connects the esophagus to the remaining stomach or small intestine.

  • Distal Pancreatectomy and Splenectomy: Part of radical gastrectomy to remove potentially cancerous lymph nodes.

Additional Treatments:

  • Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy: Platinum-based triplet regimen administered before surgery to improve survival rates. (ECF- Epirubicin, Cisplatin, 5-Flurouracil)

  • Palliative Treatment: For incurable diseases, options include chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and palliative surgery to relieve symptoms and improve quality of life.

Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by total gastrectomy (Option A) is often used for advanced gastric cancer to shrink the tumor before surgery, making it easier to remove and improving survival rates.

Subtotal gastrectomy with D1 lymph node dissection (Option B) is appropriate for tumors in the distal stomach (such as the antrum). However, a D1 lymph node dissection involves only the removal of the perigastric lymph nodes and is considered less extensive than a D2 dissection.

Palliative chemotherapy (Option D) is used to relieve symptoms and improve the quality of life in cases of incurable or metastatic gastric cancer. Since the patient has no distant metastases and the disease is potentially curable with surgery, palliative chemotherapy is not indicated in this situation.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1152-1153, 1174-1177

question: Which of the following is not typically performed as a bariatric surgery for obesity management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding (LAGB) is a restrictive bariatric procedure in which an adjustable silicone band is placed around the proximal stomach to create a small gastric pouch, thereby limiting food intake.

  • It is the only commonly performed bariatric procedure that is reversible, as the band can be adjusted or removed laparoscopically if necessary.

Chylolymphatic Cyst

Enterogenous Mesenteric Cyst
  • Cyst has chylous collection.
  • Congenitally misplaced lymphatics in the ileum with afferent lymphatics only.
  • Absence of efferent lymphatics → collection of chyle → progressive increase in the size of the cyst.
  • Independent vascular supply and there is no shared wall.

Explanation:

  • Pseudomyxoma peritonei (PMP) is a rare condition characterized by the progressive accumulation of tumor deposits in the peritoneum, along with mucinous ascites and the formation of an omental cake.
  • PMP is typically caused by the perforation of a mucinous appendiceal tumor.

Clinical Features of pseudomyxoma peritonei:

  • Many patients remain asymptomatic during the early stages.
  • Abdominal distension is common.
  • Colicky pain, particularly after eating, results from partial intestinal obstruction.
  • There is a progressive decline in overall health as amino acids are diverted for the production of the jelly-like substance.
  • On physical examination:
    • Multiple hernias may be observed due to increased intra-abdominal pressure.
    • Ascites is present but lack shifting dullness, owing to the accumulation of a semi-solid substance.

Investigation:

  • High-resolution CT scan of both the abdomen and pelvis, incorporating oral and intravenous contrast

Treatment:

  • Cytoreductive Surgery (CRS): This includes multiple peritonectomy procedures and may involve extensive multivisceral resections to achieve complete tumor removal (complete cytoreduction).
  • Hyperthermic Intraperitoneal Chemotherapy (HIPEC): Following CRS, HIPEC is administered to target any remaining microscopic disease. Common agents used are mitomycin C or oxaliplatin.

Ovarian cystic tumor (Option A) may present with abdominal distension and pelvic mass, but they typically produce serous or hemorrhagic fluid, not thick mucinous (“jelly-like”) ascites.


Ascitic fluid due to liver cirrhosis (Option C) is free-flowing fluid, which shows shifting dullness on examination. It is transudative and watery, not thick or gelatinous.


Colorectal carcinoma (Option D) usually presents with altered bowel habits, bleeding per rectum, and obstruction. While it can metastasize to the peritoneum, it does not produce the classical “jelly belly” mucinous ascites seen in pseudomyxoma peritonei.

Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1349-1353

  • This systemic condition is characterized by dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates rich in IgG4-positive plasma cells, storiform fibrosis, and often elevated serum IgG4 levels.
  • The CT findings of a retroperitoneal mass encasing the ureters, along with the biopsy showing dense fibro-collagenous tissue with chronic inflammation, are typical of IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis.


Category of Secondary RPF
Drugs

  • M – Methysergide (Most important drug)
  • A – Amphetamines
  • H – Hydralazine
  • E – Entacapone
  • B – Beta-blockers,
  • Bromocriptine

  • Non-Hodgkin lymphoma

  • TB
  • Histoplasmosis
Others

  • Radiation exposure


Metastatic prostate cancer (Option B) can involve the retroperitoneum, but it typically presents with irregular mass lesions, lymphadenopathy, or bone metastasis, rather than diffuse fibrocollagenous encasement of ureters. Histology would show malignant cells, not benign fibrotic tissue with chronic inflammation.


Methysergide use (Option C) is a known cause of secondary retroperitoneal fibrosis, but the question does not provide any history of drug intake. In the absence of such history, the most common cause remains idiopathic IgG4-related disease, making this option less likely.


Erdheim–Chester disease (Option D) is a rare non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis that can cause retroperitoneal fibrosis, but it is usually associated with:

  • Skeletal involvement (long bone sclerosis)
  • Xanthogranulomatous infiltration
  • Histology showing foamy histiocytes, not fibrocollagenous tissue

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Biopsy of the involved site with mycobacterial culture and nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT):

  • It’s the most definitive method for diagnosing abdominal TB, and allows for the direct demonstration of M. tuberculosis in tissue or fluid samples, providing conclusive evidence of the infection.

Diagnostic Method

Details

Definitive Diagnosis (Option D)

M. tuberculosis Demonstration:

  • Peritoneal fluid (in ascites)
  • Biopsy specimen (peritoneum, intestine, liver)
  • Mycobacterial culture and/or NAAT:
  • Histopathology: The presence of caseating granulomas suggests TB but is not pathognomonic

Radiographic Imaging

CT with Enterography Protocol: (Option B ruled out)

Preferred for cross-sectional evaluation

  • Intestinal TB: Concentric mural thickening in the ileocecal region, lymphadenopathy with hypodense centers
  • Peritoneal TB: Ascites, lymph nodes, mesentery and omental thickening, peritoneal thickening
  • Hepatic TB:
    • Miliary disease: Multiple low-density micronodules throughout the liver
    • Local disease: Large solitary nodule or 2-3 low-density nodules with calcification and peripheral enhancement

Ultrasound:

Detects lymphadenopathy, ascites, peritoneal thickening, omental thickening, bowel wall thickening

Other Imaging:

  • Small bowel follow-through/barium enema: Mucosal ulcerations, strictures, deformed cecum, incompetent ileocecal valve
  • Plain radiography: Air fluid levels, dilated small bowel loops, hepatic calcifications
  • Chest radiography: For suspected abdominal TB

Ascitic Fluid Analysis

Routine Tests:

  • Cell count and differential, albumin and protein concentration, Gram stain

TB-specific Tests:

  • ADA level (Option C ruled out), AFB smear, mycobacterial culture, NAAT for M. tuberculosis (if available)

Typical Findings:

  • Lymphocytic ascites with SAAG <1.1 g/dL in noncirrhotic patients (Option A ruled out)
  • Straw-colored ascites
  • leukocyte count 150-4000 cells/mm³
  • relative lymphocytic pleocytosis
  • Protein content >3.0 g/dL

The sensitivity of AFB smear and mycobacterial culture is low

Biopsy Specimens
  • Laparoscopy: Visualization of peritoneum, peritoneal biopsy
  • Endoscopy: Biopsies in the setting of intestinal involvement
  • Radiographic-guided interventions
  • Histopathology:
    • Caseating granulomas and positive acid-fast stain in fewer than 33% of cases
    • Confluent granulomas, granulomas >400 micrometres, >5 granulomas in one segment, and submucosal granulomas suggest TB enteritis

Additional Diagnostic Tools
  • Tuberculin skin test/interferon-gamma release assay: Positive in abdominal TB but limited value (does not differentiate active disease from latent infection)
  • Stool PCR: Useful adjunctive tool for diagnosing intestinal TB

correctAnswer: B. The ileum can compensate for a resected jejunum due to better absorption.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The ileum has tighter intercellular junctions and superior fluid absorptive capacity. (Option D ruled out)
  • The ileum can compensate for the loss of the jejunum, making it capable of taking over some of the jejunal functions.
  • But the jejunum cannot compensate for a missing ileum. (Option A ruled out)
  • Therefore, jejunal resections are better tolerated because of the adaptability of the ileum.
  • Short bowel syndrome usually affects the distal small intestine more than the proximal, and distal bowel loss results in a more severe form of SBS. (Option C ruled out)


Reference:

Bailey and Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1316

question: A 65-year-old male presents with sudden onset severe abdominal pain that started 30 minutes after his last meal. He is tachycardic and hypotensive and laboratory investigations reveal leukocytosis and elevated chromogranin A levels. A CT scan shows bowel wall enhancement and free fluid in the abdomen. Which of the following is the most preferred treatment?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient's history of facial flushing, diarrhea, and a newly detected heart murmur, coupled with symptoms of right-sided heart failure (such as leg swelling and shortness of breath), strongly points toward carcinoid heart disease.
  • Carcinoid heart disease is a complication of carcinoid syndrome, which results from the release of serotonin and other vasoactive substances by a carcinoid tumor.

Pathophysiology:

  • Plaque-like deposits composed of smooth muscle cells, myofibroblasts, extracellular matrix and an overlying endothelial layer which lead to valve dysfunction.
  • Valvular dysfunction can lead to edema, ascites and right-sided heart failure.
  • Pulmonary heart disease primarily affects the right side of the heart.
  • Within the right heart, the tricuspid valve is the first to be affected, followed by the pulmonary valve.
  • Regurgitant lesions are more common than stenotic lesions.

question: What is the most peculiar feature of gastric carcinoid tumor?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient presents with flushing, diarrhea, and bronchospasm, which are classical features of carcinoid syndrome. This syndrome occurs due to excessive secretion of serotonin and other vasoactive substances. The presence of multiple masses in the ileum strongly points toward a midgut carcinoid tumor, as midgut tumors commonly arise from the jejunum, ileum, appendix, and right colon and are the most common cause of carcinoid syndrome. These tumors produce large amounts of serotonin, leading to the characteristic symptoms.


Foregut carcinoid tumors (Option A) arise from the stomach, duodenum, pancreas, or bronchus. They typically produce 5-HTP (serotonin precursor) rather than serotonin and often lack the enzyme to convert it efficiently. As a result, classical carcinoid syndrome is uncommon, and serotonin levels are usually not markedly elevated.

Hindgut carcinoid tumors (Option C) arise from the distal colon and rectum. These tumors are usually non-functional and rarely secrete serotonin, so they do not typically produce carcinoid syndrome. Hence, this option is unlikely.

Non-syndromic neuroendocrine tumors (Option D) do not secrete active hormones and therefore do not cause symptoms like flushing, diarrhea, or bronchospasm. The presence of clear hormonal symptoms and elevated serotonin rules out this option.



Reference:
  1. SRB’s Manual of Surgery, 6th Edition, Page 868
  2. pathology.jhu.edu/pancreas/neuroendocrine/syndromic-vs-non-syndromic#

question: Which of the following statements is correct?

correctAnswer: B. Acquired origin due to smooth muscle motor dysfunction
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Jejunal diverticula are acquired in origin.
  • They are false diverticula, meaning they involve herniation of the mucosa and submucosa through the muscular layer of the intestine.
  • They result from a motor dysfunction of the smooth muscle or the myenteric plexus.
  • This dysfunction causes abnormal contractions of the small bowel, leading to increased pressure inside the lumen and subsequent herniation of the mucosal and submucosal layers through the weakest parts of the bowel wall.
  • Acquired diverticula of the small intestine most commonly occur in the duodenum.


Congenital origin due to incomplete recanalization of the duodenum (Option A): This describes conditions like duodenal atresia or stenosis, which are congenital anomalies seen in neonates. Jejunal diverticula, however, are acquired lesions in adults and are not related to recanalization defects.


Remnant of the omphalomesenteric duct (Option C): This refers to Meckel’s diverticulum, which is a true congenital diverticulum located in the ileum, not the jejunum. It contains all layers of the intestinal wall and is unrelated to increased intraluminal pressure.


Protrusion of the entire intestinal wall layers (Option D): This describes a true diverticulum, whereas jejunal diverticula are false (pseudodiverticula) involving only mucosa and submucosa. Hence, this option is incorrect.



Reference:

Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page 1286,1288,1289

question: A 28-year-old patient with gastrointestinal tuberculosis presents with abdominal pain and intermittent diarrhea. Imaging studies reveal a long, narrow filling defect in the terminal ileum. What is the most likely diagnosis based on these findings?

correctAnswer: B. Ulcerative tuberculosis with transverse ulcers and serosal thickening.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Ulcerative tuberculosis is characterized by multiple transverse ulcers in the terminal ileum and the thickening of the serosa.

Pathological Variants of GI Tuberculosis:

Variant

Description

Ulcerative Tuberculosis (Option B)
  • Caused by ingestion of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, often in those with pulmonary TB.
  • Results in multiple transverse ulcers, primarily in the terminal ileum.
  • Leads to thickening and inflammation of the serosa, covered in tubercles.

Hyperplastic Tuberculosis

(Option A ruled out)
  • Develops in individuals with high resistance to Mycobacterium tuberculosis who ingest the bacteria.
  • Commonly affects the ileocaecal region and distal ileum.
  • Causes chronic inflammation in lymphoid follicles, thickening of the intestinal wall, and narrowing of the lumen.
  • Less likely to cause abscesses and fistulas, and often presents with regional lymph node involvement with potential caseation.



Reference:

Bailey and Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1308

question: A patient with pulmonary tuberculosis is diagnosed with ulcers in the terminal ileum. Which form of gastrointestinal tuberculosis is characterized by this presentation?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient presents with abdominal pain, weight loss, and right iliac fossa tenderness, along with a history of pulmonary tuberculosis, which strongly suggests intestinal tuberculosis.
  • The barium follow-through showing a long, narrow filling defect in the terminal ileum is characteristic of hyperplastic tuberculosis, where there is marked bowel wall thickening and luminal narrowing due to chronic granulomatous inflammation.
  • The ileocaecal region is the most common site of involvement in gastrointestinal tuberculosis.


Etiopathogenesis of Gastrointestinal Tuberculosis (GI TB)

Hyperplastic Tuberculosis

Cause

Ingestion of Mycobacterium tuberculosis by individuals with high resistance.

Affected Area

The ileocaecal region; can also affect the distal ileum

Characteristics
  • Chronic inflammation in lymphoid follicles.
  • Thickening of the intestinal wall and lumen narrowing.
  • Rare abscess and fistula formation.
  • Early involvement of regional lymph nodes, which may caseate

Barium follow-through and CT
  • Long narrow filling defect
  • CT shows a narrowed segment with proximal distension


Crohn’s disease (Option A) can also involve the terminal ileum and cause strictures, but it typically shows skip lesions, cobblestone appearance, and string sign due to transmural inflammation. There is no history of tuberculosis, and systemic features like perianal disease or fistulae are more common. The presence of prior pulmonary TB strongly favors intestinal TB over Crohn’s disease.


Appendicitis (Option C) presents with acute onset pain, usually starting in the periumbilical region and localizing to the right iliac fossa. It is an acute condition, not associated with chronic weight loss or long-segment narrowing on imaging. Hence, this diagnosis is unlikely.


Carcinoma of the ileum (Option D) is rare and usually presents as a short, irregular constricting lesion (“apple-core” lesion) rather than a long, smooth narrowing. It is more common in older individuals and is not typically associated with a history of tuberculosis.



Reference:

Bailey and Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 933,1308

Explanation:

Laparoscopic duodenojejunostomy is the preferred surgical option for treating superior mesenteric artery syndrome after conservative management has failed due to its minimally invasive approach.


Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA) Syndrome:

  • Description: This rare condition is characterized by compression of the third portion of the duodenum between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery.
  • Symptoms: This leads to proximal small bowel obstruction, especially in individuals with significant weight loss or other risk factors.

Surgical Treatments for SMA Syndrome

Treatment Type

Description

Strong Procedure

Duodenum is mobilized by dividing the ligament of Treitz. Once the duodenal jejunal junction is mobilized, the duodenum is positioned to the right of the superior mesenteric artery

Laparoscopic Duodenojejunostomy (Option A)

Optimal definitive treatment; involves creating a bypass from the duodenum to the jejunum.

Open Surgical Procedures (Option B & D ruled out)

Employed when laparoscopic methods are not feasible or have failed.

Other Interventions

Conservative management (dietary modifications, nutritional support) is attempted first but often fails. (Option C ruled out)
