question: Which of the following characteristics is true regarding Meckel's diverticulum?

correctAnswer: C. The blood supply to the jejunum typically features four or five separate arcades with shorter vasa recta.
explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C) The blood supply to the jejunum typically features four or five separate arcades with shorter vasa recta.

Explanation:

The blood supply to the jejunum typically features four or five separate arcades with shorter vasa recta: This description is actually characteristic of the blood supply to the ileum.

  • The jejunum has fewer (one or two) prominent vascular arcades but longer, less branching terminal vessels called vasa recta.
  • The ileum has many (three to five or more) smaller, complex vascular arcades but shorter vasa recta.
  • The duodenum is demarcated from the jejunum by the Ligament of Treitz.(Option A)-The Ligament of Treitz is indeed the surgical landmark separating the fixed fourth part of the duodenum from the mobile jejunum.

The ileum makes up approximately three-fifths of the small intestine's total length (Option B) The ileum is the longer segment, comprising approximately 60% (three-fifths) of the total jejunoileal length.

The jejunum has a larger circumference and is thicker-walled than the ileum(Option D). It is typically thicker-walled and has a wider lumen (caliber) than the ileum, due to its more numerous and prominent circular folds (plicae circulares).

question: Regarding the anatomical differences and blood supply of the jejunum and ileum, which statement below presents an inaccurate description of the small intestine's surgical anatomy?

correctAnswer: B. A single-layer extramucosal (serosubmucosal) suture technique is commonly preferred
explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B) A single-layer extramucosal (serosubmucosal) suture technique is commonly preferred

Explanation:

  • Single-layer extramucosal (serosubmucosal) anastomosis is widely preferred in small bowel surgery, including in children, as it includes the submucosa, the strongest layer, while minimising tissue trauma and preserving blood supply. Clinical studies have shown this technique to be safe and effective with low complication rates. However, it is not mandatory, and full-thickness techniques may also be used depending on surgical judgment.

A double-layer full-thickness anastomosis is mandatory to prevent leakage (Option A): Double-layer techniques are not mandatory and may increase tissue ischemia and operative time without clear benefit.

The mucosa must be completely excluded from all sutures to prevent infection (Option C): Avoidance of mucosal penetration is not absolute; proper inclusion of submucosa and good technique are more important for successful healing.

Rapidly absorbable sutures such as chromic catgut are routinely recommended (Option D): Chromic catgut is generally avoided due to unpredictable absorption; synthetic absorbable sutures are preferred.



Reference:

https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3893620/

Correct Answer: D) Ileocolic

Explanation:

The presentation is classic for intussusception, characterised by intermittent colicky pain, vomiting, and passage of “red currant jelly” stools (blood and mucus). Ultrasonography showing a concentric “target sign” confirms the diagnosis.

  • Most intussusceptions occur between 2 months and 2 years; however, they can also occur in older children.
  • More than 80% are ileocolic, where the terminal ileum telescopes through the ileocaecal valve into the colon (usually ascending colon).
  • In younger children, the condition is usually idiopathic and often related to Peyer’s patch hyperplasia.
  • In older children (>2 years), a pathological lead point such as Meckel’s diverticulum, duplication cyst, or lymphoma is more likely; however, the most common anatomical location still remains ileocolic.

Colocolic (Option A): Colocolic intussusception is uncommon in children and is more often associated with pathological lesions, particularly in adults.

Rectosigmoid (Option B): This is not a typical site for intussusception and is more commonly associated with other colonic conditions rather than telescoping of bowel.

Ileoileal (Option C): Ileoileal intussusception may occur, especially in the presence of a pathological lead point (more common in older children), but it is less frequent than ileocolic intussusception.



Reference:

Bailey & Love Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 260
question: A 6-year-old child presents with recurrent episodes of colicky abdominal pain and vomiting. On examination, the abdomen is distended, and a firm mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant. Later, the child passes stools mixed with blood and mucus. Ultrasonography reveals the following finding. What is the most likely anatomical location of this pathology?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The “triple bubble” sign indicates proximal jejunal obstruction, with gas in the stomach, duodenum, and proximal jejunum and absence of distal bowel gas.

  • The operative finding of two blind bowel ends connected by a fibrous cord with an intact mesentery is characteristic of Type II jejunoileal atresia.
  • This distinguishes it from Type I (mucosal web with intact continuity) and Type III (which involves a mesenteric defect due to vascular insult). Type IV consists of multiple atresias.

Griesfeld modification of Martin’s Classification:

  • Type I: Mucosal web with intact bowel wall and normal mesentery
  • Type II: Two blind ends connected by a fibrous cord; mesentery intact
  • Type IIIa: Complete separation of bowel ends with V-shaped mesenteric defect
  • Type IIIb: Apple-peel (Christmas tree) atresia with large mesenteric defect and single arterial supply
  • Type IV: Multiple atresias (“string of sausages”)



Reference:

SRB’s manual of surgery, 6th Edition, Page 916
question: A neonate develops bilious vomiting soon after birth with minimal abdominal distension. An abdominal X-ray is provided. At laparotomy, a segment of proximal small intestine shows complete luminal discontinuity, with the proximal and distal ends connected by a fibrous cord. The mesentery is intact. Which type of jejunoileal atresia best corresponds to these findings?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Cimetidine, an H₂ receptor antagonist, is the most commonly used agent to increase the sensitivity of 99mTc-pertechnetate scintigraphy for Meckel diverticulum.

  • It acts by decreasing peptic secretion without affecting radionuclide uptake, thereby reducing the release of pertechnetate and increasing its retention within ectopic gastric mucosa in the diverticulum.
  • This results in higher tracer concentration in the diverticular wall and improved visualisation.
  • The sensitivity of this scan is approximately 85% in children (with a specificity of around 95%), but decreases in adults due to reduced ectopic gastric mucosa.
  • False-negative results may occur in the absence of gastric mucosa, or in the presence of inflammation, necrosis, obstruction, or anaemia.

Omeprazole (Option A): Although it reduces gastric acid secretion, it is not routinely used to enhance the sensitivity of Meckel scintigraphy.

Pentagastrin (Option C): This increases uptake of pertechnetate by stimulating the gastric mucosa but is less commonly used than cimetidine.

Glucagon (Option D): This reduces intestinal motility and may help reduce tracer washout, but it is used as an adjunct rather than the primary agent.



Reference:

Sabiston Textbook of Surgery: The Biological Basis of Modern Surgical Practice, 21st Edition, Pages 1289-1290

  • On barium study, characteristic findings include a pulled-up (contracted) caecum, obtuse ileocaecal angle, narrowing of the terminal ileum, and rapid transit of contrast through the diseased segment (Stierlin sign).
  • These reflect fibrosis, stricturing, and inflammatory involvement of the ileocaecal region.

Intestinal lymphoma (Option B): Classically causes aneurysmal dilatation of the bowel due to destruction of the muscular layer, rather than strictures and caecal contraction.

question: A 35-year-old man presents with chronic right lower abdominal pain, low-grade fever, intermittent diarrhoea, and weight loss over 2 months. On examination, there is tenderness in the right iliac fossa. A barium meal follow-through image is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. Transverse ulcers arranged parallel to each other
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In typhoid fever, infection of Peyer’s patches in the terminal ileum leads to necrosis and ulceration.

  • These ulcers are multiple, arranged parallel to each other, and located along the antimesenteric border.
  • They are oriented transversely (perpendicular to the long axis of the bowel) and commonly perforate in the third week of illness.
  • Perforation typically occurs due to necrosis of Peyer’s patches and may be single (most common) or multiple.
  • The condition is often associated with systemic toxicity, relative bradycardia, and neutropenia.
  • On imaging, pneumoperitoneum (gas under the diaphragm) may be seen following perforation.

Longitudinal ulcers along the mesenteric border (Option A): These are characteristic of Crohn’s disease, where ulcers run along the long axis of the bowel and are associated with transmural inflammation and skip lesions.

Flask-shaped ulcers with undermined edges (Option C): These are seen in amoebic colitis, typically involving the caecum and ascending colon.

Deep fissuring ulcers with skip lesions (Option D): These are features of Crohn’s disease, reflecting transmural inflammation and discontinuous bowel involvement.



Reference:

SRB's Manual of Surgery, 6th Edition, Page 859

question: A 28-year-old man with a history of prolonged fever presents with sudden onset severe abdominal pain. On examination, there is abdominal distension with signs of peritonitis. At laparotomy, a perforation is identified in the terminal ileum along the antimesenteric border. Multiple ulcers are noted in the surrounding bowel. Which of the following best describes the orientation and arrangement of these ulcers?

correctAnswer: B. Aggressive fluid resuscitation, correction of electrolytes, nasogastric decompression, and close monitoring
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This presentation is consistent with postoperative paralytic ileus, a transient impairment of bowel motility commonly seen within the first 2-3 days after abdominal surgery. It is usually self-limiting and managed conservatively.

  • Initial management includes aggressive fluid resuscitation, correction of electrolyte imbalances (especially hypokalemia), nasogastric decompression, and discontinuation of opioids, all of which help restore bowel motility.
  • Early mobilisation and use of non-opioid analgesia (e.g., epidural or NSAIDs) further aid recovery.
  • Imaging typically shows diffuse bowel dilatation without a transition point, helping differentiate ileus from mechanical obstruction.
  • In contrast, mechanical obstruction may require similar initial resuscitation but mandates close monitoring for signs of deterioration (fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, peritonitis), which would necessitate urgent surgery.

Immediate exploratory laparotomy (Option A): Reserved for suspected bowel ischemia, perforation, strangulation, or clinical deterioration-not for uncomplicated postoperative ileus.

Broad-spectrum antibiotics (Option C): Not indicated unless there is evidence of infection or intra-abdominal sepsis; they do not treat ileus.

Continue opioids and start oral feeding (Option D): Opioids worsen ileus by reducing gut motility, and oral feeding should be delayed until bowel function returns.



Reference:

Sabiston Textbook of Surgery: The Biological Basis of Modern Surgical Practice, 21st Edition, Page 263

question: A 60-year-old man undergoes elective laparotomy for small bowel resection. On postoperative day 2, he develops abdominal distension, mild nausea, and absence of bowel movements. He is afebrile, hemodynamically stable, and laboratory values are normal. Abdominal X-ray shows diffuse bowel dilatation without a clear transition point. What is the most appropriate initial management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Spontaneous closure of an enterocutaneous fistula depends on several factors, including output, anatomy, and presence of sepsis.

  • Although low output, short tract, and absence of distal obstruction favour closure, the presence of intra-abdominal sepsis is the most critical factor preventing healing.
  • Ongoing infection sustains inflammation and fistula output, making spontaneous closure unlikely until sepsis is controlled.

Management follows the SNAP principle:

  • S - Sepsis control: Identify and drain collections (often CT-guided)
  • N - Nutrition: Enteral or parenteral support (TPN for high-output/proximal fistulae)
  • A - Anatomical assessment: Contrast studies to define tract and bowel length
  • P - Planned surgery: Delayed until sepsis is controlled and nutrition is optimised

Low-output fistula (Option A): Favours spontaneous closure but does not override the negative impact of sepsis.

Short fistula tract (Option B): A favourable anatomical factor, but less decisive than the presence of infection.

Absence of distal obstruction (Option D): Promotes closure but is insufficient in the presence of ongoing sepsis.



Reference:

Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1315-1316
question: A 42-year-old man develops an enterocutaneous fistula 3 weeks after abdominal surgery. The fistula output is approximately 200 mL/day. He is nutritionally stable, and imaging shows no distal obstruction. However, CT scan reveals a small intra-abdominal collection adjacent to the fistula tract. Which of the following factors most strongly predicts failure of spontaneous closure?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The presence of pneumoperitoneum in an asymptomatic patient without signs of peritonitis suggests a benign cause rather than gastrointestinal perforation.

  • Pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis is characterised by gas-filled cysts in the submucosal and subserosal layers of the intestine, most commonly in the jejunum.
  • These cysts may rupture into the peritoneal cavity, causing sterile pneumoperitoneum without peritonitis.
  • It is associated with conditions such as increased intraluminal pressure, chronic pulmonary disease, bowel obstruction, and connective tissue disorders.
  • Despite the presence of free air, patients are often asymptomatic or have mild, nonspecific symptoms.

Diverticulosis (Option B): Does not produce free intraperitoneal air unless complicated by perforation, which would present with abdominal pain and peritonitis.

Perforated peptic ulcer (Option C): Typically presents with acute severe abdominal pain, guarding, rigidity, and systemic signs; asymptomatic presentation is highly unlikely.

Band with Meckel’s diverticulum (Option D): May cause intestinal obstruction but does not lead to pneumoperitoneum in the absence of perforation.



Reference:

SRB's Manual of Surgery, 6th Edition, Page 861
question: A 28-year-old woman undergoes a routine chest X-ray as part of a pre-employment evaluation. She is asymptomatic, with normal appetite and bowel habits. Physical examination and vital signs are normal. The X-ray reveals free air beneath both domes of the diaphragm. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Acute mesenteric ischemia classically presents with sudden severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical findings, especially in elderly patients with risk factors such as atrial fibrillation, which predisposes to embolism of the superior mesenteric artery.

  • Early features include central abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, and early passage of altered blood due to mucosal ischemia.
  • The abdomen may be soft with minimal tenderness initially, with rigidity developing later as infarction progresses.
  • The condition progresses rapidly, and irreversible bowel injury may occur within hours (often within ~6 hours).
  • Patients develop metabolic acidosis, elevated lactate, leukocytosis, and shock due to hypovolemia and sepsis.

Acute appendicitis (Option A): Typically presents with gradually progressive pain localizing to the right iliac fossa.

Perforated peptic ulcer (Option C): Causes sudden pain but is associated with early peritonitis and rigid abdomen, unlike the initially soft abdomen here.

Small bowel obstruction (Option D): Presents with colicky pain, distension, and vomiting, not severe pain out of proportion to examination.



Reference:

Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1312-1313
question: A 68-year-old man with a history of atrial fibrillation presents with sudden onset severe central abdominal pain. He has persistent vomiting and passes blood-stained stools. On examination, the abdomen is soft with only mild tenderness. Over the next few hours, he develops hypotension and signs of shock. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Radiation enteritis shows a clear dose-response relationship.

  • Serious late complications are uncommon when the total radiation dose is below 4000 cGy, while the risk increases significantly at doses above 5000 cGy due to progressive vascular and fibrotic injury.
  • Radiation damages rapidly dividing intestinal mucosal cells and small submucosal blood vessels, leading to obliterative arteritis, ischemia, and submucosal fibrosis.
  • Acute enteritis:
    • Occurs during or shortly after radiotherapy (often by the 3rd week) with diarrhoea, abdominal pain, bloating, and urgency; usually resolves within weeks.
  • Chronic enteritis:
    • Develops months to years later and is characterised by fibrosis, vascular thrombosis, strictures, malabsorption, obstruction (most common), fistula formation, and rarely perforation.
  • Risk factors include prior abdominal surgery (adhesions fixing bowel in the radiation field), vascular disease, diabetes, hypertension, and concurrent chemotherapy.


Reference:

Sabiston Textbook of Surgery: The Biological Basis of Modern Surgical Practice, 21st Edition, Page 1295
question: A 55-year-old woman undergoes pelvic radiotherapy for cervical cancer. She is concerned about the risk of developing chronic radiation enteritis. What is the minimum total radiation dose below which serious late complications are uncommon?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Short bowel syndrome leads to intestinal failure when the remaining bowel cannot maintain adequate fluid, electrolyte, and nutritional balance without intravenous support.

  • Although patients with 100-200 cm of jejunum and an intact colon may sometimes maintain nutrition, those with 50-100 cm have variable outcomes.
  • In this case, despite 90 cm of jejunum, the presence of persistent diarrhoea, weight loss, and malnutrition indicates intestinal failure.
  • Therefore, home parenteral nutrition (HPN) is required for long-term management.
  • Medical therapy with antidiarrhoeal agents (loperamide, codeine) (Option A), proton pump inhibitors, and bile salt binders (cholestyramine) (Option B) can reduce stool output and improve absorption.
  • Vitamin and trace element supplementation is also necessary. However, these measures alone are insufficient to maintain nutrition.
  • Adjuncts such as growth factors or GLP-2 analogues (Option D) may aid intestinal adaptation.
  • Intestinal transplantation is considered only if complications of long-term parenteral nutrition develop.


Reference:

Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1316
question: A 45-year-old male underwent extensive small bowel resection for mesenteric ischemia and now has only 90 cm of jejunum anastomosed to an intact colon. He presents with persistent diarrhoea, weight loss, and signs of malnutrition despite oral nutritional support. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Evaluation of small bowel tumours is challenging due to their vague presentation and difficult anatomical location.

  • CT enteroclysis is the most comprehensive investigation, as it combines optimal luminal distension with cross-sectional imaging.
    • It provides excellent visualisation of mucosa, bowel wall, lymph nodes, and adjacent structures, with an accuracy of around 90%.
  • CT abdomen (Option B) is useful for assessing masses, lymphadenopathy, and complications, but is less sensitive for detecting early mucosal lesions.
  • Barium meal follow-through (Option C) is less sensitive and may miss subtle lesions.
  • MRI (Option D) offers good soft-tissue contrast but is mainly used for further evaluation rather than initial diagnosis.


Reference:

SRB's Manual of Surgery, 6th Edition, Page 865
question: A 52-year-old man presents with intermittent abdominal pain, unexplained anaemia, and features of partial intestinal obstruction. Upper GI endoscopy and colonoscopy are normal. A small bowel tumour is suspected. Which of the following is the investigation of choice for evaluation?

correctAnswer: B. Radical resection is required for small primary tumours &lt;1 cm without lymph node involvement.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Carcinoid tumour management depends on tumour size, location, and nodal involvement.

  • In small bowel tumours <1 cm without lymph node involvement, segmental resection with anastomosis is sufficient.
  • Radical resection is reserved for larger tumours, multiple lesions, or nodal disease, making option B incorrect.
  • Symptomatic control is achieved with somatostatin analogues such as Octreotide, which provide significant relief of flushing and diarrhoea.
  • Pasireotide, a second-generation analogue with broader receptor activity, is also effective.
  • In patients with liver metastases, hepatic resection, embolisation, or other liver-directed therapies are used for disease control.

Long-acting somatostatin analogues (Option A): Mainstay for symptom relief.

Liver-directed therapies (Option C): Standard approach in metastatic disease.

Pasireotide (Option D): Effective second-generation somatostatin analogue.



Reference:

SRB's Manual of Surgery, 6th Edition, Page 869

question: A 50-year-old man presents with acute abdominal pain, and bilious vomiting. Physical examination reveals a distended abdomen, and he has not had a bowel movement for three days. An abdominal X-ray is shown below. What is the most appropriate next step in management ?

correctAnswer: D. Presence of centrally located featureless loops without haustra is typical of large bowel obstruction
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Centrally located, smooth, featureless loops without haustra describe small bowel obstruction, not large bowel obstruction.
  • The X-ray provided shows features of large bowel obstruction, including peripheral dilated bowel loops with visible haustral markings that are irregularly spaced and do not span the full diameter of the bowel.
  • These are classic characteristics of large bowel dilation.

Features of large bowel obstruction:

  • Haustral folds are irregularly spaced and do not cross the entire lumen (Option A).

  • Dilated large bowel loops appear peripherally on a supine film (Option B).

  • Haustral folds do not form complete mucosal rings (Option C).

question: Based on the findings visible in the X-ray, all of the following are true, except:

correctAnswer: C. A collapsed caecum during laparotomy suggests a large bowel obstruction.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A collapsed caecum indicates that the obstruction is in the small bowel.
  • In contrast, a distended caecum is indicative of a large bowel obstruction.

Management of Large Bowel Obstruction:

  • Surgical Management:
    • Malignant Lesions:
      • Resectable Lesions: Perform emergency right hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis if the patient's condition allows.
      • Non-Resectable Lesions: Consider proximal stoma (colostomy or ileostomy) or ileo-transverse bypass.
    • Splenic Flexure Obstruction: Extended right hemicolectomy with ileo-descending anastomosis.
    • Left Colon or Rectosigmoid Junction Obstruction: Immediate resection unless contraindicated.
  • Emergency Procedures:
    • Imminent Perforation: Perform emergency caecostomy or loop colostomy/ileostomy to stabilize the patient. (Option B)
  • Intraoperative Considerations:
    • Colostomy: Often performed if the distal bowel cannot be closed; Hartmann’s procedure if the distal bowel is not suitable for closure.
    • Anastomosis: Consider using proximal colon if feasible, with on-table colonic lavage for decompression and cleaning.
  • Palliative and Preoperative Stenting:
    • Self-Expanding Metal Stent: Preferred in palliative care.
    • Stenting as a Bridge to Surgery: Recommended for potentially curable left-sided colon cancer.
  • Alternative to Stenting:
    • Decompressing Stoma: If colonic stenting is not feasible
  • Adhesions: Perform adhesiolysis.
  • Malignancy: Resection and anastomosis (for peritoneal carcinomatosis)
  • Hernia: Perform reduction
  • Crohn's Disease: Resection and anastomosis (Option D)

Laparotomy Findings:

  • Distended Caecum: Indicates large bowel obstruction. (Option A)
  • Collapsed Caecum: Indicates small bowel obstruction.


Reference:

Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1389.

question: A 75-year-old male patient, bedridden after hip surgery, presents with a 4-day history of progressive abdominal distension, nausea, and constipation. On physical examination, his abdomen is distended but non-tender, with decreased bowel sounds. An abdominal X-ray shows dilated loops of colon, particularly in the cecum, but no air-fluid levels or evidence of mechanical obstruction. His vital signs are stable, and there is no fever. Which of the following drugs is commonly used in pharmacologic treatment of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Based on the clinical presentation and coffee bean sign in the X-ray abdomen, the most probable diagnosis is sigmoid volvulus
  • Long pelvic mesocolon allows the sigmoid colon to move excessively, predisposing it to twist upon its own mesenteric axis causing sigmoid volvulus.

Sigmoid volvulus:

  • It is the twist (rotation) in the axis of the loop of the bowel

Predisposing factors:

  • High-residue diet
  • Elderly patients with chronic constipation (Option A ruled out)
  • Chronic psychotropic drug
  • Anticholinergic drugs (Option B ruled out)
  • Mentally-retarded individuals (Option C ruled out)
  • Adhesions; Peridiverticulitis
  • Overloaded redundant pelvic colon
  • Long pelvic mesocolon (Option D)
  • Narrow attachment of sigmoid mesocolon

Investigations:

  • Plain X-ray
    • omega sign- single grossly distended loop of colon arising out of the pelvis and extending towards the diaphragm.
    • Coffee-bean sign or Bent-inner tube sign

  • Contrast enema:
    • Bird's beak sign (ace of spades appearance)- Upper end of the barium column tapers into the spirally twisted distal sigmoid colon.



Reference:
  1. Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery- 28th Edition, Page 1293, 1380, 1383, 1385, 1390
  2. SRB’s Manual of Surgery- 6th Edition, Page 922, 923.

question: A 72-year-old male presents with a 2-day history of progressive abdominal distension, constipation, and colicky pain. He has a history of chronic constipation and has been bedridden for the past few months due to a hip fracture. On examination, his abdomen is distended and tympanic, with mild tenderness. Abdominal guarding and rigidity not observed. X-ray of the abdomen is shown below. Which of the following factors does not predispose to this condition?

correctAnswer: C. In caecal bascule, there is axial twisting
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The caecal bascule is the upward folding of the caecum and there is no axial twisting

Caecal volvulus:

  • Caecum, terminal ileum, and right colon are involved in the volvulus (Option B ruled out)
  • Caecal bascule is the upward folding of the cecum anteriorly and there is no axial twisting.
  • Only caecum is involved in this.
  • Rotation is more commonly clockwise (Option A ruled out)

Clinical features:

  • Since the ileum is involved, patients have signs and symptoms of small bowel obstruction (Option D ruled out)
    • Colicky pain
    • Multiple episodes of bilious vomiting
    • Obstipation
  • Ischaemia is common

question: Which of the following is/are components of Hartmann’s procedure?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In early Crohn's disease, aphthous ulcers - small, superficial, punched-out ulcers surrounded by a rim of erythematous mucosa are the earliest visible endoscopic lesions. These result from the expansion of submucosal lymphoid follicles.

Cobblestoning and deeper serpiginous ulcers develop as the disease progresses and becomes more severe. (Option A, B ruled out)

Pseudopolyps (inflammatory polyps) (Option D) are seen in both Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis as a result of healing and regeneration; they are not an early finding.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1329.
question: Which of the following endoscopic findings is considered the earliest and most characteristic lesion seen in Crohn's disease?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image shows a flat, bright red vascular lesion with a fern-like or spider-like pattern of dilated mucosal vessels, characteristic of colonic angiodysplasia.

  • Angiodysplasia is a common cause of painless lower GI bleeding in the elderly.
  • These are degenerative vascular lesions that appear endoscopically as flat, red, fern-like or stellate patches, most commonly located in the cecum and right colon.
  • Diverticular bleeding is also common but typically presents with abrupt, painless maroon or bright red bleeding and is often seen in the sigmoid colon.

Diverticular bleeding (Option A): Diverticular bleeding typically appears as active bleeding or a visible vessel in a diverticulum, not as a flat, fern-like vascular lesion. It is also more common in the left colon.

Colonic carcinoma (Option B): Colonic carcinomas are usually polypoid, ulcerated, or mass-like lesions, not flat, red, fern-like vascular lesions.

Ulcerative colitis (Option D): Ulcerative colitis presents with diffuse mucosal inflammation, ulceration, and friability starting in the rectum, not as an isolated cecal vascular lesion.



Reference:

Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page 1163.
question: A 75-year-old patient presents with recurrent episodes of painless lower gastrointestinal bleeding. Colonoscopy is performed, and the image above is obtained. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The splenic flexure (Griffith's point) is the most common site for ischemic colitis because it is a watershed area between the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) and inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) circulations.
  • The marginal artery of Drummond may be tenuous here, making this region particularly susceptible to low-flow states or arterial occlusion.
  • The rectosigmoid junction (Sudeck's point) is another watershed area but is less commonly affected than the splenic flexure.

Cecum (Option A): The cecum is supplied by the ileocolic artery (from the SMA) and is less commonly affected in typical non-occlusive ischemic colitis compared to watershed areas.

Hepatic flexure (Option B): The hepatic flexure is supplied by the right colic artery (from the SMA) and is not a classic watershed zone like the splenic flexure.

Rectum (Option C): The rectum has a dual blood supply (superior rectal artery from the IMA and middle/inferior rectal arteries from the internal iliac arteries), making it relatively resistant to ischemia.



Reference:

Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Page 1309.
question: Which colonic region is most vulnerable to ischemic colitis due to its watershed vascular supply?

correctAnswer: B. Colonic submucosal oedema or haemorrhage
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Thumbprinting on abdominal X-ray refers to smooth, rounded, thumb-like impressions along the colonic wall caused by submucosal oedema or haemorrhage.
  • This nonspecific sign can be seen in conditions such as ischemic colitis, pseudomembranous colitis, inflammatory bowel disease, or infectious colitis.
  • It reflects thickening of the bowel wall rather than an intraluminal or extrinsic process.

Intraluminal faecal impaction (Option A): Faecal impaction appears as a large, heterogeneous intraluminal mass with stool density, not as regular, thumb-like indentations of the colonic wall.

Extrinsic compression by an abdominal mass (Option C): Extrinsic compression typically causes a smooth, broader indentation from outside the bowel, not multiple, rounded, submucosal-type impressions like thumbprinting.

Pneumatosis intestinalis (Option D): Pneumatosis intestinalis appears as linear or cystic intramural gas, not as soft‑tissue thumb‑like projections into the lumen.



Reference:

Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page 1359

options.text: Extrinsic compression by an abdominal mass

question: The radiographic finding of "thumbprinting" on a plain abdominal X-ray is most indicative of which pathological process?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image shows yellow-white pseudomembranes adherent to the colonic mucosa on endoscopy, characteristic of pseudomembranous colitis caused by Clostridioides difficile.

  • For the first recurrence of C. difficile infection (including moderate cases), oral fidaxomicin is the preferred drug of choice due to its narrow spectrum and lower recurrence rates compared to vancomycin.
  • Oral vancomycin is an alternative.

Oral metronidazole (Option A): Metronidazole is no longer recommended for recurrent CDI except when other agents are unavailable, due to higher relapse rates and potential toxicity with prolonged use.

Intravenous vancomycin (Option B): Intravenous vancomycin does not achieve adequate luminal concentrations in the colon and is ineffective for treating CDI. Only oral/enteral vancomycin is effective.

Oral ciprofloxacin (Option D): Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic that can precipitate CDI and is not used for its treatment.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 1069.
question: A 64-year-old woman was recently treated for antibiotic-associated diarrhea and initially improved. Two weeks later, she returns with recurrent abdominal cramps and foul-smelling watery diarrhea. Stool toxin assay is positive for Clostridioides difficile. Sigmoidoscopy findings are shown above. What is the preferred antibiotic for management at this stage?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Colovesical fistula secondary to diverticulitis is more common in men because the sigmoid colon lies in direct anatomical proximity to the bladder without an intervening uterus.
  • In women (Option A), the uterus normally separates the sigmoid colon from the bladder, providing a protective barrier; however, women who have undergone a hysterectomy (Option C) are at increased risk due to the loss of this separation.

Men and women equally (Option B): There is a significant male predominance (≥3:1) in colovesical fistulas.



Reference:
  1. Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1369, 1370.
  2. Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Page 1288.

options.text: Women who have had a hysterectomy

question: In which patient population is a colovesical fistula due to diverticulitis most commonly seen?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Pneumaturia (air in urine) and fecaluria, in the setting of recurrent diverticulitis, are classic for a colovesical fistula, which is an abnormal communication between the colon (usually sigmoid) and the bladder.
  • This results from inflammatory erosion of a diverticulum into the adjacent bladder wall, allowing passage of gas and faecal material into the urinary tract.
  • Emphysematous cystitis can cause pneumaturia, but it is due to gas-forming bacteria in the bladder wall, not a fistula.

Emphysematous cystitis (Option A): Emphysematous cystitis is a rare infection of the bladder wall with gas-forming bacteria, which can cause pneumaturia but is not associated with fecaluria or diverticulitis history.

Pericolic abscess (Option C): A pericolic abscess presents with localised pain, fever, and possibly a palpable mass, but not with pneumaturia or fecaluria.

Diverticular bleeding (Option D): Diverticular bleeding manifests as acute, painless hematochezia, not urinary symptoms like pneumaturia or fecaluria.



Reference:
  1. Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1369, 1370.
  2. Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Page 1288.
question: A patient with multiple episodes of diverticulitis develops UTIs and says the urine sometimes contains air and particles resembling stool. What is the likely complication?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In the setting of faecal peritonitis from perforated diverticulitis, the preferred emergency surgery is Hartmann’s procedure.

  • Resection of the affected sigmoid colon, creation of an end colostomy, and closure of the distal rectal stump.
  • This avoids a high-risk primary anastomosis in a contaminated, unstable patient. The colostomy can potentially be reversed later.

Primary anastomosis without diversion (Option A): Primary anastomosis is generally contraindicated in faecal peritonitis due to the high risk of anastomotic leak and mortality in this septic, hemodynamically unstable setting.

Loop ileostomy (Option B): A loop ileostomy is typically used for diversion with an anastomosis (e.g., in ulcerative colitis surgery) or to protect a low rectal anastomosis, not as the primary resectional procedure for perforated diverticulitis.

Total colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis (Option D): This extensive resection is not indicated for localised sigmoid diverticular disease. It is reserved for conditions like toxic megacolon, ischemic colitis, or synchronous colonic pathology.



Reference:
  1. Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1369.
  2. Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Pages 1286, 1287.
question: A patient presents with generalised peritonitis due to perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with faecal contamination. Which surgical procedure is most appropriate in this emergency setting?

correctAnswer: B. CT-guided percutaneous drainage and intravenous antibiotics
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • For a complicated diverticulitis with an abscess larger than 5 cm, especially in an elderly patient with comorbidities, the recommended initial management is CT-guided percutaneous drainage combined with intravenous antibiotics.
  • This approach stabilises the patient and may allow for elective surgery later, if needed, rather than urgent high-risk surgery.
  • Immediate surgery is reserved for peritonitis, perforation, or failure of percutaneous drainage.

Immediate surgical resection (Option A): Emergency surgery is typically reserved for perforation with generalised peritonitis (Hinchey III/IV) or failure of percutaneous drainage. Initial drainage and antibiotics are preferred for an accessible abscess.

Outpatient oral antibiotics and liquid diet (Option C): This conservative approach may be used for uncomplicated diverticulitis. A 6 cm abscess is complicated and requires drainage and IV antibiotics, often with hospitalisation.

Colonoscopic drainage (Option D): Colonoscopic drainage is not standard for pericolic abscesses due to the risk of perforation and incomplete drainage. Percutaneous CT-guided drainage is safer and more effective.



Reference:
  1. Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1369, 1370.
  2. Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Pages 1286, 1287

question: An elderly patient with multiple comorbidities presents with acute complicated diverticulitis and a pericolic abscess measuring 7 cm on CT scan. What is the most appropriate initial intervention?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The Hinchey classification for complications of acute diverticulitis is as follows:

Stage

Description

Stage I

Pericolic or mesenteric abscess (Option A)

Stage II

Pelvic abscess (Option B)

Stage III

Purulent peritonitis (Option C)

Stage IV

Faecal peritonitis (perforation with faecal contamination of the peritoneal cavity)


Reference:
  1. Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page 1338.
  2. Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1368.
question: According to the Hinchey classification of acute diverticulitis, which stage is characterised by faecal peritonitis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis is the standard imaging modality for acute diverticulitis. It can accurately detect colonic wall thickening, periodic fat stranding, abscess formation, and complications like perforation, while also assessing extracolonic structures.

Barium enema is contraindicated in acute settings due to the risk of perforation and extravasation. (Option A ruled out)

Plain abdominal radiography (Option B): Plain films are nonspecific and insensitive for diagnosing diverticulitis. They may show ileus or free air, but cannot confirm inflammation or complications like CT can.

Colonoscopy (Option D) is avoided in acute diverticulitis due to the risk of perforation. It is performed later (after 6–8 weeks) to confirm the diagnosis and rule out malignancy.



Reference:
  1. Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1342.
  2. Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Page 1286-1287.
question: What is currently the preferred initial imaging modality for evaluating suspected acute diverticulitis?

correctAnswer: B. False diverticula involving mucosa and submucosa only
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image shows a barium enema demonstrating multiple small outpouchings from the colonic wall consistent with colonic diverticulosis.

  • Colonic diverticula in diverticulosis are acquired false diverticula (pseudodiverticula), which involve herniation of only the mucosa and submucosa through weakened points in the muscularis propria, typically where nutrient arteries penetrate the wall.
  • They are associated with low-fibre diets and are most common in the sigmoid colon.

True diverticula involving all bowel layers (Option A) are rare in the colon and are characteristic of congenital conditions (e.g., Meckel's diverticulum), not acquired diverticulosis.

Congenital outpouchings are most common in the cecum (Option C): Congenital cecal diverticula are rare true diverticula, while typical diverticulosis is acquired, left-sided (sigmoid), and age-related.

Inflammatory pseudopolyps associated with ulcerative colitis (Option D): Pseudopolyps are inflammatory regenerative tissue in colitis, not diverticula. They have no structural or pathological resemblance to diverticula.



Reference:

Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 10th Edition, Page 1286.

False diverticula involving mucosa and submucosa only

question: A 62-year-old man presents with intermittent lower abdominal discomfort and altered bowel habits. A contrast radiographic study of the colon is performed, and the image is shown above. The outpouchings seen in this condition are best described as which of the following?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

An ulcerative colitis patient with an abdominal X-ray showing a dilated colon with loss of haustrations, points towards toxic megacolon.

  • Toxic megacolon is a severe, life-threatening complication of ulcerative colitis (and rarely Crohn's disease) characterised by acute colonic dilation (>6 cm), systemic toxicity, and loss of haustral markings on imaging.
  • It is often precipitated by severe inflammation, electrolyte imbalance, or narcotics.
  • Urgent colectomy may be required if medical management fails or if perforation occurs.

Sigmoid volvulus (Option A) typically shows a “coffee‑bean” shaped loop arising from the pelvis, not generalised transverse colon dilation with loss of haustra in the setting of active colitis.

Crohn’s disease flare (Option B): While Crohn’s can cause severe colitis, the combination of megacolon, systemic toxicity, and known ulcerative colitis points specifically to toxic megacolon as the acute complication.

Ogilvie’s syndrome (Option D): Ogilvie’s (acute colonic pseudo‑obstruction) causes massive dilation but usually occurs in hospitalised, elderly, or postoperative patients without active colitis, and it lacks the systemic inflammatory signs of toxic megacolon.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1319.
question: A patient with severe ulcerative colitis presents with high fever, abdominal distension, and tenderness. An abdominal X-ray shows the following findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. The probability of symptomatic relapse increases with time since resection
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Crohn’s disease is chronic and relapsing.

  • Endoscopic recurrence occurs early (weeks-months), but clinical relapse increases progressively with time. (Option A ruled out) (Option C)
  • Surgery relieves complications but is not curative. (Option D ruled out)
  • Active disease at margins increases risk but does not guarantee recurrence. (Option B ruled out)


Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1332.

options.text: The risk of relapse is highest immediately after surgery and decreases over time.
The presence of active disease at the resection margins guarantees early recurrence.

question: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding the postoperative recurrence of Crohn's disease?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The cecum, located in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen, is the first part of the large intestine and is typically the first structure visualized during surgery for suspected intestinal obstruction.
  • It helps in differentiating between small and large intestine obstructions:
    • Dilated cecum: Indicates a large bowel obstruction, as it is proximal to the blockage.
    • Collapsed cecum with dilated small intestines: Suggests a small bowel obstruction.
  • Identifying the cecum first allows surgeons to accurately determine the obstruction site and guide appropriate surgical management.


Reference:
  1. SRB's Manual of Surgery, 6th Edition, Page 913.
  2. Gray’s Anatomy, 42nd Edition, Page 1189.

question: A 45-year-old male presents with severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and abdominal distension along with tenderness. X-ray shows dilated bowel loops with air-fluid levels. The patient is taken for exploratory laparotomy. Which of the following structures is most likely to be visualized first to differentiate between small intestine and large intestine obstruction?

explanationHtml:
The most likely diagnosis in the above case scenario is Cowden disease.


Cowden disease / Multiple Hamartomas:

  • Loss of PTEN function leads to activation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, promoting cell proliferation and survival.
  • Clinical manifestations such as Hamartomas, Trichilemmomas, papillomatous papules, acral keratoses, Oral papillomas, Multinodular goiter, and adenomas.

  • Patients need to have two major criteria to be diagnosed with Cowden disease. (One of the two must be either Lhermitte-Duclos disease or macrocephaly)
    • Lhermitte-Duclos disease
    • Thyroid carcinoma
    • Macrocephaly
    • Breast cancer
  • Treatment: Surveillance, Removal of symptomatic hamartomas or cancers, and cutaneous lesions treated with surgical excision and 5-fluorouracil.


Neurofibromatosis (Option A) presents with neurofibromas, café-au-lait spots, axillary freckling, and lisch nodules in the iris. It does not present with oral papillomas, trichilemmomas, or PTEN-related features.


Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (Option C) is characterized by mucocutaneous pigmentation (around lips, buccal mucosa) and hamartomatous GI polyps. There are no papillomas or trichilemmomas, and pigmentation (not wart-like lesions).


Gardner syndrome (Option D) presents with multiple colonic adenomatous polyps, osteomas, epidermoid cysts, and desmoid tumors. It does not show mucocutaneous papillomas or trichilemmomas.



Reference:
  1. www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK525984/
  2. Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page 672

question: A 35-year-old woman presents with multiple oral papillomas, facial trichilemmomas, and a history of thyroid nodules. She also reports that her mother had breast cancer at a young age. On examination, multiple small, wart-like growths on her hands is noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient presents with recurrent colorectal cancer along with a strong family history of endometrial and ovarian cancers, which is highly suggestive of Lynch syndrome (Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer, HNPCC). It is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes such as MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2, leading to microsatellite instability.

Lynch syndrome is characterized by:

  • Early-onset colorectal cancer
  • Association with endometrial cancer (most common extracolonic malignancy)
  • Increased risk of ovarian, gastric, small bowel, and urinary tract cancer

The family history involving multiple Lynch-associated cancers across generations strongly supports this diagnosis.


Amsterdam II Criteria
  • Three or more family members with Lynch syndrome-related cancer, one of whom is a 1° relative
  • Two or more successive affected generations
  • At least one tumor diagnosed before the age of 50 years
  • FAP excluded


Cowden Syndrome (Option A) is associated with mutations in the PTEN gene and presents with:

  • Multiple hamartomas
  • Increased risk of breast, thyroid (follicular), and endometrial cancers
  • It is not primarily associated with colorectal cancer recurrence or mismatch repair defects.


Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome (Option C) is characterized by:

  • Hamartomatous polyps in the GI tract
  • Mucocutaneous pigmentation (around lips, buccal mucosa)
  • Although there is an increased cancer risk, the hallmark features are pigmentation and polyps, which are not mentioned in this case.


MUTYH-Associated Polyposis (MAP) (Option D) is an autosomal recessive condition characterized by:

  • Multiple adenomatous polyps (similar to attenuated FAP)
  • Increased risk of colorectal cancer
  • However, it is not associated with strong extracolonic cancers like endometrial and ovarian cancers, and the inheritance pattern does not fit the family history.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1358

question: Which variant of Familial Adenomatous Polyposis is associated with both colorectal cancer and brain tumors?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient is a 16-year-old boy with rectal bleeding, a strong family history of early-onset colorectal cancer, and colonoscopy showing hundreds of polyps, which is classical for Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP).

  • Itis an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutation in the APC gene (chromosome 5q21)
  • It is characterized by the development of numerous (>100) adenomatous polyps in the colon during adolescence
  • If left untreated, FAP carries a near 100% risk of progression to colorectal cancer, usually by the 3rd–4th decade, making early diagnosis and prophylactic surgery essential


Crohn’s disease (Option A) presents with abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and skip lesions on endoscopy. It does not present with hundreds of colonic polyps, and there is no strong hereditary polyposis pattern as seen in this case.


Lynch syndrome (Option C) is characterized by early-onset colorectal cancer without multiple polyps. Patients typically have few or no polyps, unlike the hundreds of polyps seen in this patient, making this diagnosis unlikely.


Juvenile polyposis syndrome (Option D) involves hamartomatous polyps, usually fewer in number (not typically hundreds). It presents in childhood but does not show the massive adenomatous polyposis characteristic of FAP.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1356, 1357

question: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his mother due to rectal bleeding. His father died of colon cancer at age 40. Colonoscopy reveals hundreds of polyps throughout the colon. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient presents with intermittent abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, and characteristic mucocutaneous pigmentation over the lips, buccal mucosa, and digits, along with a positive family history, which is classical for Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS).

  • It is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a mutation in the STK11 (LKB1) gene
  • The gastrointestinal symptoms are due to hamartomatous polyps, most commonly in the small intestine, which can lead to intussusception, obstruction, and bleeding.
  • The pigmented macules (dark blue-brown spots) on mucocutaneous surfaces are a hallmark feature and are often present since childhood.

  • Associated with increased risk of gastrointestinal, pancreatic, breast, ovarian, cervical, and testicular cancers


Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP) (Option A) is characterized by hundreds to thousands of adenomatous polyps in the colon with a high risk of colorectal cancer. It does not present with mucocutaneous pigmentation, which is a key feature in this case.


Lynch Syndrome (Option B) presents with early-onset colorectal cancer and extracolonic malignancies but does not involve polyposis or mucocutaneous pigmentation. The absence of these hallmark features rules it out.


Cowden Syndrome (Option D) is associated with oral papillomas, trichilemmomas, and a PTEN mutation, along with an increased risk of breast and thyroid cancers. It does not present with pigmented macules on the lips and digits, making it unlikely.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1309, 1310

Definition
  • Inflammation or infection of diverticula in the colon.

Etiology
  • Obstruction (fecal matter or food): Trapped fecal matter or food causes pressure and inflammation.

  • Pain management (analgesics)

Physiological functions of the colon

Function

Description

Water and Electrolyte Absorption
  • Absorbs water, sodium (Na+), and chloride (Cl-) to maintain fluid and electrolyte balance.

Secretion

  • In a large bowel obstruction at the descending colon, perfusion to the obstructed segment depends on collateral pathways between SMA and IMA.
  • The artery most consistently providing collateral flow is the Marginal Artery of Drummond, which forms a continuous arterial arcade along the colon.
  • It is the primary and most reliable collateral pathway between SMA and IMA.
  • Runs along the inner border of the colon.
  • Supplies descending colon when IMA flow is compromised (as in obstruction, stenosis, or ligation during surgery).

Anatomy of the Large Intestine

Segments:

Blood supply of the Large Intestine

Arterial Supply
  • Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA):
    • Supplies the cecum, ascending colon, and proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon. (Option A)
  • Inferior Mesenteric Artery (IMA):
    • Supplies the distal one-third of the transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, and rectum. (Option B)
  • Marginal Artery of Drummond:
    • An important arterial anastomosis running along the inner border of the colon, connecting branches of the SMA and IMA, ensuring continuous blood supply and providing collateral circulation. (Option C)
  • Arc of Riolan / Meandering mesenteric artery:
    • It is a collateral branch running close to the mesentery, connecting superior mesenteric artery to inferior mesenteric artery.
    • It also connects proximal part of middle colic artery to left colic artery (Option D)

Venous Drainage

Blood from the colon drains into the superior mesenteric vein and inferior mesenteric vein, which then drain into the portal vein leading to the liver.

Lymphatic Drainage

Lymph from the colon drains into the mesenteric lymph nodes and ultimately into the thoracic duct.

The 99mTc-labelled red blood cell (RBC) scintigraphy is the most sensitive modality for detecting active GI bleeding at the lowest bleeding rates, typically ≥0.1 mL/min. It is especially useful for intermittent or slow bleeding, as it allows continuous monitoring over several hours.

Selective mesenteric angiography (Option B): Detects bleeding at ≥0.5-1 mL/min; allows for therapeutic embolisation.

question: Which diagnostic modality can detect active gastrointestinal bleeding at the lowest rate of blood loss?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The guaiac faecal occult blood test (gFOBT) is more sensitive for lower GI bleeding (colon) because haemoglobin from upper GI sources is often degraded by digestive enzymes during transit, reducing its peroxidase activity. For the test to be positive, faecal haemoglobin typically needs to exceed about 10 mg/g of stool, which corresponds to a daily blood loss of roughly 10 mL.

Upper GI tract (e.g., stomach) (Option A): Upper GI bleeding often results in degraded heme (by digestive enzymes and gastric acid), making gFOBT less sensitive compared to tests like immunochemical FOBT (iFOBT) or upper endoscopy.

Small intestine (Option B): Sensitivity is lower because bleeding may be intermittent, and haemoglobin is partially degraded.

Oesophagus (Option C): Oesophagal bleeding (e.g., varices, esophagitis) is an upper GI source; like gastric bleeding, heme is often degraded, reducing gFOBT sensitivity.



Reference:

Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Page 1251.

The paracolic lymph nodes are the primary (first-tier) nodes in the colonic lymphatic drainage pathway. They lie adjacent to the colon along the course of the marginal artery of Drummond, which runs parallel to the colon and connects the SMA and IMA circulations. Lymph then drains sequentially to intermediate nodes and finally to principal nodes at the root of the mesentery.

Superior mesenteric artery (Option A): Lymph nodes along the superior mesenteric artery are central or intermediate nodes (e.g., ileocolic, right colic, middle colic groups), not the paracolic group.

Inferior mesenteric vein (Option C): The inferior mesenteric vein ascends retroperitoneally and does not have a constant anatomical relationship with the paracolic lymph nodes, which follow the marginal artery.

Middle colic artery (Option D): The middle colic artery supplies the transverse colon, and its associated nodes are part of the middle colic group, not the paracolic group.

question: A 3-month-old infant presents with chronic constipation, abdominal distension, and failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life. A rectal biopsy confirms aganglionosis of the distal colon, consistent with Hirschsprung disease. Which surgical procedure is considered a definitive treatment for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The aganglionic segment in Hirschsprung disease typically begins at the internal anal sphincter and extends proximally. The normal physiological hypoganglionic zone extends up to 2 cm above the dentate line. Therefore, a biopsy should be taken at least 2 cm above the dentate line to avoid sampling this normally sparse area and obtaining a false-positive result.

The biopsy will show hypertrophied nerve trunks and the absence of ganglion cells in the diseased segment.

0.5 cm (Option A): Biopsy at 0.5 cm is within the normal aganglionic/hypoganglionic zone and would likely show absent ganglia, leading to a false-positive diagnosis.

1.0 cm (Option B): Biopsy at 1.0 cm may still sample the transitional hypoganglionic area and risk a false-positive result.

5.0 cm (Option D): While 5.0 cm is safely above the hypoganglionic zone, it is higher than the standard recommendation (2–3 cm) and may miss very short-segment disease. The ideal distance is ≥2 cm.



Reference:

Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page 1860.

Explanation:

Ischemic Colitis

Definition

Ischemic colitis is the most common form of gastrointestinal ischemia. It occurs when there is insufficient blood flow to the colon, leading to tissue injury.

Causes
  • Thrombotic occlusion: Often linked to atherosclerosis; presents with abdominal pain, raised white cell count, and rectal bleeding.
  • Embolic events: Can cause acute ischemia with severe pain, bloody diarrhea, and hemodynamic instability.
  • Low-flow states: Conditions like septic shock, heart failure, and hypotension increase the risk.

Risk Factors
  • Predominantly affects older adults, women, and individuals with comorbidities.
  • Increased risk in case of atherosclerosis, abdominal surgeries, certain medications, and illicit drug use.

Clinical Presentation
  • Symptoms: Sudden abdominal pain, tenesmus, bloody diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, low-grade fever, abdominal distension, and tenderness.
  • Mild cases may have nonspecific symptoms; severe cases can lead to shock and require urgent treatment.

Diagnosis
  • Imaging:
    • Abdominal plain films may show "thumb-printing";
    • CT scans with contrast are preferred.
  • Colonoscopy: Gold standard for diagnosis, showing characteristic mucosal changes.
  • Vascular Imaging: Used in suspected acute mesenteric ischemia.

Treatment
  • Conservative Management: Includes bowel rest, IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and addressing underlying conditions.
  • Surgical Intervention: Necessary for severe cases; involves removing gangrenous bowel and ensuring adequate blood supply.

Acute mesenteric ischemia (Option A) usually presents with severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical findings, often without early bloody diarrhea. It is more acute and catastrophic, commonly due to arterial embolism or thrombosis, and patients rapidly progress to peritonitis and shock. The relatively stable presentation with bloody diarrhea favors ischemic colitis instead.


Diverticulitis (Option C) presents with left lower quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis, but bloody diarrhea is uncommon. It is primarily an inflammatory condition, not ischemic, and does not typically present with acute bowel ischemia on imaging.


Crohn’s disease (Option D) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease presenting with recurrent abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and skip lesions. It does not typically present with sudden onset severe pain and acute bloody diarrhea in an elderly patient with vascular risk factors, making it unlikely.

The patient presents with colon cancer, bladder cancer, a strong family history of similar malignancies, and sebaceous adenomas, which is highly suggestive of Muir-Torre syndrome, a variant of Lynch syndrome (HNPCC).

Liver cancer (Option B) is not a classical association with Lynch or Muir-Torre syndrome. While metastasis to the liver can occur from colorectal cancer, it is not a primary associated malignancy in this syndrome.


Pancreatic cancer (Option D) can be seen in some hereditary syndromes (like BRCA or Peutz-Jeghers), but it is not associateed with Muir-Torre syndrome.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Adenoma-carcinoma sequence:
    • The adenoma-carcinoma sequence describes the progression from normal colonic epithelium to colorectal cancer.
    • This process involves a series of genetic and epigenetic changes that occur in a specific order.

  1. Dysplasia:
    • This is an early step in the process.
    • Dysplasia refers to abnormal cell growth and organization within the epithelium. It is characterized by hyperproliferation of cells and is considered a precancerous change.
  2. DNA methylation:
    • DNA methylation can silence tumor suppressor genes, contributing to the progression of the adenoma.
  3. Intermediate adenoma:
    • As the genetic and epigenetic changes accumulate, the lesion progresses from an early to an intermediate adenoma.
    • This stage represents a more advanced precancerous lesion.
  4. 18q loss (DCC gene):
    • The loss of the long arm of chromosome 18, which includes the DCC (Deleted in Colorectal Cancer) gene, typically occurs in the transition from intermediate to late adenoma.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The Bethesda guidelines are used to identify individuals with colorectal cancer who should be tested for microsatellite instability (MSI) or mismatch repair (MMR) deficiency to screen for Lynch syndrome.

Bethesda criteria for testing colorectal tumors for microsatellite instability (MSI).

Tumors from individuals in the following situations should be tested for MSI:

1. Colorectal cancer diagnosed in a patient before age 50.

2. Presence of synchronous/metachronous colorectal or other hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC)-related tumors (including endometrial, stomach, ovarian, pancreas, ureter and renal pelvis, biliary tract, brain (usually glioblastoma), sebaceous gland adenomas and keratoacanthomas, and carcinoma of the small bowel), regardless of age.

3. Colorectal cancer with the MSI histology (defined by the presence of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, Crohn-like lymphocytic reaction, mucinous/signet-ring differentiation, or medullary growth pattern) diagnosed in a patient before age 60.

4. Colorectal cancer diagnosed in at least one first-degree relative with an HNPCC-related tumor in which one cancer was diagnosed before age 50.

5. Colorectal cancer diagnosed in at least two first- or second-degree relatives with HNPCC-related tumors, regardless of age.

Amsterdam II criteria (Option A): The Amsterdam II criteria are used for clinical diagnosis of Lynch syndrome in families, but are highly specific and insensitive; they are not used to select tumours for MSI testing.

Revised Geneva criteria (Option C): The revised Geneva criteria are for the pretest probability of pulmonary embolism, not Lynch syndrome.

Dukes staging system (Option D): Dukes staging is a pathological staging system for colorectal cancer, not a criterion for genetic testing.

  • A major limitation of CT colonography (virtual colonoscopy) is that it is a diagnostic imaging study only and cannot obtain tissue biopsies or remove polyps.

Advantages:

  • Noninvasive
  • Sensitivity may be as good as a colonoscopy for colorectal cancers and polyps greater than 1 cm in size.

Disadvantages:

  • Requires bowel preparation
  • Insensitive for small polyps
  • Minimal experience and data
  • A colonoscopy is required for a positive result
  • False-positive results from retained stool, diverticular disease, haustral folds, and motion artefacts
  • Inability to detect flat adenomas


Reference:
  • Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Page 1294.

question: A 58-year-old man undergoes CT colonography as part of colorectal cancer screening because he refuses an invasive procedure. The scan reveals a suspicious colonic lesion. He is advised to undergo another procedure for definitive diagnosis and management. Which of the following represents a key limitation of CT colonography compared with conventional colonoscopy?

correctAnswer: B. Colonoscopy every 3–5 years starting at age 40
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Individuals with a first‑degree relative diagnosed with colorectal cancer before age 60 are considered at higher risk. Screening is recommended with colonoscopy every 3–5 years, starting at age 40 or 10 years before the youngest affected relative’s age at diagnosis (whichever is earlier).
  • Average‑risk individuals start at age 45–50 with a colonoscopy every 10 years. For Lynch syndrome, screening begins at age 20–25 every 1–2 years.

Screening Guidelines for Colorectal Cancer

Population

Recommended Screening Test

  • Flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 y or
  • Annual FOBT and flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 y or
  • Air-contrast barium enema every 5 y or
  • Colonoscopy every 10 y

Adenomatous polyps

50 y
  • Colonoscopy at first detection; then colonoscopy in 3 y.
  • If no further polyps, colonoscopy every 5 y
  • If polyps, colonoscopy every 3 y
  • Annual colonoscopy for >5 adenomas

Colorectal cancer

At diagnosis
  • Pretreatment colonoscopy; then at 12 mo after curative resection; then colonoscopy after 3 y; then colonoscopy every 5 y, if no new lesions

Ulcerative colitis, Crohn’s colitis

At diagnosis; then after 8 y for pancolitis, after 15 y for left-sided colitis
  • Colonoscopy with multiple biopsies every 1–2 y

10–12 y

  • Upper endoscopy every 1–3 y after polyps appear

20 y

  • Upper endoscopy every 1–3 y after polyps appear

20–25 y

FAP: Familial adenomatous polyposis, FOBT: Fecal occult blood testing, HNPCC: Hereditary nonpolyposis colon cancer

Colonoscopy every 10 years starting at age 50 (Option A): This schedule is meant for average-risk individuals. A first-degree relative with colorectal cancer diagnosed before 50 places the patient in a high-risk category, requiring earlier and more frequent screening.

Colonoscopy every 1–2 years starting at age 20 (Option C): Such early and frequent screening is recommended for hereditary colorectal cancer syndromes (e.g., FAP, Lynch syndrome), not for a single affected first-degree relative.

No screening until age 50 (Option D): Delaying screening ignores the increased familial risk. In high-risk individuals, screening must start earlier than 50 to detect premalignant lesions promptly.
