question: For an asymptomatic 40‑year‑old individual with a first‑degree relative diagnosed with colorectal cancer at age 45, what is the recommended colonoscopy screening schedule?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In the Vogelstein model of colorectal carcinogenesis:

  • APC mutation initiates adenoma formation.
  • KRAS mutation promotes progression to an intermediate adenoma.
  • p53 mutation is a late event driving the transition from late adenoma to invasive carcinoma.
    • Mutations in the p53 gene are present in approximately 75% of colorectal cancers.

APC mutation (Option A): APC mutation is typically the earliest event in the sequence, driving initiation of adenoma formation.

KRAS mutation (Option B): KRAS mutation usually occurs at the intermediate adenoma stage, promoting growth but not invasion.

MSH2 mutation (Option C): The MSH2 mutation is involved in Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer) via mismatch-repair deficiency, rather than the classic adenoma-carcinoma sequence of sporadic colorectal cancer.



Reference:

Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Pages 1289, 1290.
question: In the classic adenoma-carcinoma sequence of colorectal cancer, which genetic mutation is most associated with the progression from a late adenoma to invasive carcinoma?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Sessile (flat) polyps carry a higher risk of malignancy compared to pedunculated polyps, as they are more likely to have submucosal invasion and be difficult to completely remove.

Other high-risk features:

  • Size >2 cm
  • Villous histology (villous > tubulovillous > tubular).3

Pedunculated morphology (Option A): Pedunculated polyps have a lower risk of containing invasive carcinoma compared to sessile lesions, as the stalk often provides a margin of safety before invasion reaches the submucosa.

Size <0.5 cm (Option B): Polyps <0.5 cm have a very low risk of malignancy (<1%).

Tubular adenoma histology (Option D): Tubular adenomas have a lower risk of malignancy compared to villous or tubulovillous adenomas.



Reference:
  • Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Pages 1290, 1291.
  • Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1355.
question: A 64-year-old man undergoes a screening colonoscopy, which reveals multiple colonic polyps. The gastroenterologist is concerned about the risk of invasive carcinoma within a polyp. Which of the following polyp features is associated with the highest risk of containing invasive carcinoma?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A high intake of dietary fibre (from fruits, vegetables, and whole grains) is associated with a reduced risk of colorectal cancer.
  • In contrast, high-calorie diets, low fibre intake, high animal fat, red/processed meat, and alcohol consumption increase the risk.
  • Protective micronutrients include calcium, selenium, and vitamins A, C, and E.

Polyunsaturated fats (Option A): High intake of certain fats, especially omega-6 fatty acids, may increase colorectal cancer risk.

Plant phenols (polyphenols) (Option B) are antioxidants and are protective; a low intake removes this benefit.

Oleic acid (monounsaturated fat, e.g., olive oil) (Option D) is generally neutral or protective; a low intake is not beneficial.



Reference:

Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Page 1289.
question: Which dietary component is considered protective against colorectal cancer?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Cholecystectomy is associated with an increased risk of colorectal cancer, particularly right-sided colon cancer, possibly due to altered bile acid metabolism and increased secondary bile acids in the colon.

Other risk factors:

  • Ulcerative colitis
  • Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP)
  • Smoking
  • Ureterosigmoidostomy
  • Low-fibre diet
  • Red/processed meat consumption.


Reference:
  • https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10331452/
  • Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Pages 1288, 1289.
question: Which of the following is a known risk factor for the development of colorectal carcinoma?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Overall, the rectum is the most common site for colorectal adenocarcinoma, followed by the sigmoid colon.
  • Together, the rectosigmoid region accounts for the majority of colorectal cancers.
  • Proximal (right-sided) colon cancers (e.g., cecum, ascending colon) are more common in older individuals and in hereditary syndromes like Lynch syndrome.

Sites of development of CRC: Rectum > Sigmoid colon > Cecum > Transverse colon > Ascending colon > Descending colon > Splenic flexure > Hepatic flexure

Cecum (Option A): The cecum and right colon are common sites for sporadic MSI‑high tumours and present about 15–20% of cases, but not the most common overall.

Sigmoid colon (Option B): The sigmoid colon is a common site (~20–25%) but less frequent than the rectum.

Transverse colon (Option C): The transverse colon accounts for a smaller proportion (~5–10%) of colorectal cancers.



Reference:
  • Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1358.
  • https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK586003/
question: A 62-year-old man presents with altered bowel habits and intermittent rectal bleeding. Colonoscopy reveals an ulceroproliferative mass in the distal large bowel. Biopsy confirms colorectal adenocarcinoma. Overall, which anatomical site is the most common location for colorectal adenocarcinoma?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Villous adenomas have the highest risk of malignancy (up to 40%) among adenomatous polyps, followed by tubulovillous and then tubular adenomas.

Risk increases with:

  • Polyp size (>1 cm)
  • Degree of villous architecture
  • High-grade dysplasia.

All adenomatous polyps are considered premalignant and should be removed.

Classification of intestinal polyps

Inflammatory

Inflammatory polyps (pseudopolyps in ulcerative colitis)

Hamartomatous
  • Peutz–Jeghers polyp
  • Juvenile polyp

Serrated polyps (serrated lesions)
  • Hyperplastic polyp
  • Sessile serrated lesion
  • Sessile serrated lesion with dysplasia
  • Traditional serrated adenomas
  • Mixed polyp

Adenoma
  • Tubular
  • Tubulovillous
  • Villous

Malignant polyp

Adenocarcinoma

Tubular adenoma (Option A): Tubular adenomas have the lowest malignant potential (~5% risk when >1 cm) among conventional adenomas.

Tubulovillous adenoma (Option B): Tubulovillous adenomas have an intermediate risk (between tubular and villous), approximately 15–20% risk when >2 cm, but not the highest.

Sessile serrated adenoma (Option D): Sessile serrated adenomas (SSAs) carry an increased risk of malignancy, but among the listed histological subtypes of adenomatous polyps, villous adenoma is classically considered the highest risk.



Reference:
  • Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Page 1242.
  • Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1355, 1356.
question: Among the histological subtypes of colonic adenomatous polyps, which one carries the highest risk of malignancy?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Muir-Torre syndrome is a variant of Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) characterised by:

  • Sebaceous skin tumours (adenomas, epitheliomas, carcinomas)
  • Keratoacanthomas, along with internal malignancies, most commonly colorectal and endometrial cancers.

It is caused by germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair genes (e.g., MSH2, MLH1).

Turcot syndrome (Option A): Turcot syndrome is the association of colorectal adenomatous polyposis and primary brain tumours, not sebaceous adenomas.

Gardner syndrome (Option C): Gardner syndrome is a variant of FAP with osteomas, soft tissue tumours, and desmoid tumours, not sebaceous adenomas.

Peutz‑Jeghers syndrome (Option D): This syndrome features hamartomatous polyps and mucocutaneous pigmentation, not sebaceous adenomas.



Reference:
  • Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page 1373.
question: A patient presents with multiple sebaceous adenomas of the skin and has a family history of colorectal and endometrial cancers. Which variant of Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) is most likely?

correctAnswer: C. Accelerated tumour progression but normal initiation
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In Lynch syndrome (HNPCC), colorectal cancers exhibit accelerated progression from adenoma to carcinoma due to defective DNA mismatch repair, but tumour initiation occurs at a normal rate.

Other features include early age of onset (mean ~44 years) (Option B)

proximal (right-sided) predominance (Option A) occurring in the ascending colon, and increased risk of synchronous/metachronous tumours.

Excellent prognosis with low rates of metachronous cancers (Option D): While Lynch syndrome cancers may have a better stage‑for‑stage prognosis compared to sporadic MSI‑low tumours, the risk of metachronous colorectal cancer is high (~16–30% at 10 years after segmental resection), necessitating subtotal or total colectomy.



Reference:
  • Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Pages 1292, 1293.
  • Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1358.

options.text: Accelerated tumour progression but normal initiation
Excellent prognosis with low rates of metachronous cancers

question: A 41-year-old man presents with iron-deficiency anaemia and altered bowel habits. He has a strong family history of early-onset colorectal cancer affecting multiple relatives across generations. Colonoscopy reveals a proximal colon adenocarcinoma with mucinous features. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in a DNA mismatch repair gene. Which of the following is a characteristic feature of colorectal cancers in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In Lynch syndrome (HNPCC), caused by germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, the most common extracolonic malignancy in women is endometrial carcinoma, which may even present before colorectal cancer.
  • Other associated cancers include ovarian, gastric, urinary tract, small bowel, and hepatobiliary cancers.
  • Screening for endometrial and ovarian cancer is recommended in women with Lynch syndrome.

Amsterdam II criteria

  • Three or more family members with a Lynch syndrome-related cancer (colorectal, endometrial, small bowel, ureter, renal pelvis), one of whom is a first-degree relative of the other two
  • Two or more successive affected generations
  • FAP excluded
  • At least one tumour diagnosed before the age of 50 years
  • Tumours verified by pathological examination

Ovarian cancer (Option A): Ovarian cancer risk is elevated in Lynch syndrome (~10–12% lifetime risk), but it is less common than endometrial cancer.

Gastric cancer (Option C): Gastric cancer risk is increased in Lynch syndrome (especially in certain populations), but it is not the most common extracolonic malignancy in women.

Pancreatic cancer (Option D): Pancreatic cancer risk is modestly elevated in Lynch syndrome, but it is far less frequent than endometrial or colorectal cancers.



Reference:
  • Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Pages 324,325.
  • Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1358.
question: In Lynch syndrome, what is the most common extracolonic malignancy in women?

correctAnswer: B. Total proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA)
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The standard prophylactic surgery for FAP is total proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA), which removes the entire colon and rectum while preserving continence. This eliminates the near 100% risk of colorectal cancer.
  • Ileorectal anastomosis (IRA) may be considered in selected cases with mild rectal polyposis but requires lifelong rigorous surveillance of the rectal stump.

Segmental colectomy (Option A): Segmental resection leaves the remaining colon and rectum at high risk for cancer and is not appropriate for prophylactic treatment of FAP.

Total colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis (IRA) (Option C): IRA is an option in selected patients with mild rectal polyp burden and good compliance with surveillance, but it leaves the rectum at risk for cancer. IPAA is preferred when rectal polyposis is significant or to eliminate rectal cancer risk.

Proctocolectomy with permanent end ileostomy (Option D): This is a valid cancer‑preventing operation but is typically reserved for patients with low rectal cancer, poor sphincter function, or contraindications to IPAA. It is not the first‑choice prophylactic procedure in a patient with intact sphincters.



Reference:
  • Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Pages 1292, 1293.
  • Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1357.

options.text: Total proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA)

question: What is the definitive prophylactic surgical procedure of choice for a patient with classical familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) to prevent colorectal cancer?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image shows a brain tumour in a patient with multiple colorectal adenomatous polyps, a combination characteristic of Turcot's syndrome.

  • Turcot's syndrome is characterised by the combination of multiple colorectal adenomas (FAP phenotype) and primary central nervous system tumours, most commonly medulloblastoma or glioblastoma.
  • It is considered a variant of familial adenomatous polyposis (resulting from an APC gene mutation) or, less commonly, Lynch syndrome (resulting from an MMR gene mutation).

Gardner's syndrome (Option A): Gardner’s syndrome is a variant of FAP with osteomas, soft tissue tumours, and desmoid tumours, not primary brain tumours.

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (Option C): This syndrome involves hamartomatous polyps (not adenomatous) and mucocutaneous pigmentation, not brain tumours.

Lynch syndrome (Option D): Lynch syndrome (hereditary non‑polyposis colorectal cancer) features few adenomas and increased risk of various cancers (colorectal, endometrial, etc.), but brain tumours are not a defining component except in the rare Turcot‑type variant associated with mismatch‑repair mutations.



Reference:
  • Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Page 1292.
  • https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK534782/#:~:text=Introduction,2%20(BTPS1%20and%20BTPS2).
question: A 16-year-old patient presents with headache and vomiting. MRI of the brain reveals a space-occupying lesion, as shown below. Further evaluation reveals numerous adenomatous polyps throughout the colon. Which syndrome best explains the association of these findings?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Desmoid tumours (aggressive fibromatosis) are benign but locally invasive mesenchymal tumours strongly associated with FAP. They commonly arise in the abdominal wall, mesentery, or extremities.
  • In FAP patients, they are a major cause of morbidity and can complicate surgical management.
  • Diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy (beta-catenin positive), and MRI is the preferred imaging modality.

Lipoma (Option A): While lipomas can occur in FAP, they are soft, benign fatty tumours, not typically described as firm, slowly growing masses. Desmoid tumours are more characteristic.

Metastatic colorectal cancer (Option C): Metastatic cancer would be more aggressive and likely associated with other systemic signs. Desmoid tumours are a primary benign but locally invasive lesion associated with FAP.

Lymphoma (Option D): Lymphoma is not specifically associated with FAP and usually presents with systemic symptoms (e.g., fever, weight loss, night sweats) and lymphadenopathy.



Reference:
  • Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1356.
  • Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Pages 1086, 1087.
question: A patient with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) presents with a firm, slowly growing abdominal wall mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Gardner's syndrome is a variant of FAP characterised by colorectal polyposis plus extracolonic manifestations such as:

  • Osteomas (most commonly in the mandible)
  • Dental anomalies
  • Epidermoid cysts
  • Desmoid tumors

Medulloblastoma (Option A): Medulloblastoma is associated with Turcot syndrome (FAP with CNS tumours), not specifically Gardner’s syndrome.

Café-au-lait spots (Option C): Café‑au‑lait spots are characteristic of neurofibromatosis type 1 and other conditions like McCune‑Albright syndrome, not Gardner’s syndrome.

Pheochromocytoma (Option D): Pheochromocytoma is associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2) and von Hippel‑Lindau disease, not Gardner’s syndrome.



Reference:
  • Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Pages 1292, 1293.
  • Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1356.
question: A 22-year-old man with a strong family history of colorectal cancer is evaluated for multiple asymptomatic bony swellings over the jaw and skull. Colonoscopy reveals numerous adenomatous polyps throughout the colon. On examination, multiple epidermoid cysts are also noted on the skin. Which of the following additional findings is most characteristic of his underlying condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Patients with FAP have a significantly increased risk of duodenal and periampullary adenocarcinoma due to adenomatous polyps in the duodenum.
  • Duodenal cancer is the leading cause of death in FAP patients after prophylactic colectomy.
  • Gastric polyps in FAP are usually fundic gland polyps with low malignant potential.

Gastric adenocarcinoma (Option B): Gastric adenomas and cancer can occur in FAP but are less common than duodenal/ampullary malignancies.

Oesophageal carcinoma (Option C): Oesophageal cancer is not significantly associated with FAP.

Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour (Option D): Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours are not a characteristic extracolonic manifestation of FAP.



Reference:

Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Pages 1292, 1293.
question: In patients with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), duodenal adenomatous polyps are associated with an increased risk of which of the following malignancies?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image shows multiple lesions of congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE), a characteristic extracolonic manifestation associated with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP).

  • Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a germline mutation in the APC (adenomatous polyposis coli) gene on chromosome 5q21.
  • It leads to the development of hundreds to thousands of colorectal adenomas, with a near 100% risk of colorectal cancer if untreated.
  • Congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE) is an early extracolonic marker of colorectal cancer.
  • Prophylactic surgery is indicated to prevent colorectal cancer
  • Polyps and malignant tumours can develop, particularly around the duodenal ampulla

BRCA1 (Option A) mutations are associated with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome, not FAP.

MSH2 (Option B) mutations are involved in Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer, HNPCC), which typically presents with few adenomas, rather than the polyposis phenotype.

STK11 (Option D) mutations cause Peutz‑Jeghers syndrome, characterised by hamartomatous polyps, not adenomatous polyps.



Reference:
  1. Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1356, 1357.
  2. Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Pages 1292, 1293.
question: A 19-year-old man undergoing evaluation for a suspected hereditary colorectal cancer syndrome is noted to have multiple pigmented retinal lesions on fundoscopic examination, as shown in the image below. The underlying condition associated with this finding most commonly results from a mutation in which of the following genes?

Explanation:

Haggitt's classification is used for pedunculated malignant polyps:

  • Level 1: Invasion limited to the head of the polyp.
  • Level 2: Invasion into the neck of the polyp.
  • Level 3: Invasion into the stalk.
  • Level 4: Invasion into the submucosa of the bowel wall below the stalk but above the muscularis propria.

question: According to Haggitt's classification for malignant polyps, invasion of the submucosa of the bowel wall by carcinoma is classified as which level?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The histological image shows elongated colonic crypts with a serrated (saw-toothed) appearance of the epithelial lining without cytologic dysplasia, characteristic of a hyperplastic polyp.

  • Hyperplastic polyps are characterised histologically by elongated, serrated (saw-toothed) crypts due to delayed shedding of surface epithelial cells.
  • They are the most common colorectal polyps, typically small, located in the rectosigmoid, and have no malignant potential in their usual form.
  • In contrast, adenomatous polyps show dysplasia, and sessile serrated lesions (a distinct subtype) may have malignant potential.

Glandular dysplasia (Option A): Dysplasia is a feature of adenomatous polyps, not hyperplastic polyps.

Villous projections (Option C): Villous structures are seen in villous or tubulovillous adenomas, not hyperplastic polyps.

Signet ring cells (Option D): Signet ring cells are a feature of signet‑ring cell adenocarcinoma, not hyperplastic polyps.



Reference:
  • Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page 1365.
  • https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7726909/

  • Budesonide is a first-line treatment for inducing remission in mild to moderate Crohn's disease, especially when the disease is localized in the ileocecal region.
  • It is a corticosteroid with a high first-pass metabolism, resulting in fewer systemic side effects than corticosteroids like prednisone.

Category

Mild Crohn's Disease

Moderate to Severe Crohn's Disease

Induction Therapy
  • First-line: Budesonide (Option D) (preferred for ileocecal disease)or aminosalicylates (e.g., mesalamine).
  • Prednisone (Option A) for those who do not respond to budesonide.
  • Alternative: Enteral nutrition.
  • First-line: Corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone for short term) or biologics
    Anti-TNF agents (Infliximab (Option C), Adalimumab)
  • Anti-integrin therapy (Vedolizumab)
  • Anti-interleukin therapy (Ustekinumab)
  • Combination therapy: Anti-TNF agents plus immunomodulators (Azathioprine, 6-MP) (Option B)

Maintenance Therapy
  • First-line: Continue aminosalicylates if effective.
  • Alternative: Thiopurines (azathioprine, 6-MP) for patients intolerant to aminosalicylates.
  • Anti-TNF monotherapy: Long-term for maintaining remission.
  • Combination therapy: Anti-TNF agents with immunomodulators (for severe cases or history of nonresponse to biologics).
  • Continue anti-integrin or anti-interleukin agents for those induced by these therapies

Monitoring
  • Regular follow-up to monitor symptoms and inflammation.
  • Ileocolonoscopy 6-12 months post-remission. Drug level monitoring and fecal calprotectin to assess mucosal healing.

question: Which of the following macroscopic features is most characteristic of Crohn's disease compared to ulcerative colitis?

correctAnswer: B. Total Abdominal Colectomy with End Ileostomy
explanationHtml:
Explanation:


The patient's severe symptoms and lab abnormalities, along with X-ray findings of significant colonic dilation, suggest a critical condition like toxic megacolon.

  • The most appropriate surgical procedure is Total Abdominal Colectomy with End Ileostomy, as it has been associated with lower mortality compared to segmental colectomy, especially in the presence of colonic perforation or necrosis.


Management of Toxic megacolon:

Therapies
  • IBD-Related: Intravenous glucocorticoids (e.g., hydrocortisone 100 mg every 6-8 hours) as first-line therapy; infliximab or cyclosporine if no response within 3 days
  • C. difficile Colitis: Stop inciting antibiotics; steroids not used; metronidazole, vancomycin, or fidaxomicin for medical therapy; fecal microbial transplantation considered in some cases

Surgical Indications
  • Absolute indications: Perforation, life-threatening hemorrhage, worsening toxicity, worsening dilatation
  • IBD: Colectomy if no improvement after 24-48 hours; subtotal colectomy preferred for emergency surgery
  • C. difficile: Surgery for perforation, necrosis, or severe complications; early colectomy reduces the mortality rate

Procedure

Indications

Advantages

Disadvantages

Total Abdominal Colectomy with End Ileostomy

Colonic perforation, necrosis, abdominal compartment syndrome

Diagnosis and Evaluation of Toxic Megacolon

Diagnosis Criteria

Radiographic Evidence: Colonic dilation (diameter >6 cm)

PLUS at least three of the following:

  • Fever >38ºC
  • Heart rate >120 beats/min
  • Neutrophilic leukocytosis >10,500/microL
  • Anemia

PLUS at least one of the following:

  • Altered sensorium (Option B)
  • Electrolyte disturbances (Option D)
  • Hypotension (Option C)

  • Congenital megacolon (Hirschsprung's disease).
  • Acquired megacolon (chronic constipation).
  • Chagas megacolon.
  • Colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome).

question: A 58-year-old male comes to the hospital complaining of intermittent pain in the anal region and intermittent diarrhea for 6 months. On examination, he was found to have complex perianal fistulas bilaterally, with skin tags, as shown in the image. His blood investigations reveal anemia. What could be the possible diagnosis leading to this?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation is characteristic of Crohn's disease with perianal involvement.

  • Crohn's disease causes transmural intestinal inflammation, predisposing to complex fistulas, recurrent abscesses, fissures, and large edematous ("elephant ear") skin tags.
  • Perianal disease occurs in approximately 20-30% of patients and may precede intestinal manifestations.

Characteristic anorectal features include:

  • Multiple complex, branching perianal fistulas, often bilateral
  • Large edematous "elephant ear" skin tags
  • Broad-based anal fissures, frequently away from the midline
  • Recurrent anorectal abscesses
  • Anal ulceration and anorectal strictures

Management focuses on controlling sepsis, treating the underlying intestinal inflammation, and preserving sphincter function:

  • Drainage of anorectal abscesses and placement of a loose seton when indicated
  • Antibiotics (e.g., metronidazole or ciprofloxacin) as adjunctive therapy
  • Immunomodulators
  • Anti-TNF biologic agents (infliximab or adalimumab) for fistulizing disease
  • Sphincter-preserving procedures, such as advancement flap repair in selected patients
  • Temporary fecal diversion may be considered for severe refractory perianal disease.

Ulcerative colitis (Option B): Although mild perianal lesions may occasionally occur, multiple complex fistulas, large edematous skin tags, and non-midline fissures are characteristic of Crohn's disease rather than ulcerative colitis.

Carcinoma rectum (Option C): Rectal carcinoma typically presents with rectal bleeding, altered bowel habits, tenesmus, and weight loss. Complex bilateral perianal fistulas with characteristic skin tags are not typical features.

Hemorrhoids (Option D) commonly present with bleeding, prolapse, or pain (if thrombosed) but do not cause multiple complex fistulas, elephant-ear skin tags, or chronic inflammatory perianal disease.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has undergone total proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA), which is the surgery of choice for ulcerative colitis requiring definitive treatment. This procedure involves creating an ileal pouch (J-pouch) and anastomosing it to the anal canal. Common complications of IPAA include:

  • Pouchitis (most common): It presents with increased stool frequency, urgency, abdominal cramps, and sometimes bleeding, and is a hallmark complication of this surgery
  • Anastomotic leak (Option A)
  • Pelvic sepsis (Option C) can occur due to anastomotic leak or infection of the pelvic cavity after surgery
  • Pouch fistula, strictures, and pouch failure
  • Anastomosis and pouch line leaks (Option A)

Peritonitis, however, is not considered a direct or typical complication of the procedure itself. It is more commonly related to disease-related complications (like perforation) or secondary to severe intra-abdominal infection, rather than a complication of IPAA.

question: A patient with a history of ulcerative colitis (UC) has undergone a total proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (TPA + IPAA) as part of their treatment. Which of the following is not a possible complication of the procedure?

correctAnswer: B. Total Proctocolectomy with Ileal Pouch-Anal Anastomosis (TPA+IPAA)
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Total Proctocolectomy with Ileal Pouch-Anal Anastomosis (TPA + IPAA)

Indications:

  • Definitive treatment for ulcerative colitis, especially in young patients.
  • Eliminates risk of colorectal cancer and colitis-related symptoms.

Typically done in two stages:

  • Proctocolectomy and ileal pouch creation.
  • Closure of the ileostomy after pouch healing.

Proctocolectomy (First Stage)

Remove the colon and rectum.

Preserve the anal canal.

↓

Ileal Pouch Creation

Create a J-shaped ileal pouch from a segment of the ileum.

Connect the pouch to the anal canal (ileal pouch-anal anastomosis).

↓

Anastomosis and Ileostomy

Anastomose the J-pouch to the anal canal.

Perform a covering loop ileostomy to divert intestinal contents and protect the pouch.

↓

Post-operative Imaging

Conduct a Gastrografin contrast enema to confirm the integrity and healing of the pouch.

↓

Closure of Ileostomy (Second Stage)

Close the ileostomy once pouch healing is confirmed through imaging.

↓

Post-surgical Outcomes

Monitor for adjustment to stool frequency and management of minor issues like urgency or fecal incontinence, which usually improve over time.


TPC + End Ileostomy (Option A) is preferred for older patients and patients with fecal incontinence.

TPC + mucosectomy with hand-sewn IPAA (Option C) is a procedure done in case of the presence of rectal dysplasia.

Total abdominal colectomy with very low Hartmann closure with end ileostomy (Option D) is done in more debilitating cases and those who can’t tolerate long duration of surgery. The rectum is spared here.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Permanent fecal diversion following total colectomy is one of the major indications for Ileostomy.

  • An end ileostomy is indicated following total colectomy for conditions such as Rectal carcinoma or familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP).
  • This results in a permanent stoma, where the ileum is brought to the surface, and the patient manages the stoma for life.
  • The absence of the colon necessitates this approach, making it specific to conditions involving the entire colon removal.

Feature

Ileostomy

Colostomy

Location

Typically located in the right iliac fossa

Typically located in the left iliac fossa

Stool Consistency

Usually results in liquid or semi-liquid stool

Produces a more formed stool

Spout

Ileostomy is usually spouted

Colostomy is usually flush

Use
  • To defunction the rest of the bowel in order to protect a distal anastomosis
  • To evacuate stool from the body if the entire colon has been removed (such as in colorectal cancer, IBD)
  • To relieve bowel obstruction
  • To protect a distal anastomosis or allow healing away from the faecal flow
  • Following resection when anastomosis is unsafe or not possible
  • To relieve obstruction when resection is not feasible
  • To reduce disease activity (e.g. Crohn’s disease)
  • To allow alternative bowel control (incontinence)

Fluid and electrolyte problems

More likely

Less likely

Appliances

Requires bags that often need to be emptied frequently due to the liquid consistency of the stool

Uses appliances that may be changed as needed, depending on the type of colostomy and stool consistency

Image

A colostomy can be used to relieve obstruction when resection isn't possible (Option A), such as in cases of obstructing rectal cancer or sigmoid volvulus. It helps divert stool away from the obstruction site.

A colostomy is commonly used to protect a distal anastomosis (Option B), especially after rectal surgery, by diverting fecal flow and allowing the anastomosis to heal without the risk of contamination from fecal material.

While ileostomy may sometimes be used in Crohn's and other inflammatory diseases, colostomy can also be indicated, particularly when the disease is localized to the colon and perianal regions (Option C). It helps manage fecal diversion in severe cases, allowing perianal lesions to heal.

Ulcerative Colitis (UC)

  • UC is an inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) characterized by chronic inflammation primarily affecting the mucosal layer of the colon.
  • Unlike Crohn's disease, which can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract and involves deeper bowel layers, UC is limited to the colon and involves only the mucosal layer.

Contributing factors
  • Defective mucin production: Mucosal immunological reactions
  • Autoimmune factors (Cytotoxic T cells, anticolon antibodies)
  • HLA DR2 association
  • Family history
  • Cow's milk allergy
  • Stress and lifestyle associations

Protective factors
  • Appendicectomy
  • Smoking

Sites of involvement
  • UC is confined to the large intestine.
  • Always involves the rectum; extends proximally continuously.
  • Extent of involvement:
    • Proctitis/Proctosigmoiditis (Limited to the rectum and sigmoid colon)
    • Left-Sided Colitis
    • Pancolitis (Entire colon)

Colonoscopy Findings
  • Continuous inflammation from the dentate line of the rectum and extends proximally.
  • Initially, mucosa appears erythematous, granular, or roughened; it worsens over time.
  • Ulcers are long, serpentine, covered in fibrin, with a "bear claw" appearance.
  • Significant bleeding can occur due to ulcer erosion into blood vessels.

Microscopic Findings
  • Inflammation limited to the mucosal layer
  • Polymorphonuclear leukocytes in lamina propria.
  • Depletion of mucin in goblet cells.
  • Crypt abscesses contain inflammatory cells within Lieberkühn crypts.
  • No granulomas, deep fissural ulcers, or transmural lymphoid aggregates.

Explanation:

In acute appendicitis, the initial pain is visceral, colicky, and poorly localised to the periumbilical region (T8–T10 dermatomes), resulting from luminal obstruction and distention of the appendix. Right lower quadrant, sharp and constant (Option A): This describes later somatic pain after peritoneal involvement, not the initial presentation.

Epigastric, burning (Option B): Epigastric burning is typical of peptic ulcer disease or gastritis, not appendicitis.

question: What is the typical initial location and character of abdominal pain at the onset of acute appendicitis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Pseudomyxoma Peritonei is a rare condition characterised by gelatinous mucinous ascites diffusely coating peritoneal surfaces. It occurs due to rupture of a mucin-producing epithelial tumour with peritoneal dissemination of mucin.

  • Most common primary site:
    • Appendix (mucinous cystadenoma / low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm).
    • Ovarian mucinous tumours are usually secondary.
  • Clinical features: Progressive abdominal distension, vague abdominal pain, weight loss, bowel obstruction (late).
  • Treatment: Cytoreductive surgery + hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC).
  • Prognosis: Depends on tumour grade and completeness of cytoreduction; better in low-grade disease.

Colonic adenocarcinoma (Option A): While colorectal cancer can cause peritoneal carcinomatosis, it typically presents with solid metastases and ascites, not the classic diffuse gelatinous mucin of pseudomyxoma peritonei.

Ovarian serous cystadenocarcinoma (Option C): Ovarian carcinomas cause malignant ascites and peritoneal spread but are not the classic source of pseudomyxoma peritonei, which is mucin‑producing and often indolent.

Gastric signet-ring carcinoma (Option D): Gastric signet‑ring cell carcinoma causes peritoneal carcinomatosis (linitis plastica‑like) with mucin‑producing cells but not the extensive, acellular gelatinous ascites characteristic of pseudomyxoma peritonei.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1351.
question: Pseudomyxoma peritonei most commonly arises from rupture or leakage of which type of tumour?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Yersinia enterocolitica infection typically causes acute terminal ileitis, mesenteric lymphadenitis, and right lower quadrant pain that can closely mimic acute appendicitis. It is a common cause of acute mesenteric lymphadenitis in children and young adults. At surgery, the appendix is normal, but enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes are present.

Salmonella typhi (Option A) causes typhoid fever, which can lead to ileocecal lymphoid hyperplasia or perforation, but it is not the most common cause of isolated mesenteric lymphadenitis mimicking appendicitis.

Campylobacter jejuni (Option B): Campylobacter typically causes enterocolitis with diarrhoea.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Option C): Tuberculous lymphadenitis can involve mesenteric nodes but usually presents with chronic symptoms, weight loss, and systemic features.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1340.
question: Which pathogen is classically associated with mesenteric lymph node enlargement producing symptoms similar to acute appendicitis?

explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C) Observation only

Explanation:

For carcinoid tumours <1 cm located in the appendix with negative margins and no high-risk features (mesoappendiceal invasion, lymphovascular invasion, base involvement), observation alone is sufficient after appendectomy, as the risk of metastasis is extremely low. Right hemicolectomy is reserved for tumours≥2 cm or smaller tumours with adverse features.

Completion right hemicolectomy (Option A): Right hemicolectomy is reserved for tumours>2 cm or those with high-risk features (location at base, mesoappendix invasion >3 mm, positive margins, lymphovascular invasion).

Adjuvant chemotherapy (Option B): Chemotherapy has no role in localised, low-grade carcinoids completely resected with low-risk features.

Radiation therapy (Option D): Radiation is not indicated for low-risk, completely resected appendiceal carcinoids.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1349, 1350.
question: An incidental 0.5 cm carcinoid tumour at the tip of the appendix with clear margins and no high-risk features is discovered after an appendectomy. What is the appropriate management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Appendiceal carcinoids < 2 cm, located at the tip, with clear margins and no mesoappendiceal invasion, carry a low risk of metastasis. Therefore, right hemicolectomy is not indicated, and the appropriate next step is observation alone.

  • Most are benign
  • Appendiceal carcinoids 1–2 cm in size located in the tip with no high-risk features (mesoappendiceal invasion, lymphovascular invasion, positive margins, or base involvement) are treated with a simple appendectomy.
  • Right hemicolectomy (Option B) is considered for:
    • Tumours ≥2 cm
    • Mesoappendiceal invasion
    • Lymph node involvement.

Chemotherapy (Option C): Chemotherapy has no role in localised, low‑risk appendiceal carcinoids treated with complete surgical resection.

Repeat appendectomy with wider margins (Option D): Wider margins are unnecessary if the initial resection margins are negative and the tumour is low‑risk (≤2 cm, tip location).



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1349, 1350.
question: A 1.8 cm carcinoid tumour is found at the tip of the appendix on histopathology after an appendectomy. There is no invasion of the mesoappendix, and margins are clear. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

correctAnswer: C. Tip (distal third) of the appendix
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Appendiceal carcinoid tumours most commonly arise in the tip (distal third) of the appendix. They are the most common primary tumours of the appendix, but are usually discovered incidentally.

  • Diagnosis: Based on immunohistochemical staining for synaptophysin and chromogranin A.
  • Classified as grade 1–3 according to their proliferative capacity (determined by the Ki-67 index and mitotic rate).

Base of the appendix (Option A): Carcinoids at the base are less common and carry a higher risk of obstruction or involvement of the cecum, often requiring more extensive resection.

Mid-appendix (Option B): Mid‑appendix carcinoids occur but are less frequent than those at the tip.

Appendiceal orifice (Option D): This location is rare and may be associated with involvement of the cecal wall, but it is not the most common site.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1349.
question: What is the most common site within the appendix for a carcinoid tumour to arise?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

To minimise the risk of stump appendicitis (inflammation of residual appendiceal tissue after appendectomy), the residual stump should be no longer than 5 mm. Leaving a longer stump increases the chance that retained faecal material or inflammation can occur in the remnant. Stump appendicitis typically presents with symptoms similar to acute appendicitis and may require reoperation.

1 mm (Option A): While shorter is generally better, a 1 mm stump is technically difficult to achieve consistently and is not a standard requirement.

3 mm (Option B): Although short, this is not the accepted upper limit cited in surgical guidelines.

10 mm (Option D): A 10 mm (1 cm) stump is excessively long and significantly increases the risk of complications.



Reference:

Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Page 1338.
question: A surgeon performing an appendectomy ensures that only a very short appendiceal stump is left behind to avoid stump appendicitis. What is the recommended maximum length of the residual appendiceal stump?

correctAnswer: B. External oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis muscles
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The Rutherford Morison incision is an oblique muscle-cutting extension of the gridiron incision, made when greater exposure is needed.
  • It involves the division of the external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis muscles along the line of the incision. In contrast, the standard gridiron incision splits these muscles along their fibre directions without cutting them.

Only the external oblique muscle (Option A): This describes only the initial step of the gridiron incision, where the external oblique aponeurosis is split, not cut.

Rectus abdominis muscle only (Option C): The rectus abdominis is not typically involved in a standard Rutherford Morison extension for appendectomy; this muscle lies medial to the common appendiceal incisions.

External oblique and transversus abdominis muscles only (Option D): The internal oblique muscle must also be divided to convert to a Rutherford Morison incision; it is not spared.

question: When converting a gridiron (McBurney) incision to a Rutherford Morison incision during an appendectomy, which of the following muscle layers are divided?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

For a stable patient with an appendiceal mass (phlegmon or abscess) that is already walled off, the recommended initial approach is the Ochsner-Sherren (conservative) regimen:

  • Bowel rest
  • Intravenous antibiotics
  • Hydration and close observation.

Surgery at this stage can be difficult and risks spreading localised infection. If the mass resolves, an interval appendectomy may be performed 6–8 weeks later. Percutaneous drainage is considered if an abscess >3-4 cm is present.

Immediate appendectomy (Option A): Immediate surgery in the setting of a well‑contained mass is technically difficult, carries a high risk of injury to adjacent inflamed structures (e.g., bowel, ureter), and is associated with higher complication rates.

Percutaneous drainage of the mass (Option C): Percutaneous drainage is reserved for a clearly defined abscess that fails to respond to antibiotics or causes persistent sepsis. It is not the first step for all appendiceal masses, especially phlegmons.

Laparoscopic exploration (Option D): Laparoscopy in the presence of an established mass is challenging and risky due to adhesions and inflammation; conservative management is preferred initially.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1343.
question: A patient with a palpable, tender right lower quadrant mass and a history of abdominal pain for 5 days is diagnosed with an appendiceal mass. The patient is hemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate initial management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In perforated appendicitis, the most common anaerobic pathogen isolated is Bacteroides fragilis, found in approximately 80% of cases. The most common aerobic pathogen is Escherichia coli. Antibiotic coverage for complicated appendicitis should target both gram-negative aerobes and anaerobes.

Escherichia coli (Option A): E. coli is the most common aerobic Gram-negative bacterium isolated in appendicitis; however, the question asks for the most common anaerobic bacterium.

Clostridium perfringens (Option C): Clostridium perfringens can be found, but is less prevalent than Bacteroides fragilis in perforated appendicitis.

Klebsiella pneumoniae (Option D): Klebsiella is an aerobic Gram‑negative rod that may be present but is not the predominant anaerobic isolate.



Reference:

Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page 1302.
question: A 28-year-old man presents with fever, right lower quadrant pain, and signs of peritonitis. Exploratory laparotomy reveals a perforated appendix with purulent peritoneal fluid. Cultures are obtained. Which anaerobic organism is most commonly isolated in this scenario?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

For pediatric patients with suspected appendicitis, ultrasonography is the preferred initial imaging study because it avoids ionising radiation and can reliably diagnose appendicitis when performed by an experienced operator.

In adults, a CT scan is generally the most accurate modality. MRI is also radiation-free, but is less commonly used as a first-line test due to availability and cost.

Plain abdominal X-ray (Option A): Plain films have low sensitivity and specificity for appendicitis and still involve radiation exposure. They are not the preferred initial imaging choice.

CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis (Option B): CT involves significant radiation and is typically reserved for cases where ultrasound is equivocal or not diagnostic, especially in older children or when complications are suspected.

MRI of the abdomen (Option D): MRI avoids radiation but is less widely available, more time‑consuming, often requires sedation in young children, and is not the first‑line imaging choice. It may be used selectively if ultrasound is nondiagnostic.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1342.

question: In a pediatric patient with suspected acute appendicitis, what is the preferred initial imaging modality to avoid radiation exposure?

explanationHtml:

The CT image demonstrates an enlarged, thickened appendix consistent with acute appendicitis.

  • Ballance's sign is associated with ruptured spleen, not appendicitis.
  • It is characterised by fixed dullness in the left flank (due to clotted blood) and shifting dullness in the right flank (due to liquid blood in the peritoneal cavity).

Psoas sign (Option A): The psoas sign is associated with acute appendicitis (especially retrocecal appendicitis).

Rovsing's sign (Option B): Rovsing's sign is a classic physical finding in acute appendicitis.


McBurney's sign (Option D): Tenderness at McBurney's point (one-third the distance from the ASIS to the umbilicus) is a hallmark sign of acute appendicitis.

question: A 26-year-old patient presents with acute right lower quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and low-grade fever. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen is obtained and is shown above. Which of the following physical examination findings is not typically associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image demonstrates passive extension of the patient’s right hip to stretch the psoas muscle, which produces pain in cases of retrocecal appendicitis, known as the psoas sign.

  • The psoas sign is positive when pain is elicited by passive extension of the right hip or by flexion of the hip against resistance.
  • This occurs because an inflamed retrocecal appendix lies in contact with the psoas muscle, and stretching the muscle irritates the adjacent peritoneum.

Obturator sign (Option A): The obturator sign involves pain on internal rotation of the flexed right hip, not hyperextension.

Rovsing's sign (Option B): Rovsing's sign is pain in the right lower quadrant upon palpation of the left lower quadrant.

Murphy's sign (Option D): Murphy's sign is right upper quadrant tenderness on inspiration, associated with cholecystitis, not appendicitis.

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1339.
question: A 24-year-old man presents with acute onset of right lower abdominal pain, fever, and nausea. During physical examination, the manoeuvre shown in the image is performed, which elicits pain in the right lower quadrant. This clinical finding is known as:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Rovsing's sign is elicited by palpation or deep pressure in the left lower quadrant, which causes referred pain in the right lower quadrant due to displacement of colonic gas toward an inflamed appendix. This is a classic sign of acute appendicitis.

Psoas sign (Option A): The psoas sign involves pain on right hip extension (e.g., with the patient lying on their left side), indicating an inflamed appendix overlying the psoas muscle, not left-sided palpation.

Obturator sign (Option B): The obturator sign is pain on internal rotation of the flexed right hip, suggesting an inflamed appendix in contact with the obturator internus muscle.

Murphy's sign (Option C): Murphy's sign is right upper quadrant tenderness with inspiration, associated with acute cholecystitis, not appendicitis.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1339.
question: Which physical examination manoeuvre, when performed in the left lower quadrant, elicits pain in the right lower quadrant and is suggestive of acute appendicitis?

correctAnswer: A. The appendix's pelvic location masking classic right lower quadrant signs
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Pelvic appendicitis occurs when the appendix is anatomically located in the pelvis, which happens in about 20-30% of the population.

  • In these cases, the classic signs and symptoms of appendicitis may be altered, leading to a delayed diagnosis.
  • The patient's presentation with vague lower abdominal pain, low-grade fever, and dysuria is consistent with pelvic appendicitis.


The pelvic location of the appendix can mask the classic right lower quadrant signs by:

  • Altering the location of pain and tenderness (more suprapubic or diffuse lower abdominal)
  • Reducing the likelihood of a positive Rovsing's sign
  • Potentially causing a positive obturator sign due to irritation of the obturator internus muscle

Other locations of the appendix and their presentations:

Location

Presentation

Retrocecal

May present with flank or back pain

Subcecal

Can mimic gynecological disorders or urinary tract infection

Pre-ileal

May cause small bowel obstruction symptoms

Post-ileal

May cause small bowel obstruction symptoms

Paracecal

Can present with typical right lower quadrant pain

Subhepatic

Can be mistaken for cholecystitis

Pelvic

Can mimic symptoms of pelvic inflammatory disease or ovarian pathology

Misinterpretation of urinary symptoms as a primary urological issue (Option B): Urinary symptom is a consequence of the appendix's pelvic location rather than the primary cause. The proximity to the bladder can cause urinary symptoms making it a presentation of pelvic appendicitis .

In pelvic appendicitis, the migration pattern (Option C) might not be as noticeable due to the appendix’s atypical location. However, this does not fully explain a delayed diagnosis, as some degree of migration can still occur or other signs may be evident. Therefore, this option is not the best explanation for the delayed diagnosis.


Absence of typical anorexia and vomiting in early appendicitis (Option D): While anorexia and vomiting are commonly associated with appendicitis , their absence is not a significant cause of delayed diagnosis. Appendicitis can present with or without these symptoms, and their absence doesn’t necessarily obscure the diagnosis.



Reference:

Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1339

question: A 28-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of vague lower abdominal pain, low-grade fever, and urinary frequency. Initial pelvic examination and urinalysis were inconclusive. Acute appendicitis most commonly begins with luminal obstruction, often by a fecalith (appendicolith), lymphoid hyperplasia, or, less commonly, by a foreign body or tumour.

Ischemic injury due to arterial embolism (Option B): Primary arterial occlusion (e.g., embolism) is a rare cause of appendicitis; ischemia in typical appendicitis results from venous outflow obstruction secondary to luminal blockage.

Bacterial translocation from the colon (Option C): Bacterial invasion is a secondary event following mucosal compromise due to obstruction and ischemia, not the initial trigger.

Autoimmune inflammation (Option D): Appendicitis is not an autoimmune process; inflammation is secondary to obstruction and bacterial proliferation.

question: Which pathological process marks the starting point in the evolution of acute appendicitis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The fold of Treves (ileocecal fold) is an antimesenteric peritoneal fold at the ileocecal junction that contains no significant blood vessels, hence called the "bloodless fold."
  • It is used intraoperatively as a landmark to locate the appendix and guide the extent of coagulation to avoid thermal injury to adjacent bowel.
  • The Gerlach valve is a mucosal fold at the appendiceal orifice, and the Jackson membrane is an adhesion from the abdominal wall to the ascending colon.

Jackson membrane (Option A): Jackson’s membrane is a peritoneal fold sometimes covering the ascending colon, not a specific ileocecal landmark.

Gerlach valve (Option B): This is an alternative name for the ileocecal valve itself, not an external peritoneal fold.

Mesoappendix (Option D): The mesoappendix is the mesentery of the appendix containing the appendicular artery, not an avascular fold marking the ileocecal junction.

question: Which anatomical structure serves as a surgical landmark to identify the ileocecal junction during appendectomy?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The appendicular artery, a branch of the lower division of the ileocolic artery, runs within the mesoappendix and is the primary vessel ligated during appendectomy. It is an end-artery supplying only the appendix. Thrombosis of this artery in acute appendicitis can lead to gangrene and perforation of the appendix.

Ileocolic artery (Option A): The ileocolic artery is the parent vessel but is not ligated during a routine appendectomy; only its terminal branch, the appendicular artery, is divided.

Right colic artery (Option B): The right colic artery supplies the ascending colon and is not involved in the blood supply of the appendix or the mesoappendix.

Middle colic artery (Option D): The middle colic artery supplies the transverse colon and is unrelated to the appendix or its mesentery.

question: A 30-year-old female presents with right lower quadrant abdominal pain and is diagnosed with acute appendicitis. During surgery, a small mass is found at the tip of the appendix, which is subsequently identified as a carcinoid tumour. Which of the following statements about carcinoid tumours in the appendix is correct?

correctAnswer: B. Rising pulse rate with increasing size of the appendix mass
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A rising pulse rate with increasing size of the appendix mass strongly suggests worsening infection, potential abscess formation, and failure of conservative management, necessitating urgent surgical intervention.

Appendicular Perforation

Appendix rupture causes peritoneal contamination, leading to peritonitis.

Risk Factors
  • Extremes of age (<5 years, >65 years)
  • Immunosuppression
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Faecolith obstruction
  • Pelvic appendix
  • Previous abdominal surgery

Pathophysiology
  • Lumen obstruction (often by faecolith) increases intraluminal pressure.
  • Venous obstruction and ischemia occur.
  • Bacterial invasion through the appendix wall.
  • Ischemic necrosis leads to rupture and contamination of the peritoneum.

Clinical Presentation
  • Initial colicky periumbilical pain, progressing to intense RLQ pain.
  • Signs of diffuse peritonitis (rigid abdomen, systemic sepsis).
  • Systemic signs (fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis).

Management: Preoperative
  • Intravenous fluid resuscitation
  • Broad-spectrum antibiotics
  • Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis
  • Hyperpyrexia treatment in children

Surgical Approach
  • Laparoscopic appendectomy is preferred for quicker recovery and reduced wound infection risk.
  • Indicators for stopping conservative treatment of an appendix mass and planning surgical intervention:
    • Rising Pulse Rate: Indicates worsening infection and potential sepsis; requires immediate surgical intervention.
    • Spreading Abdominal Pain: Suggests peritonitis, moving beyond the right iliac fossa; necessitates immediate surgery.
    • Increasing Mass Size: Indicates potential abscess growth or inadequate infection containment; requires surgical drainage and possible appendicectomy.
  • Drain abscess if present.


Reference:

Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1337-1338; 1343-1344

question: A 55-year-old male with a history of appendicitis presents with severe right lower quadrant pain, fever, tachycardia, and tenderness. An ultrasound shows an appendix mass. Despite conservative treatment, his condition worsens. Which sign or symptom indicates the need for surgical intervention?

correctAnswer: B. Continue IV antibiotics and observe
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient in this scenario is presenting with an appendix mass. This occurs when the inflamed appendix becomes encased in a phlegmonous mass due to the adherence of the greater omentum and loops of the small bowel.
  • When a patient presents with an appendix mass, the standard treatment is the conservative Ochsner-Sherren regimen, which prioritizes observation and a non-operative approach unless necessary.
  • Given that the patient has demonstrated significant clinical improvement after 48 hours of IV antibiotics, with the resolution of fever and improvement in abdominal pain, the most appropriate next step is to continue the conservative management with IV antibiotics and observe for further improvement.

Pain significantly reduced Minimal abdominal pain, improving tenderness Worsening abdominal pain or peritonitis
Able to tolerate oral diet Tolerating full oral diet & oral meds Persistent vomiting, unable to take oral meds
Hemodynamically stable Ambulating comfortably Hemodynamic instability (low BP, high HR)
WBC improving No signs requiring inpatient monitoring Rising WBC or metabolic abnormalities
No enlarging abscess on imaging No complications on imaging CT shows enlarging abscess/phlegmon
No nausea/vomiting Follow-up arranged & patient reliable Social issues preventing safe discharge

Laparoscopic appendectomy (Option C): Not preferred in appendicular mass; high risk of bowel injury due to dense adhesions.

Colonoscopy (Option D): Has no role in acute appendicitis; used only in suspected colonic pathology (e.g., carcinoma)

question: A 16-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of abdominal pain. The pain was initially periumbilical and colicky in nature but has since localized to the right iliac fossa. He has also experienced one episode of vomiting and has no appetite. His Alvarado score is 5. What is the inference of this score?

correctAnswer: B. The hyperesthesia is due to irritation of the T10-L1 nerve roots by the inflamed appendix
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Sherren's triangle:

  • It is a clinical sign in acute appendicitis characterized by cutaneous hyperesthesia in the right lower quadrant.
  • The area is roughly triangular, bounded by lines joining the anterior superior iliac spine, umbilicus, and pubic symphysis.
  • It is caused by irritation of the nerves supplying the anterior abdominal wall (T10-L1) by the inflamed appendix.


Clinical features of Appendicitis

Symptoms

Pain

Initial: Vague, dull pain around the umbilicus.

Progression: Pain localizes to the right lower quadrant (RLQ) due to parietal peritoneum involvement.

Nausea and Vomiting

Due to abdominal inflammation.

Anorexia

Loss of appetite.

Signs

Tenderness

Tenderness at McBurney's point (one-third of the distance from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus on the right side).

Rebound Tenderness

Increased pain upon sudden release of pressure on the abdomen, indicating peritoneal irritation.

Rovsing's Sign

Positive when palpation of the left lower quadrant causes pain in the right lower quadrant, suggesting peritoneal irritation.

Psoas Sign

Pain on passive extension of the right hip, indicating irritation of the iliopsoas muscle group.

Obturator Sign

Pain elicited by internal rotation of the right thigh while supine, suggesting irritation of the obturator internus muscle.

Dunphy's Sign

Increased pain in the RLQ with coughing, indicating peritoneal irritation.

Aaron's Sign

Referred pain in the epigastrium upon pressure over McBurney's point.

Ten Horn Sign

Increased pain during gentle traction or pulling of the right testicle in male patients, suggesting an inflamed appendix close to the right spermatic cord.


Sherren’s triangle (Option A) is not specific to retrocecal appendicitis. It can be seen in appendicitis irrespective of the position of the appendix.


Sherren’s triangle (Option C) is not highly specific for appendicitis and does not rule out other causes of right lower quadrant pain, such as mesenteric adenitis, ureteric colic, or gynecological conditions.


The presence of Sherren’s triangle (Option D) does not influence the choice of surgical approach. Laparoscopic appendectomy remains safe and is commonly preferred depending on patient factors and surgeon expertise.



Reference:
  1. Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1338, 1339
  2. litfl.com/sherren-triangle/

question: A 28-year-old male presents with right lower quadrant pain, nausea, and low-grade fever. Upon examination, he exhibits rebound tenderness at McBurney's point. Which of the following is the most likely initial event in the pathogenesis of this patient's condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The LIFT (Ligation of the Intersphincteric Fistula Tract) procedure is a sphincter-preserving technique that disconnects the internal opening of the fistula from the tract while minimizing damage to the anal sphincter.
  • This approach is particularly suitable for patients who are concerned about maintaining continence post-surgery, making it the most appropriate option for the patient in this scenario.

Fistula-in-Ano:

  • A chronic abnormal communication between the anorectal lumen (internal opening) and an external opening on the skin of the perineum, buttock, or, rarely, the vagina in women.

Common Treatment Options

Treatment

Description

Indications

Fistulotomy

(Option A ruled out)

Opening the fistula tract to heal by secondary intention.

Used for intersphincteric and trans-sphincteric fistula involving <30% of external sphincter; not for anterior fistula in women.

Fistulectomy

(Option B ruled out)

Removal of the fistula using diathermy cautery for better visualization of anatomy.

Effective for understanding the fistula's anatomy and extensions.

Setons

(Option C ruled out)

Materials are inserted into the fistula tract for drainage or gradual cutting.

Loose setons promote drainage; tight/cutting setons cut through muscle over time.

Advancement Flaps

Closing the internal opening with a flap of anorectal mucosa is used when the sphincter complex is not extensively indurated.

Effective for certain fistula configurations.

question: A 35-year-old woman with a recurrent anal abscess has developed an anal fistula. She is concerned about continence after surgery. Which surgical option is best to treat her condition while minimizing incontinence risk?

correctAnswer: B. Initial colostomy followed by definitive pull-through operation
explanationHtml:
Explanation:
A rectovestibular fistula is a type of high fistula in girls, which typically requires an initial colostomy to manage the bowel function. A definitive pull-through operation (posterior sagittal anorectoplasty) is then performed as a second stage to correct the malformation.

Anorectal Malformations (ARM):

Cause

Results from the imperfect fusion of the post-allantoic gut with the proctodaeum.

Incidence

Occurs in 1 in 4500 newborns; associated with anomalies like VATER/VACTERL, including cardiac, trachea-esophageal fistula, renal, and spinal anomalies.

Types
  • Male: Rectobulbar fistula (the fistula originating distal to the puborectalis)
  • Female: Rectovestibular fistula.

Investigations
  • Wangenstein's invertogram is used to determine the level of the rectal pouch relative to the pubococcygeal (Stephen’s) line.
  • Murugassu's technique: Involves aspiration of meconium from the rectum and dye injection to assess fistula level.
  • USG abdomen, cardiac function evaluation, MRI spine.

Treatment
  • Low Fistula: Single-stage reconstruction like anoplasty, ano vestibuloplasty, anal dilation, or incision of the anal membrane with excellent outcomes.
  • High Fistula: Initial colostomy followed by a definitive “Pull-through operation” (posterior sagittal anorectoplasty) and later colostomy closure.

Complications
  • Infection
  • Fecal fistula
  • Stenosis
  • Colitis
  • Malnutrition
  • Fecal incontinence

Single-stage anoplasty (Option A) is generally suitable for low fistulas, not high fistulas like the rectovestibular type.

Wangenstein's Invertogram to determine the level of the rectal pouch (Option C) is useful as a diagnostic tool rather than a treatment method.

Aspiration of meconium and dye injection for fistula assessment (Option D), Murugassu’s technique is used for assessing the level of the fistula, but it is not a treatment method.



Reference:
  1. Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1398

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient’s symptoms and examination & diagnostic findings, lead us to the diagnosis of solitary rectal ulcer syndrome (SRUS)
  • The STARR procedure (Stapled Transanal Resection of the Rectum) is the preferred surgical treatment for rectal intussusception associated with SRUS, addressing both the underlying intussusception and the ulcer.


Solitary Rectal Ulcer Syndrome (SRUS)

  • SRUS can be associated with obstructed defecation syndrome.
  • Location: Typically presents as an ulcer on the anterior wall of the rectum, 6–8 cm from the anal verge.
  • The ulcer may heal and leave a polypoid appearance.
  • Diagnostic Tools:
    • Proctography: May reveal rectal intussusception or anterior rectal wall prolapse.
    • Histology: Confirms the diagnosis.
  • Treatment:
    • Surgical Options:
      • STARR Procedure: Stapled Transanal Resection of the Rectum.
      • Abdominal Rectopexy: Resuspension of the rectum.

Abdominal Rectopexy (Option B) is another surgical option for rectal prolapse but is generally more invasive and typically reserved for cases of full-thickness rectal prolapse, not the localized intussusception seen in SRUS.

Histology (Option C) is crucial for confirming the diagnosis of SRUS, but it is a diagnostic tool, not a treatment modality.

Colostomy (Option D) is not indicated in the management of SRUS; it is typically reserved for more severe anorectal malformations or cases where bowel rest is required.

question: A 28 y/o female presents with a history of chronic constipation, rectal pain, and bleeding. On examination, an ulcer is found on the anterior wall of the rectum, 7 cm from the anal verge. explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The preferred treatment for carcinoma of the anal canal, particularly in the absence of distant metastasis and with localized inguinal lymph node involvement, is chemoradiation (Nigro regimen).

Treatment of Carcinoma of the Anal Canal

  1. Chemoradiation (Nigro regimen): The preferred treatment modality for carcinoma of the anal canal.
    • Chemotherapy Drugs: Commonly used drugs include 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), bleomycin, vincristine, and adriamycin.
    • Radiotherapy: Often used alone in advanced cases where the tumour is not resectable.
  2. Surgical Interventions:
    • Abdominoperineal Resection (APR) with Colostomy: Indicated for persistent or recurrent disease after combined modality therapy (CMT), or for cases where the tumor does not respond to chemoradiation.
    • Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy: Involves using 5-FU, cisplatin, and mitomycin C before surgery to shrink the tumour.

Abdominoperineal Resection (APR) with Colostomy (Option A)

  • APR is not the initial treatment.
  • Reserved for residual or recurrent disease after chemoradiation.

Radiotherapy alone (Option C)

  • Inferior outcomes.
  • Chemoradiation is superior for anal canal cancer.

Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgery (Option D)

  • Not standard for anal canal carcinoma.
  • Surgery is only for failures of chemoradiation.

correctAnswer: C. Local excision is indicated for early-stage rectal cancers with good prognostic factors.
explanationHtml:
Explanations:

  • Local excision is appropriate for early-stage cancers(T1 & T2), allowing for the removal of the tumour while preserving the rectum and anal sphincter, thus minimizing the impact on bowel function.

Treatment Options for Rectal Carcinoma

Surgical Treatment

  • Goals of Surgery: Achieve complete oncological clearance by removing the tumour, surrounding mesorectum, and lymph nodes (Total Mesorectal Excision - TME) to minimize local recurrence risk.
  • TME is a curative and gold-standard approach to completely removing rectal cancer. (Option A ruled out)
  • Neoadjuvant Therapy:
    • Chemoradiotherapy is often used before surgery to downstage cancer, facilitating easier removal and improving resection success. (Option B ruled out)

Surgical Techniques:

Technique

Indications

Local Excision

(Option C)

Suitable for early-stage cancers (T1 and selected T2) with good prognostic factors; preserves rectum and anal sphincter, minimizing bowel function impact.

Anterior Resection

Preferred for most cancers in the middle and lower rectum; involves removing affected rectal parts and reconnecting the colon to the remaining rectum.

Abdominoperineal Excision (APR)

(Option D ruled out)

Reserved for low-lying, extensive tumours unsuitable for sphincter-saving; involves removing rectum, anus, and surrounding tissues, creating a permanent colostomy.

Hartmann's Procedure

Involves removing the rectum and creating a temporary colostomy, suitable for elderly or frail patients.

Pelvic Exenteration: Radical surgery for advanced cases with cancer spread to adjacent organs; removes rectum, bladder, prostate (in men), and/or reproductive organs (in women) for clear margins.

Non-Surgical Treatment:

  • Wait and watch:
    • Considered for patients with complete clinical response to neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (about 20% of cases); involves close monitoring with potential surgery if recurrence occurs.
  • Endoluminal Stenting:
    • Used palliatively to relieve obstruction from inoperable tumours or to facilitate elective surgery; suitable for tumours in the upper rectum or rectosigmoid junction.
  • Palliative Colostomy:
    • Indicated in inoperable rectal cancer or cancers causing obstruction.

Adjuvant Therapy

  • Radiotherapy:
    • May be used pre- or post-surgery to destroy remaining cancer cells and reduce recurrence risk.
  • Chemotherapy:
    • Typically 5-fluorouracil(5-FU) based regimens are often combined with radiotherapy or given post-surgery to eliminate remaining cancer cells.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1409, 1412-1415

question: A 62 y/o woman diagnosed with rectal carcinoma is being evaluated for treatment options. Which of the following statements regarding the treatment strategies for rectal carcinoma is true?

correctAnswer: A. Perform a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient’s clinical examination & investigation findings point toward the diagnosis of rectal cancer.
  • Performing a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis is the correct next step to assess the extent of the disease and check for any distant metastases, which is essential for staging rectal carcinoma.

Investigations and Diagnosis of Rectal Carcinoma

  • Digital Rectal Examination:
    • Used to assess the size, consistency (hard), shape (Irregular), and mobility (mobile, tethered, or fixed).
    • A vaginal examination is recommended for women to check for involvement of the posterior vaginal wall.
  • Rigid Sigmoidoscopy:
    • Outpatient procedure for visualizing the neoplasm and obtaining biopsies
  • Biopsy and Histological Analysis:
    • Crucial for confirming the diagnosis and distinguishing rectal carcinoma from conditions that may mimic it, such as inflammatory strictures, granulomas, and benign adenomas.
  • Staging Investigations:
    • CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis.
    • Local pelvic imaging with MRI and/or endoluminal ultrasonography provides detailed information about local tumour spread, including infiltration into surrounding tissues and lymph node involvement.
  • Colonoscopy:
    • Essential for most patients to rule out synchronous tumours elsewhere in the colon.
    • Techniques like "dye spray" colonoscopy help differentiate benign from malignant lesions based on mucosal 'pit patterns'.
    • Proximal adenomas can be removed during the procedure; finding synchronous carcinomas may alter surgical strategy.
  • CT Colonography or Barium Enema:
    • Alternatives to colonoscopy if full visualization of the colon is not possible due to stenosing cancer.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1406

Clinical Features of Rectal Carcinoma:

  1. Commonly seen in >55 years of age (Option C ruled out)
  2. Early Symptoms:
    • Bleeding per rectum: The most common early symptom, often bright red and painless, which can be mistaken for hemorrhoidal bleeding.
    • Tenesmus: It is an important early symptom. It is the feeling of incomplete evacuation, often present with lower rectal tumours, leading to frequent attempts to pass stool or gas. (Option A ruled out)
    • Diarrhoea: Early morning diarrhoea may occur. (Option B ruled out)
  3. Late Symptoms:

    • Weight loss indicates metastatic disease.
  4. Abdominal Examination Findings:
    • Early cases may be normal while obstructing tumours can show signs of subacute bowel obstruction.
    • Palpable liver enlargement may indicate liver metastases, and cachexia can be present.
    • Ascites may be found in cases of peritoneal spread.
  5. Rectal Examination Findings:
    • The tumour is palpable within 7-8 cm of the anal verge, appearing as a raised, hard mass. If ulcerated, it may present as a depression with everted edges. (Option D)
    • Mobility and distance from the anal sphincter complex are important for assessing resectability and surgical planning.

question: A 24-year-old male presents with recurrent painful swelling and discharge at the natal cleft. He has coarse hair and reports worsening after prolonged sitting. On examination, a tender fluctuant swelling with a midline pit is noted.What is the most appropriate initial management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Lateral Internal Sphincterotomy involves dividing a portion of the internal anal sphincter, which reduces sphincter tone and allows the fissure to heal.
  • It is designed to maintain continence while addressing the fissure.
  • Management of anal fissures involves a combination of conservative and surgical interventions if conservative measures are ineffective.

Conservative Management

Lifestyle and Dietary Modifications

Aim: To soften stools and reduce pain

  • Increase fiber intake
  • Adequate fluid intake
  • Warm Sitz baths to relax the anal sphincter.
  • Topical anaesthetics.
  • Anorectal biofeedback: Helps patients learn to relax the anal sphincter and improve bowel control.

Pharmacological Treatment

1. Topical medications:

  • Glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) ointment (0.2%): Applied 2-3 times daily; a nitric oxide donor that promotes relaxation but may cause headaches.
  • Diltiazem (2%): Applied twice daily; a calcium channel blocker that induces sphincter relaxation with fewer side effects compared to GTN.

2. Botulinum toxin injections: 10-100 units injected into the internal anal sphincter to reduce pressure and allow healing by blocking acetylcholine release.

Surgical Interventions

Consider if conservative measures fail, especially for chronic cases.

Lateral Internal Sphincterotomy

Divides a small portion of the internal anal sphincter.

Approaches:

  • Closed Method: Small incision over the intersphincteric groove to divide the sphincter under the mucosa.
  • Open Technique: Incision through the anoderm for direct access to the internal sphincter.

Fissurectomy (Option A ruled out)
  • Excision of the fissure, including fibrotic edges and associated skin tags.
  • Often combined with an anal advancement flap.

Anal Advancement Flap

(Option C ruled out)
  • Used when there’s an increased risk of incontinence after sphincterotomy, especially in women post-childbirth.
  • Involves advancing a flap of healthy skin from the perianal area to cover the fissure, promoting healing and reducing tension.

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1428, 1429
