question: A 45-year-old man presents with persistent bleeding from haemorrhoids despite dietary changes and non-operative treatments. Examination reveals third-degree internal haemorrhoids. Which of the following is not an indication of hemorrhoidectomy?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Prolapsed haemorrhoids that cannot be reduced manually are classified as 4th-degree haemorrhoids.
  • Operative hemorrhoidectomy is the standard treatment for fourth-degree addressing both the prolapse and associated symptoms.
  • It is the elective resection of symptomatic haemorrhoids by decreasing blood flow and excising redundant tissue.
    • Used in 3rd and 4th-degree haemorrhoids.

Treatment of Hemorrhoids

Medical Therapy

  • Dietary and Lifestyle Changes: Increased dietary fibre, stool softeners, fluid intake, and avoiding straining can improve first- and second-degree haemorrhoids. (Option A ruled out)

Procedures

Rubber Band Ligation

Effective for persistent bleeding in first, second, and selected third-degree haemorrhoids by strangulating tissue to prevent further bleeding or prolapse. (Option B ruled out)

Infrared Photocoagulation:

Suitable for small first and second-degree haemorrhoids, coagulating the underlying plexus.

Sclerotherapy

Involves injecting sclerosing agents into first, second, and some third-degree haemorrhoids to cause fibrosis. (Option C ruled out)

Excision of Thrombosed External Hemorrhoids

Elliptical excision under local anaesthesia for acutely thrombosed external haemorrhoids causing intense pain.

Surgical Procedures

Operative Hemorrhoidectomy

Elective resection of symptomatic haemorrhoids by decreasing blood flow and excising redundant tissue.Used in 3rd and 4th-degree haemorrhoids (Option D)

Doppler-Guided Hemorrhoidal Artery Ligation

Uses a Doppler probe to identify and ligate arteries feeding the hemorrhoidal plexus, promising for symptomatic hemorrhoids but long-term effectiveness is still being evaluated.




Reference:
  1. SRB’s Manual of Surgery, 6th Edition, Page 962
  2. Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Pages 1310,1312

question: A 48-year-old patient presents with rectal bleeding during defecation and a prolapsing anal mass that requires manual reduction after bowel movements. The clinical appearance of the lesion is shown in the image above. These internal haemorrhoids are classified as which grade?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Injection sclerotherapy is most appropriate for first-degree internal haemorrhoids, particularly when painless rectal bleeding is the predominant symptom.

  • It induces endothelial inflammation, fibrosis, and fixation of the submucosa, reducing vascularity and preventing prolapse.
  • Although it may be used in selected second-degree haemorrhoids, rubber band ligation is generally the preferred office procedure for most Grade II disease because of its superior long-term efficacy.

Procedure:

  • Sclerosant: 5% phenol in arachis (almond) oil (classical agent)
  • Injection site: Above the dentate line at the apex of the hemorrhoidal pedicle, not into the hemorrhoidal cushion itself, to avoid pain and tissue necrosis.
  • Approximately 3-5 mL is injected into each hemorrhoidal pedicle, and the patient is reassessed after 6-8 weeks if further treatment is required.

Third-degree hemorrhoids (Option B): These prolapse during defecation and require manual reduction. They are generally treated with rubber band ligation (selected cases) or hemorrhoidectomy, rather than injection sclerotherapy.

Fourth-degree hemorrhoids (Option C): These are irreducible prolapsed hemorrhoids and usually require surgical hemorrhoidectomy because office-based procedures are ineffective.

External hemorrhoids (Option D): Injection sclerotherapy is not indicated for external hemorrhoids because they are covered by pain-sensitive anoderm below the dentate line. Thrombosed external hemorrhoids, when symptomatic, are managed with excision rather than sclerotherapy.



Reference:
  1. Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Page 1310.
  2. Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1431.

correctAnswer: B. Thrombus evacuation under local anaesthesia
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This presentation is classic for an acute thrombosed external haemorrhoid. If the patient presents within 48–72 hours of onset, thrombus evacuation under local anaesthesia provides immediate pain relief.

After 72 hours, pain usually subsides, and conservative management (sitz baths, analgesics, stool softeners) is appropriate.

Rubber band ligation is for internal haemorrhoids; hemorrhoidectomy is reserved for severe or recurrent cases.

Thrombosed External Haemorrhoid (Perianal haematoma)

  • Involves the superficial (external) haemorrhoidal venous plexus.
  • Clinical presentation
    • Sudden onset of severe pain
    • Olive-shaped, bluish, subcutaneous swelling at the anal margin
    • Typically located laterally at the anal verge
  • Precipitating factors: Straining at stool, coughing, lifting heavy weights
  • If untreated, may:
    • Resolve spontaneously (the majority of cases)
    • Suppurate
    • Fibrose → form a cutaneous (skin) tag
    • Burst with extrusion of the clot
    • Continue bleeding

Conservative management with sitz baths and analgesics (Option A): Conservative therapy is an option for mild or chronic symptoms, but is less effective for rapid pain relief compared to clot evacuation in an acute, painful thrombosis.

Rubber band ligation (Option C): Band ligation is for internal haemorrhoids, not thrombosed external haemorrhoids.

Emergent hemorrhoidectomy (Option D): Hemorrhoidectomy is typically reserved for large, circumferential thromboses or when conservative/evacuation measures fail, not as first‑line for a simple acute thrombosis.



Reference:
  1. Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Page 1310.
  2. Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1434.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Urinary retention is the most frequent early complication after hemorrhoidectomy, occurring in 1-15% cases, likely due to pain, reflex spasm, or opioid use.
  • Adequate pain control, limited intraoperative fluids, and avoidance of excessive anorectal packing can help reduce urinary retention.

Complications of haemorrhoidectomy

Early

  • Pain
  • Acute retention of urine
  • Reactionary haemorrhage

Late

  • Secondary haemorrhage
  • Anal stricture
  • Anal fissure
  • Incontinence

Delayed haemorrhage (Option A): Delayed (secondary) haemorrhage typically occurs 7–14 days postoperatively but is less common than urinary retention in the immediate postoperative period.

Anal stricture (Option B): Anal stricture is a late complication, not early, and is associated with excessive tissue excision or healing with fibrosis.

Faecal incontinence (Option D): Incontinence is uncommon after standard hemorrhoidectomy; it may occur if the sphincter is inadvertently injured, but it is not the most frequent early complication.



Reference:
  1. Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page 1406.
  2. Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Page 1311.
  3. Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1433, 1434.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Over 90% of anal fissures are located in the posterior midline. The posterior midline is thought to be vulnerable due to relative ischemia from the configuration of the terminal branches of the inferior rectal artery and high internal sphincter pressures.

Anal Fissure

  • A longitudinal tear in the anoderm, usually extending from the dentate line to the anal verge.
  • Common site: Posterior midline (most common); anterior fissure occurs less often, especially in women.
  • Aetiology: Passage of hard stool, constipation, or trauma → hypertonia and spasm of the internal anal sphincter → ischemia.
  • Clinical features: Severe pain during and after defecation, bright red bleeding per rectum, and fear of defecation.
  • Acute vs chronic: Acute fissure is a fresh tear; chronic fissure (>6 weeks) shows sentinel pile, hypertrophied anal papilla, and exposed internal sphincter fibres.
  • Management:
    • Acute: Conservative- high-fibre diet, stool softeners, sitz baths, topical lignocaine/nitrates.

Chronic: Lateral internal sphincterotomy is the definitive treatment.

Anterior midline (Option A): Anterior midline fissures are less common (about 10% overall) but are more frequent in women after childbirth.

Lateral position (left or right) (Option C): Lateral fissures are uncommon and should raise suspicion for secondary causes (e.g., Crohn’s disease, tuberculosis, malignancy, or sexually transmitted infections).

Circumferential (Option D): Circumferential fissures do not occur; fissures are linear tears, not circumferential.



Reference:
  1. Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1427, 1428.
  2. Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page 1407.
question: Where is the most common location for an acute anal fissure?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

According to Parks classification, the intersphincteric fistula is the most common type (about 45%).

Parks classification:

  • Interphincteric (Option A): Traverses the internal sphincter and tracks in the intersphincteric space. It runs between the internal and external anal sphincters.
  • Transsphincteric (Option B): Second most common (40%) and crosses both the internal and external sphincters.
  • Suprasphincteric (Option C): Uncommon (10%). They pass above the level of the puborectalis muscle and then curl downwards through the levators and ischioanal fossa to reach the skin.
  • Extrasphincteric (Option D): Rare (5%) and often secondary to trauma, Crohn’s disease, or pelvic infections. Run without a specific relation to the sphincters.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1436, 1237.
question: What is the most common type of anal fistula according to the Parks classification?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The X in the image is the Dentate or pectinate line. The pectinate (dentate) line is an important embryological and histological landmark.

Tumours above the pectinate line arise from the columnar epithelium of the rectum/anal transitional zone and are typically adenocarcinomas.

Tumours below the pectinate line arise from stratified squamous epithelium and are usually squamous cell carcinomas. Other rare tumours (melanoma, neuroendocrine) can occur anywhere in the anal canal.

Squamous cell carcinoma (Option A): Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common anal canal cancer overall, but arises distal to the dentate line from the stratified squamous epithelium.

Melanoma (Option C): Anal melanoma is rare and can occur anywhere in the anal canal, but it is not the most common type above the dentate line.

Neuroendocrine tumour (Option D): Neuroendocrine tumours (e.g., carcinoid) are uncommon in the anal canal and are not the predominant histology above the dentate line.



Reference:
  1. Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1418.

Goodsall’s rule states:

  • External opening anterior to the transverse anal line → internal opening follows a short, radial tract to the nearest crypt.
  • External opening posterior to the transverse anal line → tract curves to the posterior midline (6 o’clock) internal opening.

Exception: Anterior external opening >3 cm from the anus may also track to the posterior midline.

12 o’clock position (Option A): This would be expected for an anterior external opening that is >3 cm from the anus.

3 o’clock position (Option B): This would be possible for an anterior external opening close to the anus (≤3 cm) where the tract runs radially.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • For complex anal fistulas (especially in Crohn’s disease) involving a significant portion of the sphincter, a seton (cutting or draining) is preferred. A cutting seton is tightened periodically to slowly cut through the sphincter while allowing fibrosis, reducing the risk of incontinence. A draining seton controls sepsis and maintains patency.

Fistulotomy (Option A): Fistulotomy is contraindicated in high fistulas (involving significant sphincter muscle) and in Crohn’s disease due to high risk of incontinence and poor healing.

Lateral internal sphincterotomy (Option C): This is a treatment for chronic anal fissure, not for complex fistulas.

Fistulectomy (Option D): Fistulectomy (complete excision of the fistula tract) carries a high risk of sphincter injury and incontinence in complex Crohn’s‑related fistulas and is generally avoided.

question: What is the most common type of anorectal abscess?

correctAnswer: B. Dead hair with pointed ends directed inward
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image shows a midline sinus opening in the natal cleft characteristic of pilonidal sinus disease.

  • The hair found in a pilonidal sinus is usually dead, loose hair that has penetrated the skin from the outside.

  • The pointed ends of these hair shafts are directed toward the blind end of the sinus, suggesting they are driven inward by friction and negative pressure.

  • True hair follicles are almost never found in the sinus wall; the condition is primarily a foreign‑body reaction to embedded hair, not a disorder of local hair growth.

Pilonidal Sinus

  • One or more, usually non-infected, midline openings, which communicate with a fibrous track lined by granulation tissue and containing hair lying loosely within the lumen.

  • Common site: Midline of the natal cleft.

  • Aetiology (Acquired theory- accepted): Loose hairs driven into the skin by friction and suction → foreign body reaction → sinus formation.

  • Risk factors: Young adults, males, obesity, deep natal cleft, hirsutism, prolonged sitting.

  • Clinical features: Midline pits with hair, serous or purulent discharge, pain; may present as a pilonidal abscess.

  • Complications: Recurrent infection, abscess formation, multiple secondary tracts, and, rarely, squamous cell carcinoma in long-standing disease.

  • Management:

    • Acute abscess: Incision and drainage

    • Chronic sinus: Excision of sinus tracts with healing by secondary intention or flap procedures (e.g., Limberg flap)

  • Prevention/aftercare: Hair removal, hygiene, and avoiding prolonged sitting.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1423.

question: A 23-year-old man presents with pain and intermittent discharge from the natal cleft region. On examination, a small midline pit with surrounding inflammation is noted in the sacrococcygeal area, as shown in the image above. The hair found within the tract of this condition is typically:

Recurrence rates are lower with off‑midline (asymmetrical) excision and closure (e.g., Bascom, Karydakis, Limberg flap) because they flatten the natal cleft, reduce moisture/friction, and avoid a scar in the midline where recurrent hair penetration is likely.

Excision along the natal cleft (Option A): Midline excision along the natal cleft has a high recurrence rate due to the deep cleft, tension, and poor healing environment.

Primary midline closure (Option B): Primary midline closure after midline excision carries a high risk of wound breakdown and recurrence.

Leaving the wound open to heal by secondary intention (Option D): Open healing (marsupialisation) is an option, but has a longer healing time and higher recurrence compared to off‑midline flap techniques.

question: Which surgical principle helps reduce recurrence in the treatment of pilonidal sinus disease?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Perianal Paget's disease, an intraepithelial adenocarcinoma, is frequently associated with an underlying invasive malignancy, most commonly colorectal adenocarcinoma.

Other associated cancers include anal gland adenocarcinoma and urothelial carcinoma.

Perianal Paget Disease

  • A rare intraepithelial adenocarcinoma arising from apocrine sweat glands of the perianal skin.
  • Clinical features: Presents with pruritus, discharge, bleeding; lesion appears as an erythematous, eczematous plaque that may be ulcerated, crusted, or papillary.
  • Types:
    • Primary: Intraepidermal/intradermal disease
    • Secondary: Associated with anorectal or colorectal adenocarcinoma (~50% of patients have a synchronous colorectal neoplasm → full colonoscopy mandatory).
  • Other malignancies: Increased risk of synchronous or metachronous adnexal and visceral cancers.
  • Management: Wide local excision; reconstruction may require a cutaneous or myocutaneous flap.
    • Advanced disease: Abdominoperineal resection with neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy if invasive or associated with anorectal cancer.
  • Prognosis: High recurrence rate (30–60% at 5 years) → long-term follow-up essential.

Breast carcinoma (Option A): Mammary Paget's disease involves the nipple and is associated with breast carcinoma, not perianal Paget's.

Prostate adenocarcinoma (Option C): Prostate cancer is not typically linked to perianal Paget's disease.

Melanoma (Option D): Perianal melanoma is a distinct entity and not the usual malignancy underlying Paget's disease.



Reference:

Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Pages 1421, 1422.
question: Perianal Paget's disease is most commonly associated with which underlying malignancy?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) accounts for the majority of anal canal cancers. Adenocarcinomas are the next most common and are thought to arise from anal glands. Other tumours include melanoma, lymphoma, sarcoma and tumours of perianal skin.

Anal Squamous Cell Carcinoma:

  • Risk factors: iHPV infection (especially types 16/18), HIV, smoking, anal receptive intercourse, and immunosuppression
  • Anal SCC usually presents with pain and bleeding. A mass, pruritus or discharge is less common. Advanced tumours may cause faecal incontinence by invasion of the sphincters and, in women, anterior extension may result in anovaginal fistulation.
  • Lymphatic spread is to the inguinal lymph nodes.

The standard primary treatment for anal SCC is chemoradiation (Nigro protocol), with surgery reserved for salvage.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1443, 1444.
question: What is the most common histological type of anal canal carcinoma?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • As with cutaneous melanomas, the Breslow thickness (depth of invasion in mm) is the most important prognostic factor for anorectal melanoma. Thicker tumours have a worse prognosis.
  • Nodal and distant metastasis also affect outcome, but depth is the key determinant of staging and survival.
  • Overall prognosis is poor, with 5‑year survival <20%.
  • Treatment involves wide local excision if feasible; abdominoperineal resection (APR) may be used for larger tumors but does not clearly improve survival.

question: What is the primary prognostic factor for anorectal melanoma?

correctAnswer: C. Preservation of the mesorectal fascia envelope intact
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Total mesorectal excision (TME) involves sharp dissection in the embryological avascular ("holy") plane between the mesorectal fascia (fascia propria) and the parietal pelvic fascia, allowing complete removal of the mesorectum with the mesorectal fascia envelope intact.
  • This minimizes circumferential resection margin (CRM) involvement and reduces local recurrence while preserving the pelvic autonomic nerves.

Dissection medial to the endopelvic fascia (Option A): TME is performed in the embryological avascular plane between the mesorectal fascia and parietal pelvic fascia, not medial to the endopelvic fascia; this may result in an incomplete mesorectal excision.

Dissection lateral to the avascular plane around the mesorectum (Option B): Dissection outside the correct avascular ("holy") plane increases the risk of bleeding, autonomic nerve injury, and incomplete mesorectal excision.

Wide resection of the presacral fascia (Waldeyer's fascia) (Option D): Waldeyer's fascia is divided sharply only as required during posterior dissection; routine wide resection is unnecessary and increases the risk of presacral venous bleeding and nerve injury.

.

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1413.

question: A proctoscope is typically used to visualise up to what length of rectum?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image shows a proctoscope, an instrument used to visualise the anal canal and distal rectum during proctoscopic examination.

  • In an acute anal fissure, the anal canal is exquisitely tender, and digital rectal examination or anoscopy/proctoscopy is usually deferred to avoid severe pain and worsening spasm. Examination may be performed later under anaesthesia if needed.
  • In contrast, proctoscopy is commonly used to evaluate painless rectal bleeding, internal haemorrhoids, rectal prolapse, and other anorectal disorders.

question: The instrument shown in the image above is commonly used for examination of the anal canal and distal rectum. In which of the following conditions is the use of this instrument typically deferred or avoided during the initial evaluation?

correctAnswer: B. Conservative management of underlying causes
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In children, rectal prolapse is usually mucosal and often related to constipation, diarrhoea, parasitic infections, or malnutrition. Conservative management is first‑line:

  1. Digital repositioning
  2. Treat underlying causes (e.g., fibre for constipation, antiparasitics for worms, nutritional support)
  3. Encourage defecation posture changes.
  4. Submucosal injection or banding can be done.

Most cases resolve with conservative measures. Surgery is reserved for recurrent or full‑thickness prolapse.

Immediate surgical repair (Option A): Surgery is reserved for recurrent or persistent prolapse after failed conservative management.

Permanent colostomy (Option C): Colostomy is never a first‑line treatment for pediatric mucosal prolapse; it is considered only in extreme, refractory cases with full‑thickness prolapse and underlying neuromuscular disorders.

Endoscopic submucosal resection (Option D): Endoscopic resection is not a standard treatment for rectal prolapse in children.



Reference:
  • Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1397.
question: What is the initial management approach for mucosal rectal prolapse in a child?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In elderly or high‑risk patients, perineal approaches like Delorme’s mucosectomy or Altemeier rectosigmoidectomy are preferred because they avoid laparotomy, have lower morbidity, and can be performed under regional anaesthesia. However, they have a higher recurrence rate than abdominal procedures.

Delorme’s procedure:

  • The rectal mucosa is circumferentially stripped over the length of the prolapse.
  • The underlying rectal muscle is plicated with sutures, causing it to concertina toward the anal canal.
  • Excess rectal mucosa is excised, and a mucosal anastomosis is performed.
  • This creates a plicated muscular ring above the anal canal, reducing the prolapse.

Abdominal rectopexy (with or without resection) is preferred for younger, fitter patients due to better long‑term results. Thiersch’s encirclement is largely obsolete.

Perineal procedures

Abdominal procedures
  • Delorme’s mucosectomy
  • Thiersch encirclement
  • Altemeier rectosigmoidectomy
  • Anterior: Ripstein’s rectopexy,
  • Resection rectopexy (Frykman–Goldberg procedure)
  • Posterior (Well’s & Ivalon’s)
  • Suture rectopexy,
  • Mesh rectopexy

Ripstein rectopexy (Option A): Ripstein rectopexy is an abdominal procedure with mesh fixation, carrying a higher surgical risk in frail patients.

Frykman–Goldberg procedure (resection rectopexy) (Option C): This is also an abdominal procedure combining sigmoid resection with rectopexy, and is not ideal for high‑risk patients.

Thiersch’s anal encirclement (Option D): Thiersch’s procedure (anal encirclement with a suture or mesh) is a palliative perineal approach but has high recurrence and complication rates (e.g., erosion, infection, obstruction) and is not the preferred surgical repair.

  • Defecography (proctography) is the dynamic fluoroscopic study of choice for evaluating pelvic floor dysfunction, rectal intussusception, prolapse, and paradoxical puborectalis contraction. It involves injecting barium paste into the rectum and imaging during evacuation. This test is particularly useful in patients with solitary rectal ulcer syndrome, constipation, or suspected rectal prolapse to assess structural and functional abnormalities during defecation.

Barium enema (Option A): Barium enema primarily evaluates anatomical structure and mucosal details of the colon, but does not assess dynamic pelvic floor function during defecation.

CT colonography (Option B): CT colonography is used for colorectal cancer screening and detection of polyps, not for functional pelvic floor assessment.

Pelvic MRI (Option D): Static pelvic MRI provides excellent anatomical detail, but dynamic MR defecography (if available) is the functional variant, not routine pelvic MRI. Standard defecography (fluoroscopic) remains the widely accepted primary investigation.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The puborectalis muscle maintains the angle between the anal canal and rectum (the anorectal angle) and is an important component in the continence mechanism. The position and length of the anal canal, as well as the angle of the anorectal junction, depend to a major extent on the integrity and strength of the puborectalis muscle sling.

Internal anal sphincter (Option A): The internal anal sphincter provides resting tone (involuntary control) but does not maintain the anorectal angle.

External anal sphincter (Option B): The external anal sphincter provides voluntary squeeze pressure but does not shape the anorectal angle.

Levator ani muscle (Option D): While the puborectalis is a component of the levator ani, the broad term “levator ani” includes other parts (pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus) that primarily support the pelvic floor rather than specifically maintaining the anorectal angle.

Alteration in bowel habits, tenesmus, and passage of mucus are also common but often appear later. Abdominal pain and weight loss usually indicate advanced disease. Digital rectal examination and endoscopic evaluation are essential for early detection.

Abdominal pain (Option A): Abdominal pain is a later symptom, often indicating advanced disease, obstruction, or perforation.

Weight loss (Option B): Weight loss is a systemic symptom of advanced cancer and is not early or specific.

Tenesmus (Option D): Tenesmus (a feeling of incomplete evacuation) is common with rectal tumours, but it typically occurs when the tumour is larger or lower in the rectum, not necessarily the earliest symptom.

It accurately assesses tumour depth, extramural invasion, circumferential resection margin (CRM), and lymph node involvement, which is critical for planning neoadjuvant therapy and surgery.
  • EUS is also accurate for early T staging but has a limited field of view for nodal and mesorectal assessment.

CT scan of abdomen and pelvis (Option A): CT is used for distant metastasis (M) staging and evaluation of extrarctal spread, but has poor accuracy for local T and N staging compared to MRI.

Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) (Option B): EUS is excellent for early T staging (T1/T2) and can assess perirectal nodes, but it is operator‑dependent, limited by stenotic tumours, and less accurate for mesorectal fascia assessment compared to MRI.

PET‑CT scan (Option C): PET‑CT is valuable for detecting distant metastases and restaging after therapy, but lacks the anatomical detail needed for precise local T/N staging.

explanationHtml:

  • T3- Tumour invasion through the muscularis propria into the perirectal tissue
  • N1b- Involvement of two lymph nodes
  • M0- No evidence of metastasis

For stage III rectal cancer (any T, N1‑2, M0), the current standard is neoadjuvant chemoradiation (CRT) followed by total mesorectal excision (TME). This approach improves local control, may downstage the tumour, and increases sphincter‑preservation rates. Adjuvant chemotherapy is typically given postoperatively.

For early-stage I (T1‑2 N0) tumours, local excision or radical resection may be sufficient without neoadjuvant therapy.

question: For a patient with rectal cancer staged as T3 N1b M0, what is the standard treatment approach?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Low anterior resection (LAR) with total mesorectal excision (TME) is the sphincter‑preserving procedure of choice for mid- and upper-rectal cancers (typically ≥5 cm from the anal verge) when a clear distal margin (≥1-2 cm) can be achieved.

Abdominoperineal resection (APR) (Option A): APR (permanent end colostomy) is indicated for very low tumours (<5 cm from the anal verge) that invade the sphincter complex or when the distal margin cannot be achieved with sphincter preservation.

Hartmann's procedure (Option C): Hartmann's is used in emergency settings (obstruction, perforation) or for palliation, not for elective curative resection of a mid‑rectal cancer.

Transanal local excision (Option D): Local excision is reserved for small, early T1 N0 tumours with favourable histology, not for a typical T3 or node‑positive cancer at 6 cm.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1409-1411.
question: For a rectal cancer located 6 cm from the anal verge without sphincter involvement, which surgical procedure is typically preferred?

correctAnswer: B. T1 N0, well‑differentiated tumour 6 cm from anal verge, &lt;3 cm in size
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Transanal local excision is reserved for select early T1 N0 rectal cancers that are:

  • <3 cm in size
  • Well‑ to moderately‑differentiated
  • Within 8 cm of the anal verge
  • Involve <30% of the rectal circumference
  • No lymphovascular invasion or nodal involvement on imaging

T2 N0 tumor, 5 cm from the anal verge (Option A): T2 tumors have a significantly higher risk of regional lymph node metastasis and are best managed with radical resection and total mesorectal excision (TME) rather than local excision.

T3 N0 tumor, 10 cm from the anal verge (Option C): T3 tumors are locally advanced rectal cancers and require neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by radical resection with TME. Local excision is contraindicated.

T1 N1 tumor, 4 cm from the anal verge (Option D): The presence of regional lymph node metastasis (N1) is an absolute contraindication to local excision and requires radical resection with lymphadenectomy, regardless of the early T stage.



Reference:
  1. Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Pages 1299, 1300.

  • FOLFIRI (5‑FU, leucovorin, irinotecan) is used more often in metastatic disease.

question: Following surgical resection of node-positive (stage III) rectal cancer, which chemotherapy regimen is considered the standard adjuvant treatment?

correctAnswer: B. Hartmann's procedure (resection with end colostomy)
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Hartmann's procedure (resection of the tumour, closure of the rectal stump, and creation of an end colostomy) is a good option for elderly, frail patients with obstructing left‑sided colon cancer when primary anastomosis is deemed high‑risk due to poor bowel condition, compromised sphincter function, or patient comorbidities.
  • It avoids the risks of anastomotic leak. Endoscopic stenting may be used as a bridge to surgery or for palliation, but it is not a definitive curative treatment.

Low anterior resection with primary anastomosis (Option A): This is contraindicated due to poor sphincter function (would result in incontinence) and the high risk of anastomotic complications in an obstructed, unprepared bowel.

Transanal endoscopic microsurgery (TEM) (Option C): TEM is for early, small rectal tumours (T1 N0), not for obstructing rectosigmoid cancers. It does not address obstruction or nodal disease.

Endoscopic stent placement as definitive treatment (Option D): Stenting is a palliative or bridge‑to‑surgery option, not a definitive treatment for resectable cancer. It leaves the primary tumour in place and does not address cancer‑related risks.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The liver is the most common site of distant metastasis in rectal (and colon) cancer, due to drainage via the portal venous system. The lungs are the second most common site. The adrenal glands, bones, and brain are less common metastatic sites.

Lungs (Option A): The lungs are the second most common site for hematogenous spread, especially from rectal primaries due to drainage via the systemic venous system (via the inferior mesenteric vein), but less frequent than liver metastases.

Bones (Option B): Bone metastases are uncommon in colorectal cancer, typically occurring late in advanced disease.

Brain (Option D): Brain metastases are rare and usually associated with widespread systemic disease.

question: A 62-year-old man with rectal adenocarcinoma presents for staging workup. The clinician explains that rectal cancers commonly spread via the portal venous system before systemic dissemination. Which is the most common site of hematogenous metastasis in rectal carcinoma?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical scenario suggests a Spigelian hernia based on the lateral location of the swelling in the lower abdomen and a defect in the transversus abdominis aponeurosis seen on the CT scan.
  • AKA ‘lateral ventral hernia or a hernia of the semilunar line’.
  • It is the protrusion of preperitoneal fat, peritoneal sac, or organ(s) through a defect in the Spigelian fascia, which is the aponeurosis between the lateral edge of the rectus abdominis muscle medially and the semilunar line laterally.
  • Typically presents as a painful lump that becomes more prominent when standing or coughing, and can be prone to incarceration due to its location.
  • Surgical repair via an open or laparoscopic approach is recommended due to the high risk of complications.

Epigastric hernia (Option A) occurs in the midline between the xiphoid process and umbilicus, is usually small, and is often asymptomatic. It has no relation to the transversus abdominis aponeurosis.

Umbilical hernia (Option B) protrudes through the umbilicus, appearing as an outward bulge at the navel. This condition is more common in infants and obese adults, and its location at the umbilicus differs from the lateral abdominal wall.


An incisional hernia (Option D) occurs at the site of a previous surgical incision and requires a history of abdominal surgery. It can occur anywhere on the abdominal wall, not specifically related to the transversus aponeurosis



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1075

Strangulated Hernia:

  • A strangulated hernia occurs when a portion of tissue or intestine protrudes through a weakened area in the abdominal wall and becomes trapped.
  • The trapped segment loses its blood supply, leading to tissue ischemia (lack of blood flow) and potential tissue death if not promptly treated.

Clinical Features:

  • Irreducibility: The hernia cannot be pushed back.
  • Signs of Intestinal Obstruction: Colicky pain, bilious vomiting, absence of faeces and flatus.
  • History: Sudden onset of pain at the hernia site, followed by generalised abdominal pain.
  • Physical Examination Findings: Tense, extremely tender hernia with reddish or bluish skin discolouration and no cough impulse.
  • Diagnosis is primarily based on clinical examination and physical findings.

Treatment:

  • Initial Resuscitation:
    • Administer intravenous (IV) fluids.
    • Provide IV antibiotics.
    • Perform nasogastric aspiration.
    • Insert Foley's catheter.
  • Surgical intervention is done only after Initial Resuscitation.

Mesh Usage:

  • Synthetic mesh is contraindicated due to the increased risk of infection.
  • If a mesh is necessary, bioprosthetic or absorbable mesh is preferred.

question: A 62-year-old male presents with a progressively worsening right groin bulge over 6 months, causing discomfort during lifting or prolonged standing. The hernia is reducible, and he is scheduled for elective repair. What is the gold standard surgical technique for his inguinal hernia repair?

explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: D) Type 7

Explanation:

The patient's hernia, located below the inguinal ligament and extending into the femoral canal, is classified as a Type 7 (Femoral hernia) according to the Gilbert classification.

Gilbert classification system for Groin Hernias:

Type 1: Indirect, small hernia (Option A)
  • A hernia that protrudes through the deep inguinal ring.
  • It is typically small and often seen in pediatric cases.

Type 2: Indirect, medium hernia
  • An indirect hernia that is larger than Type 1 but does not yet cause significant displacement of the surrounding structures.
  • Admits one finger but less than two-finger breadth.

Type 3: Indirect, large hernia (Option B)
  • A significant indirect hernia may extend into the scrotum or cause a more noticeable displacement of structures.
  • > 2 Finger breath

Type 4: Direct hernia, involves the entire floor
  • A direct hernia that protrudes through the weakened area of the abdominal wall (Hesselbach's triangle), involving the entire floor of the inguinal canal.
  • It has an intact internal ring.

Type 5: Direct hernia, diverticular
  • A direct hernia where the sac resembles a diverticulum.
  • It has an intact internal ring.

Type 6: Combined hernia (Romberg's hernia)

(Option C)

It involves both direct and indirect components, often referred to as a pantaloon or saddleback hernia.

Type 7: Femoral hernia

(Option D)
  • A hernia that protrudes through the femoral canal, located below the inguinal ligament.
  • It is less common and more prone to complications like strangulation.


Reference:

SRB’s Manual of Surgery, 6th Edition, Page 745,746

question: What is the most common primary malignant tumour of the retroperitoneum?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A persistent omphalomesenteric (vitellointestinal) duct remnant should be suspected in a newborn with an umbilical sinus discharging mucus. This indicates a possible patent duct or sinus tract connecting the umbilicus to the ileum.

The most appropriate investigation is a fistulogram (contrast sinography):

  • Delineate the tract
  • Confirm communication with the intestine
  • Define the extent and anatomy of the remnant

During fetal development, the midgut initially communicates with the yolk sac via the omphalomesenteric (vitelline) duct. With the formation of the abdominal wall, this duct narrows, becomes incorporated into the umbilical cord, and normally obliterates, leaving the intestine free within the peritoneal cavity. Failure of complete obliteration of the duct results in various omphalomesenteric duct anomalies involving the intestine and abdominal wall.

CT abdomen with contrast (Option A) is unnecessary in a neonate due to radiation exposure and poor yield for small umbilical tracts. It is not the first-line investigation for suspected vitellointestinal duct remnants.

Ultrasound of the abdomen (Option B) may suggest an associated anomaly, but cannot reliably demonstrate luminal communication between the umbilicus and bowel.

Cystoscopy (Option D) is used to evaluate urachal anomalies, which present with urine discharge from the umbilicus.



Reference:

Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Pages 1085, 1086.

question: A newborn is noted to have an abdominal wall defect with protrusion of abdominal contents at birth, as shown in the image above. This condition is characterised by which of the following?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image shows a protruding swelling at the umbilicus consistent with an umbilical hernia in an infant, caused by failure of complete closure of the umbilical ring.

  • Umbilical hernia is a common condition in infants and young children and is usually benign in nature; it rarely strangulates.
  • Nearly 95% of umbilical hernias resolve spontaneously as the child grows and the abdominal wall strengthens.
  • Conservative treatment is indicated in children below 2 years of age when the hernia is asymptomatic.
  • Surgical repair is indicated when:
    • The hernia persists beyond 2 years of age
    • The hernia becomes symptomatic or complicated

Surgical Procedure: Herniotomy

  • A small, curved incision is made immediately below the umbilicus.
  • The neck of the hernial sac is identified and opened, and any contents are reduced into the peritoneal cavity.
  • The sac is then closed, and the redundant sac is excised.
  • The defect in the linea alba is closed with interrupted sutures using slowly absorbable material.

Mayo’s repair (Option B) is a vest-over-pants (double-breasting) fascial repair used for adult umbilical and small ventral hernias. It involves the overlapping of the rectus sheath and is not indicated in children. Paediatric umbilical hernias have good tissue healing and do not require such reinforcement.

Bassini repair (Option C) is a tissue repair for an inguinal hernia, involving suturing of the conjoint tendon to the inguinal ligament. It is not used for umbilical hernias.

Lichtenstein mesh repair (Option D) is a tension-free mesh repair used for adult inguinal hernias.



Reference:
  • Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1073.
question: An infant is brought to the clinic with a soft swelling at the umbilicus that becomes more prominent during crying or straining. The clinical appearance is shown in the image above. What is the most appropriate surgical procedure for this condition if operative treatment is required?

correctAnswer: C. They are the most common type of internal hernia.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Paraduodenal hernias are rare internal abdominal hernias, accounting for ~50% of such cases. They occur when small bowel loops become trapped in congenital peritoneal fossae (pockets) near the duodenum. They are congenital (Option D), due to abnormal mesenteric fixation during embryology.

Two Main Types:

  1. Left Paraduodenal Hernia (75% of cases) (Option A):
    • Herniation into the fossa of Landzert (posterior to the inferior mesenteric vein and left colic artery).
    • The small bowel lies posterior and to the left of the descending colon.
  2. Right Paraduodenal Hernia:
    • Herniation into the fossa of Waldeyer (Option B) (behind the superior mesenteric artery).
    • The small bowel is posterior to the mesocolon.

Symptoms: Often asymptomatic. Can cause chronic, vague abdominal pain or present acutely with obstruction or strangulation (a surgical emergency).

Diagnosis: Challenging. CT scan is key, showing clustered small bowel loops in a sac-like structure, abnormal mesenteric vessel orientation (e.g., "whirl sign"), and displaced colon.

Treatment: Surgical reduction of the hernia and closure of the hernia orifice to prevent recurrence. Laparoscopic or open approach. Do not divide the inferior mesenteric vein (left) or the superior mesenteric artery (right).



Reference:
  1. Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page 1097.
  2. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6370429/

Herniation through the umbilical ring (natural fascial defect).

question: Which surgical approach for a femoral hernia is performed through the inguinal canal?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The deep inguinal ring is an opening in the fascia transversalis, located lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. It serves as the entrance to the inguinal canal for the spermatic cord in males or the round ligament in females. The superficial inguinal ring is an opening in the external oblique aponeurosis.

Inguinal Canal

  • Location: Oblique passage in the lower anterior abdominal wall, just above the medial half of the inguinal ligament.
  • Length: ~4 cm in adults.
  • Orientation: Runs antero-inferiorly from the deep (internal) ring to the superficial (external) ring.

Boundaries

  • Anterior wall: Aponeurosis of external oblique (throughout); reinforced laterally by internal oblique fibres.
  • Posterior wall: Transversalis fascia; reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon (inguinal falx).
  • Roof: Arching fibres of the internal oblique & transversus abdominis muscles.
  • Floor: Inguinal ligament (rolled inferior edge of external oblique aponeurosis) and lacunar ligament medially.

Openings

  1. Deep (Internal) Ring:
    • Entrance into the transversalis fascia.
    • Located midway between the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) and pubic symphysis, ~1.5 cm above the inguinal ligament.
  2. Superficial (External) Ring:
    • Exit in the external oblique aponeurosis.
    • Triangular opening just superior and lateral to the pubic tubercle.

Transversus abdominis muscle (Option A): The transversus abdominis muscle lies posterior to the fascia transversalis but does not form the deep ring; the ring is a defect in the fascia.

Internal oblique aponeurosis (Option B): The internal oblique aponeurosis contributes to the conjoint tendon and the anterior wall of the canal medially but does not form the deep ring.

External oblique aponeurosis (Option D): The external oblique aponeurosis forms the superficial inguinal ring, not the deep ring.



Reference:

Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page 1109.

question: Which type of mesh is preferred in inguinal hernioplasty to minimise chronic pain and foreign‑body reaction while maintaining adequate strength?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In children, inguinal hernias are almost always indirect due to a patent processus vaginalis. The standard treatment is herniotomy: High ligation and excision of the hernia sac without repairing the inguinal floor (no muscle or fascial reconstruction).
  • Mesh repairs (e.g., Lichtenstein) and tissue‑based repairs (e.g., Bassini, McVay) are reserved for adults where weakness of the posterior wall is a contributing factor.

Bassini repair (Option B): Bassini repair (approximation of the conjoint tendon to the inguinal ligament) is an adult tissue‑based repair and is unnecessary in children.

Lichtenstein mesh repair (Option C): Mesh repairs are generally avoided in children due to growth concerns and the rarity of tissue weakness; herniotomy alone is curative.

McVay repair (Option D): McVay repair (Cooper's ligament repair) is used for adult direct or femoral hernias, not pediatric indirect hernias.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1068.
question: What is the standard surgical procedure for an uncomplicated indirect inguinal hernia in a child?

correctAnswer: B. Intra‑abdominal pressure holds it in place
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In Stoppa's repair, a large prosthetic mesh is placed in the preperitoneal space. According to Pascal's law, intra‑abdominal pressure is transmitted equally in all directions within the closed abdominal cavity, pressing the mesh firmly against the abdominal wall and keeping it in position without sutures for smaller defects. For larger or recurrent hernias, the mesh may be sutured laterally for added security. This tension‑free repair is effective for complex hernias.

Key Principles

  • Extraperitoneal approach via a lower midline or Pfannenstiel incision.
  • A single large mesh is placed in the preperitoneal space, covering the myopectineal orifices bilaterally (Fruchaud’s area).
  • Mesh extends beyond all potential hernia sites without fixation (held by intra-abdominal pressure).

Indications

  • Complex primary hernias (large, bilateral, or recurrent).
  • Multiple recurrent inguinal hernias.
  • "Hostile abdomen" (multiple previous surgeries).
  • Some incisional/ventral hernias.

Mesh adheres spontaneously to the peritoneum (Option A): While mesh may eventually incorporate, immediate fixation relies on pressure, not adhesion.

Fibrin glue is used instead (Option C): Fibrin glue is sometimes used for mesh fixation, but is not the principle behind Stoppa's sutureless technique.

The mesh is anchored by scar tissue formation (Option D): Scar tissue forms over weeks; the initial stability comes from intra‑abdominal pressure.



Reference:
  1. Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Pages 435, 436, 1125, 1126.
  2. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9055462/#:~:text=It%20(%20The%20Stoppa%20technique%20)%20has,and%20carries%20high%20morbidity%20and%20failure%20rates.

question: In Stoppa's preperitoneal mesh repair for inguinal hernia, why does the mesh often not require suturing in smaller defects?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

When the hernial sac is found medial to the epigastric artery, it is suggestive of a direct inguinal hernia. In a direct inguinal hernia, the sac lies medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, protruding through the floor of Hesselbach’s triangle.

Indirect inguinal hernia (Option A): Sac lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, exiting through the deep inguinal ring.

Femoral hernia (Option B): Sac passes below the inguinal ligament, lateral to the lacunar ligament.

Spigelian hernias (Option D): Occur through the spigelian aponeurosis (lateral to the rectus sheath, below the arcuate line), unrelated to the inferior epigastric artery in the inguinal canal.

Feature

Direct Inguinal Hernia

Indirect Inguinal Hernia

Origin

Acquired weakness of the posterior wall

Congenital patent processus vaginalis

Anatomical Exit

Through Hesselbach's triangle

Through the deep inguinal ring

Relation to Inferior Epigastric Vessels

Medial to the vessels

Lateral to the vessels

Age of Onset

Usually older adults (>40)

Any age (infancy to adulthood)

Sex Prevalence

Almost exclusively males

More common in males, but occurs in both sexes

Hernia Sac

Wide-necked, rarely descends into the scrotum

Narrow-necked, often descends into the scrotum/labia

Risk of Strangulation

Low (due to wide neck)

Higher (especially if narrow neck)

Clinical Presentation

Bulge in the medial inguinal region, diffuse

A bulge in the lateral inguinal region may extend downward

Reduction Direction

Reduces upward and laterally

Reduces upward and medially

Cough Impulse

Directly forward against the finger in the canal

Impulse from lateral to medial along the canal

Surgical Repair

Reinforcement of the posterior wall (mesh)

High ligation of sac + reinforcement

Association

Chronic straining, ageing, and connective tissue weakness

Congenital predisposition, often in younger patients


Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1065-1070.
question: During laparoscopic or open surgical exploration, a groin hernia sac found medial to the inferior epigastric artery is indicative of which type of hernia?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Femoral hernias have the highest rate of strangulation due to the narrow, rigid boundaries of the femoral canal. Therefore, elective repair is recommended at diagnosis for femoral hernias. Strangulation presents with tenderness, obstruction, and signs of ischemia.

  • More common in women (F: M ≈ 4:1) due to a wider pelvis and increased intra-abdominal pressure (e.g., pregnancy).
  • Often small and irreducible.
  • Common presentation: Sudden onset of a tender, firm lump in the groin below the inguinal ligament, or as an acute small bowel obstruction without an obvious hernia ("the great masquerader").

Management

  • Always requires surgical repair (open or laparoscopic) due to high strangulation risk.
  • Repair: Reduction of contents, excision of sac, and closure of femoral ring (often with mesh plug or suturing the inguinal to pectineal ligament).

Boundaries of the Femoral Ring (superior opening of the femoral canal):

  • Anterior: Inguinal ligament.
  • Posterior: Pectineal ligament (Cooper's ligament).
  • Medial: Lacunar ligament.
  • Lateral: Femoral vein.

Because the femoral canal is surrounded by ligamentous structures, the chances of strangulation are high in Femoral hernias.



Reference:
  1. Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 1071, 1072.
  2. Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Pages 1117, 1118.
question: Which type of hernia has the highest risk of strangulation?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

An indirect inguinal hernia confined to the inguinal canal and not extending into the scrotum is called a bubonocele.

Types of indirect inguinal hernia based on extent:

  • Bubonocele (Option B): hernia limited to the inguinal canal.
  • Funicular (Option A): hernia extends to the superior part of the scrotum, but the processus vaginalis is closed above the hernia.
  • Complete (Option C) (scrotal): hernia descends into the scrotum through a patent processus vaginalis.

Indirect hernias are more common on the right side due to the later descent of the right testis and the later closure of the processus vaginalis.

question: An indirect inguinal hernia that is confined to the inguinal canal and does not extend into the scrotum is termed:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The public tubercle is a key landmark for differentiating groin hernias:

  • Inguinal hernia: presents above and medial to the pubic tubercle.
  • Femoral hernia: presents below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.

This corresponds to their anatomical exits: inguinal hernias pass through the inguinal canal above the inguinal ligament, while femoral hernias pass through the femoral canal below the ligament.

Feature

Inguinal Hernia

Femoral Hernia

Location

Above the inguinal ligament, through the inguinal canal.

Below the inguinal ligament, through the femoral canal.

Incidence

Common (~75-80% of groin hernias).

Less common (~5-10% of groin hernias).

Sex Prevalence

More common in males (M: F ≈ 7:1).

More common in females (especially multiparous).

Anatomical Landmark

Superior to the pubic tubercle.

Inferior and lateral to the pubic tubercle.

Relation to Pubic Tubercle

The hernia sac lies above and medial.

The hernia sac lies below and laterally.

Neck Relation to Inferior Epigastric Vessels

Direct: Medial.

Indirect: Lateral.

Always lateral (but inferior to them).

Risk of Strangulation

Lower risk.

High risk (narrow, rigid femoral ring).

Clinical Presentation

Reducible groin swelling often extends to the scrotum.

Small, often irreducible bulge in the upper medial thigh.

Examination Finding

Expansile cough impulse above the inguinal ligament.

Cough impulse may be absent; often firm/irreducible.

Common Age Group

Broad (congenital to older adults).

More common in middle-aged/elderly women.


Reference:
  1. Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1071.
  2. Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Page 1607.
question: An inguinal hernia is located relative to the pubic tubercle in which position?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Indirect inguinal hernia is the most common type of hernia overall in both genders, accounting for about two‑thirds of all groin hernias. In men, indirect hernias outnumber direct hernias 2:1. In women, inguinal hernias are also most common, with indirect being the predominant type, though femoral hernias are relatively more frequent in women than in men.

Indirect Inguinal Hernia

Definition: Herniation through the deep (internal) inguinal ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, often descending into the scrotum/labia.

Mechanism: Persistence or weakness of the processus vaginalis (embryological tube connecting the abdomen to the scrotum/labium majus).

  • More common than direct hernia (~2/3 of groin hernias).
  • Congenital predisposition (patent processus vaginalis), but it can present at any age.
  • Often descends into the scrotum (in males).
  • The neck of the sac is lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.

Clinical Presentation

  • Swelling in the groin may extend to the scrotum.
  • Often reducible, may be painful with straining.
  • "Silk glove sign": Thickened spermatic cord feel on palpation.



Reference:
  1. Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page 1107.
  2. Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Page 1600.
question: What is the most common type of hernia in both men and women?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The structure forming the medial border of the triangle of doom is the vas deferens.

The triangle of doom is a critical danger zone in laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair, containing the external iliac artery and vein.

  • Boundaries:
    • Medial: Vas deferens (or round ligament in females)
    • Lateral: Gonadal vessels (testicular/ovarian)
    • Inferior: Peritoneal reflection
  • Contents:
    • External iliac artery
    • External iliac vein

Avoiding stapling or dissection in this triangle prevents vascular injury.

Triangle of Pain: The triangle of pain is another important danger zone encountered during laparoscopic (TAPP/TEP) inguinal hernia repair, mainly because it contains sensory nerves; injury leads to chronic postoperative pain. Staples, tacks, or sutures placed in this area can injure these nerves, causing chronic groin pain, meralgia paresthetica, or numbness in the thigh.



Reference:

Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Pages 1603, 1605.
question: Which structure forms the medial border of the "triangle of doom" in laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair?

correctAnswer: C. Femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve (Option C) runs lateral to the femoral sheath and supplies skin over the femoral triangle; it does not traverse the inguinal canal.

Inguinal Canal

  • Location: Oblique passage in the lower anterior abdominal wall, just above the medial half of the inguinal ligament.
  • Length: ~4 cm in adults.
  • Orientation: Runs antero-inferiorly from the deep (internal) ring to the superficial (external) ring.

Contents of the inguinal canal:

  • In both sexes: Ilioinguinal nerve (Option A) (runs outside the spermatic cord but within the canal).
  • In males: Spermatic cord (Option D)
    • Ductus deferens
    • Testicular artery
    • Pampiniform plexus
    • Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (Option B)
    • Autonomic nerves
    • Lymphatics
    • Processus vaginalis remnant.
  • In females: Round ligament of the uterus and remnants of the processus vaginalis (canal of Nuck).



Reference:

Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page 1109.

Femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve

question: Which of the following is not a content of the inguinal canal?

correctAnswer: C. It develops from the mesenchymal cells of the ventral mesogastrium.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Spleen develops from mesenchymal cells in the dorsal mesogastrium during 5th week of embryogenesis.

Anatomy of spleen:

  • Weight: 75 to 250 gm (Option A ruled out)
  • Location: left hypochondrium, along the axis of the 10th rib. (Option B ruled out)
  • It is an intraperitoneal organ. (Option D ruled out)
  • Largest lymphatic organ
  • In a healthy adult, the spleen is not usually palpable.
  • It becomes palpable when the size increases by more than 2.5 times.
  • Suspended by two ligaments: lienorenal ligament and gastrosplenic ligament.
  • Relations of the spleen:

    • It is related to the fundus of the stomach, the tail of the pancreas, the splenic flexure of the colon, and the anterior surface of the left kidney on it’s visceral surface.

question: What is the most common indication for a splenectomy?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • For patients planned for elective splenectomy, such as in hereditary spherocytosis, the best strategy to prevent overwhelming post-splenectomy infections (especially from encapsulated bacteria like Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Neisseria meningitidis) involves administering vaccines well in advance of surgery.

  • Vaccinating 10-12 weeks before surgery allows enough time for the patient’s immune system to mount an effective response and develop optimal protective antibody levels before the spleen is removed.

  • This vaccine timing provides the best opportunity for immunity to establish, minimizing the risk of severe infections after the spleen is removed.

Key vaccines to administer:

  • Pneumococcal vaccine (preferably PCV13 followed by PPSV23)

  • Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib) vaccine

  • Meningococcal vaccine (covering groups A, C, W, and Y; MenB as needed)

  • Annual influenza vaccination is also recommended

Timing of Vaccination:

Scenario Recommendation
Elective splenectomy (ideal) 10–12 weeks before surgery (optimal for immune response)
Elective splenectomy (minimum) At least 2 weeks before surgery
Emergency splenectomy At hospital discharge or 14 days post-op, whichever comes first



Reference:

explanationHtml:

  • DVT/Pulmonary embolism (Option A ruled out)- due to post-splenectomy thrombosis and prolonged immobility.

question: A 25-year-old woman with thalassemia major undergoes an elective splenectomy. She is informed about potential complications and the need for vaccinations. When is the most common Fatal late complication of splenectomy most likely to occur?

correctAnswer: A. Equal incidence in both males and females
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Acute ITP typically presents in children under the age of 5 and affects both males and females equally.
  • The sudden onset of petechiae, purpura, and spontaneous bleeding are characteristic features.

Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP)

  • Definition: An autoimmune disease where antibodies attack platelet membrane glycoproteins, leading to isolated thrombocytopenia.
  • Types:
    • Acute ITP: Occurs in children.
    • Chronic ITP: Occurs in adults.

Clinical Features

  • Chronic ITP:
    • More common in women aged 15-50. (Option B ruled out)
    • Can affect any age or sex.
  • Acute ITP:
    • Typically presents before age 5.
    • Affects males and females equally. (Option A)
  • Symptoms:
    • Skin & Mucous Membranes: Purpuric patches (ecchymoses), petechial hemorrhages.
    • Mucous Membranes: Spontaneous bleeding (e.g., epistaxis).
    • Women: Menorrhagia.
    • General: Prolonged bleeding from minor wounds.

Renal dysfunction (Option C) is not a feature of ITP but is more characteristic of conditions like Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS) or Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP).

Hemolytic anemia and jaundice (Option D) are associated with conditions like TTP or HUS, not ITP, where isolated thrombocytopenia is the primary finding.



Reference:

Bailey and Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th edition, Pages 1226, 1227

question: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with a history of sudden onset of petechial hemorrhages and purpuric patches on the skin. The mother also reports episodes of spontaneous epistaxis over the past few days. He had a flu-like illness a few weeks ago. Laboratory investigations show isolated thrombocytopenia. Which of the following statements is most accurate about the disease?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient presents with petechiae, epistaxis, and menorrhagia, which are classical features of thrombocytopenia.

  • The chronic duration of symptoms (>6 months) suggests chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).
  • In ITP, autoantibody-mediated destruction of platelets occurs primarily in the spleen, making splenectomy a definitive treatment in refractory or relapsing cases.
  • Laparoscopic splenectomy is the preferred approach in current surgical practice because it is minimally invasive and associated with reduced postoperative pain, shorter hospital stay, faster recovery, and fewer complications compared to open splenectomy.
  • It is especially suitable in ITP as the spleen is usually normal-sized or only mildly enlarged.
  • During splenectomy, it is essential to identify and remove accessory spleens (splenunculi), commonly located near the splenic hilum, tail of the pancreas, or omentum, as their persistence can lead to recurrence of the disease.
  • Preoperatively, patients should receive vaccination against encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, meningococcus, and Haemophilus influenzae) to prevent overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI).


Treatment for ITP

Acute ITP Chronic ITP (>6 months)
  • Common in children
  • Often resolves without treatment
  • Short courses of corticosteroids are effective
  • Prolonged steroid therapy is not recommended
  • Typically affects adults
  • Corticosteroids are used but prolonged use is not advised (Option B ruled out)
  • For refractory or relapsing cases, splenectomy is generally recommended


Pre-Splenectomy Considerations

  • Vaccination
  • Transfusions
    • It may be necessary before a splenectomy
    • Typically, it is not administered until the splenic vessels are controlled. (Option D ruled out)


Reference:

Bailey and Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th edition, Page 1227

question: A 30-year-old patient presents with an abdominal mass. Imaging studies reveal a cystic structure in the spleen. Based on the imaging characteristics and the absence of an epithelial lining, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Explanation:

  • Hemangioendothelioma is a type of vascular tumor that is commonly found in the spleen.
  • It arises from endothelial cells lining blood vessels, making it a likely candidate for a vascular tumor found in the spleen.

Types of Splenic Tumors

Non-Lymphoid Tumors Lymphoid Tumors
  • Vascular Tumors (most common):
    • Benign Hemangiomas
    • Littoral Cell Angiomas
    • Lymphangiomas
    • Hemangioendotheliomas
  • Other Tumors (less common):

    • Neurinoma

  • Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma
  • Histiocytic Lymphoma
  • Plasmacytoma


Histiocytic Lymphoma (Option A) is a lymphoid malignancy, not a vascular tumor. It arises from reticuloendothelial/immune cells, not endothelial cells.


Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma (Option C): Although it is the most common malignant tumor involving the spleen, it is a lymphoid tumor, not vascular. Histology would show lymphoid proliferation, not vascular channels.


Plasmacytoma (Option D) usually involves:

  • Bone (multiple myeloma)
  • Occasionally soft tissues
  • It is not a vascular tumor and rarely presents as a primary splenic lesion.

Advanced cancers invading outside the mesorectum may infiltrate the prostate or bladder anteriorly or the sacral plexus posteriorly, giving rise to severe, intractable pain.

Clinical Features of Rectal Carcinoma:

  • Commonly seen in >55 years of age
  • Early Symptoms:
    • Bleeding per rectum: The most common early symptom, often bright red and painless, which can be mistaken for hemorrhoidal bleeding.
    • Tenesmus: It is an important early symptom. It is the feeling of incomplete evacuation, often present with lower rectal tumours, leading to frequent attempts to pass stool or gas.
    • Diarrhoea: Early morning diarrhoea may occur.
  • Late Symptoms:
    • Constipation can develop with rectosigmoid junction tumours.
    • Colicky pain may indicate obstruction and advanced cancers may cause severe pain due to invasion of nearby structures (prostate or bladder anteriorly or the sacral plexus posteriorly). (Option D)
    • Weight loss indicates metastatic disease.
  • Abdominal Examination Findings:
    • Early cases may be normall while obstructing tumours can show signs of subacute bowel obstruction.
    • Palpable liver enlargement may indicate liver metastases, and cachexia can be present.
    • Ascites may be found in cases of peritoneal spread.
  • Rectal Examination Findings:
    • The tumour is palpable within 7-8 cm of the anal verge, appearing as a raised, hard mass. If ulcerated, it may present as a depression with everted edges.
    • Mobility and distance from the anal sphincter complex are important for assessing resectability and surgical planning.


Reference:

Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1406.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The image shows a dilated esophagus with a "bird beak" appearance, suggesting Achalasia Cardia, where 24-hour pH monitoring is unnecessary as the condition primarily involves structural and motility issues, not acid reflux.

Achalasia Cardia

Definition

Progressive degeneration of ganglion cells in the oesophagal wall. This leads to a loss of peristalsis in the lower oesophagus and failure of the lower oesophagal sphincter (LES) to relax during swallowing.

Clinical Features
  • Dysphagia: May initially affect liquids more than solids.
  • Regurgitation
  • Halitosis
  • Chest Pain
  • Weight Loss

Investigations

Esophageal Manometry (Option C ruled out)

  • Gold Standard: This is the definitive diagnostic test for achalasia. It measures the pressure and pattern of muscle contractions in the oesophagus.
  • Elevated resting LES pressure (typically > 45 mmHg).
  • Incomplete LES relaxation.
  • Absence of peristalsis in the esophageal body.
  • Periodic contractions with normal amplitude or high amplitude contractions (type I and II achalasia).

Barium Swallow (Esophagram) (Option A ruled out)

  • Dilated esophagus with a narrowing at the LES (Bird beak appearance).

Endoscopy (Option B ruled out)

  • Normal mucosa but may show dilated esophagus with possible food debris; it is important to rule out other causes of dysphagia, such as tumours.

Management

Pharmacological Treatments

  • Calcium Channel Blockers (reduce LES pressure)
  • Nitrates (relax the LES)
  • 5'-Phosphodiesterase Inhibitors (increase cyclic GMP to lower LES pressure)
  • Botulinum Toxin (Botox) Injections (temporarily paralyse LES muscles).

Non-Surgical Interventions

  • Bougie/Balloon Dilatation (ruptures LES muscle fibres to reduce pressure).

Surgical Treatments

  • Laparoscopic Heller's Cardiomyotomy (Most common)
    • The incision in the LES muscle to reduce pressure.
    • It is often combined with a fundoplication.
  • Partial Fundoplication
    • Prevents reflux; options include Dor or Toupet fundoplication.
  • Esophagectomy
    • Surgical removal of the esophagus (severe cases).

Endoscopic Treatments

  • Per-Oral Endoscopic Myotomy (POEM): A newer Minimally invasive procedure involving dissection of LES muscle fibres.


Reference:

Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1122-1125.

SRB's Manual of Surgery, 6th Edition, Page 790-791.

• Duodenal Fistulas can cause maximum malnutrition, as the duodenum is crucial for nutrient absorption, including proteins, fats, carbohydrates, vitamins, and minerals.
  • It occurs as a complication of:
    • Gastric resection
    • Duodenal resection
    • Biliary tract procedures
    • Pancreatic resections
    • Trauma
    • Perforated peptic ulcers
    • Cancer.
  • There is a direct connection between the duodenum and an abnormal opening, causing significant nutrient loss and malnutrition.

(A) The smaller duodenal fistula was repaired over a t-tube; (B) The larger fistula was closed with interrupted sutures. (C) Pyloric exclusion; (D) Jejuno-jejunostomy following segmental resection of jejunal fistula; (E) Feeding jejunostomy

Pancreatic fistula (Option A) leads to the loss of digestive enzymes, but the body can adapt to some extent, causing less severe malnutrition than a duodenal fistula, where nutrient absorption is directly impaired.

Distal ileal fistula (Option C) affects the absorption of bile salts and vitamin B12, but it doesn’t impact the absorption of a wide range of nutrients like the duodenum, which is responsible for absorbing most nutrients from digested food.


Colonic fistula (Option D) mainly affects water and electrolyte absorption, leading to dehydration or imbalances, but it has less impact on overall nutrient absorption compared to a duodenal fistula, which disrupts early nutrient uptake.

Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page 272.

explanationHtml:
• The loss of sensation at the root of the penis after open hernia surgery likely involves the Ilioinguinal Nerve.
  • It originates from the first lumbar nerve and passes through the inguinal canal.
  • Supplies: Sensory innervation to the upper medial thigh, the root of the penis, and mons pubis in males.
  • During open hernia surgery, this nerve can be damaged or irritated, resulting in a loss of sensation in the structures.

Hernia Surgery

  • The most common nerve injured in:
    • Open repair: Ilio-inguinal > Iliohypogastric > Genital branch of Genitofemoral nerve. (Option B)
    • Laparoscopy: Lateral Cutaneous nerve of thigh > Genito-femoral nerve.
  • Landmarks in Laparoscopic Surgery:
    • Triangle of Doom: Injury to Iliac vessels
    • Triangle of Pain: Injury to Nerves causing postoperative pain

Complications of Surgery:

  • Immediate Complications:
    • Bleeding/Hematoma: From subcutaneous or inferior epigastric vessels.
    • Urinary Retention: May require catheterization.
    • Femoral Nerve Blockade
  • Early Postoperative Issues (within the first week):
    • Pain, Bruising, Swelling: Common.
    • Seroma Formation: Often resolves spontaneously; may need aspiration.
    • Wound Infection: Less frequent; routine antibiotics not recommended.
    • Testicular Infarction: Damage to the testicular artery during dissection or repair.
  • Long-term Concerns:
    • Chronic Pain:
      • Nerve Injury: Damage to nerves such as the ilioinguinal or iliohypogastric nerves during surgery.
      • Nerve Irritation: Chronic irritation by suture material or mesh.
      • Psychological Factors
    • Hernia Recurrence: Inadequate repair or weakness in the abdominal wall; mesh-related issues may also contribute.

Iliohypogastric nerve (Option A) provides sensory innervation to the lower abdomen and the upper part of the thigh, but it does not innervate the root of the penis. It is less likely to be involved in loss of sensation at the root of the penis.

Genitofemoral nerve (Option C) does provide sensation to the skin of the genital area; it mainly innervates the scrotum and labia, not specifically the root of the penis. It is less likely to be affected in this case.


Medial cutaneous nerve to the thigh (Option D) provides sensation to the inner thigh, but it has no direct involvement in the sensory innervation of the penis. Therefore, it wouldn't cause loss of sensation over the root of the penis after surgery.



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th edition, Page 1070.

Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page, 1109.

Reason for vaccination:

Vaccine recommendations for asplenic patients:

Vaccination

Children

Adults (age 19 and older)

Pneumococcal (Option A ruled out)

  • PPSV23 8 weeks later.

MenACWY series AND MenB series

Haemophilus influenzae type B (Option C ruled out)

Hib once if 15 months or older and previously not vaccinated

Hib once

    • At Least 2 weeks before an elective surgery
    • Emergency splenectomy- At discharge or 14 days after surgery, whichever is first.
  • CDC immunisation guidelines for 2020 also recommend tetanus (Tdap or Td), human papillomavirus (HPV), measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR), varicella, zoster, influenza, hepatitis A (hep A) and hepatitis B (hep B), and meningococcal vaccines.

explanationHtml:
• In Meckel's Diverticulum, the most frequently found ectopic tissues are gastric and pancreatic tissues.
  • Persistent remnant of the Vitello-intestinal duct or omphalomesenteric duct.

Meckel's Diverticulum

Clinical features
  • Most common ectopic mucosa in Meckel’s diverticulum is Gastric > Pancreatic > Colonic (Option A) (Option B, C ruled out)
  • The most common symptom in children is gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Ulcers are formed in the surrounding area due to acid secreted from the ectopic gastric mucosa in Meckel’s diverticulum, which causes bleeding.
  • The most common symptom in adults is abdominal pain.
  • Complications: Volvulus, intestinal obstruction, intussusceptions, diverticulitis and perforation.

Investigations
  • 99mTc-pertechnetate scan: Absorbed by the ectopic gastric mucosa, allowing for visualisation.
  • Plain abdominal radiography, CT abdomen, and ultrasonography are seldom useful.
  • Endoscopy: Helpful in false-negative cases, but not the investigation of choice.

Management

  • Healthy base (no induration or ulceration): Diverculectomy (excision of the diverticulum only) + anastomosis.
  • Unhealthy base (ulceration, presence of gastric mucosa): Resection of the small bowel with the diverticulum + anastomosis.
  • Incidentally detected during an elective surgery: Diverculectomy.


Thyroid and lung (Option D) tissue are extremely rare in Meckel’s diverticulum. These tissues are not typically associated with diverticular formations in the small intestine.



Reference:

Bailey and Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1311-1312.

Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page 1288-1289.

Gallbladder Cancer is a deadly disease with a median survival of less than 6 months, a 5-year survival rate of 50% for localised cases (with chemotherapy), and 2-5% for those with distant metastasis.

Gallbladder Cancer

Etiology

  • Gallstones
  • Choledochal cyst
  • Anomalous pancreaticobiliary duct junction
  • Cholesterosis of the gallbladder
  • Gallbladder polyps
  • Porcelain gallbladder
  • Infections and inflammatory conditions
    • Chronic typhoid carriers
    • Inflammatory bowel disease
    • Hepatitis B and hepatitis C virus infections
  • Other factors:
    • Polypoid lesions (GB polyp)
    • Xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis
    • Nitrosamines
    • Carcinogens

Clinical features

  • Often indistinguishable from benign gallbladder diseases (Option C ruled out)
  • Symptoms include:
    • Biliary colic
    • Cholecystitis (especially in older individuals)
    • Jaundice (late-stage) (Option B ruled out)
    • Loss of appetite (late-stage)
    • Palpable mass (late-stage) (Option A ruled out)

Laboratory Findings
  • Non-specific indicators:
    • Anemia
    • Leukocytosis
    • Slight increase in transaminases
  • Tumor markers:
    • Elevated CA19-9
    • Elevated carcinoembryonic antigen (in ~80% of patients)

Diagnostic Imaging
  • Ultrasonography (USG): Initial diagnosis
  • CT Scans: Thorax, abdomen, and pelvis for confirmation and staging
  • MRI/MRCP: For accurate preoperative staging
  • PET Scans: To identify metastatic disease

Staging and Biopsy
  • Preoperative Staging: Crucial to assess local disease extent and rule out distant metastases
  • Percutaneous Biopsy: Guided by radiological imaging for unresectable tumours
  • Laparoscopic Examination: Detects peritoneal or liver metastases that preclude surgery

Management
  • Early disease:
    • For disease confined to the mucosa, if there is negative cystic duct margin and no recurrence on imaging- No further treatment
  • For transmural disease- Radical en bloc resection of gallbladder fossa, liver wedge, and regional lymph nodes.
  • Advanced Cancer:
    • Non-operative palliative care.
    • Endoscopic/percutaneous methods to relieve obstructive jaundice.
  • Adenocarcinoma:
    • Early-stage limited to mucosa:
  • No additional treatment is required if imaging shows no recurrence.
  • Beyond mucosa:
    • Extensive surgery involving gallbladder fossa, a portion of the liver, and nearby lymph nodes.


Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 1257-1259.
