Explanation:

The patient has significant burns involving critical areas (face, neck, and hands) and is elderly, which increases the risk of complications. Referral to a burn center for specialized treatment is the most appropriate step.

Indications of referral to burns center

Suspected airway injury
  • Burns on face/neck, hoarseness, stridor, singed facial/nasal hair

Burns needing fluid resuscitation
  • >15% TBSA in adults
  • >10% in children/elderly

Burns requiring surgery
  • Deep partial-thickness (deep dermis damage)
  • Full-thickness (entire dermis destroyed)
  • Circumferential full-thickness (restricted movement)

Significant burns
  • Burns on hands, face, feet and perineum

Psychiatric/social concerns
  • Mental health issues, substance abuse and unstable living conditions

Suspected non-accidental injury
  • Delayed presentation, inconsistent history and unexplained injuries

Extremes of age
  • Infants, elderly with thinner skin and higher risk of complications

Burns with serious sequelae
  • High-tension electrical burns, hydrofluoric acid burns, etc.

Definitive Management of Such Burns:

  • Once the patient is transferred to a burn center, management shifts from acute stabilization (ATLS) to definitive care:

1. Airway and Pulmonary Hygiene:

  • If inhalation injury is confirmed via bronchoscopy, management involves aggressive pulmonary toilet, humidified oxygen, and potentially mechanical ventilation with lung-protective strategies.

2. Wound Management and Surgery:

  • Early Escharotomy: If neck or hand burns are circumferential and full-thickness, an escharotomy may be performed to prevent respiratory distress or compartment syndrome in the limbs.

  • Debridement and Grafting: For deep partial or full-thickness burns, early excision and skin grafting (autografting) is the definitive treatment to reduce infection risk and promote functional recovery.

  • Specialized Dressings: Use of antimicrobial silver-impregnated dressings or biosynthetic skin substitutes to maintain a moist environment and prevent "burn wound sepsis."

3. Rehabilitation (The "Functional" Management):

  • Positioning and Splinting: Especially for the hands and neck, "the position of comfort is the position of contracture." Specialists use customized splints to maintain the hands in a functional position and prevent the neck from healing in a flexed (downward) position.

  • Early Physical Therapy: Crucial to maintain range of motion in the joints of the hands.

explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B) Perform an urgent endoscopy to control the bleeding

Explanation:

Urgent endoscopy is the first-line intervention for controlling gastrointestinal bleeding in patients with Cushing ulcers. It is effective even though there is a high risk of re-bleeding.

Cushing Ulcer

Pathophysiology
  • Cushing's ulcer is a gastro-duodenal ulcer caused by increased intracranial pressure (ICP), commonly due to brain tumors, head injuries or other intracranial conditions.
  • Vagal Stimulation: Overstimulation of the vagus nerve due to elevated ICP leads to increased gastric acid secretion.
  • Sympathetic Paralysis: Disruption in sympathetic pathways may exacerbate the imbalance in gastric secretions, contributing to ulcer formation.

Clinical Presentation
  • Epigastric pain
  • Nausea and vomiting.
  • Gastrointestinal bleeding, presenting as hematemesis (vomiting blood) or melena (black stools).
  • Potential complications include ulcer perforation and peritonitis, which are life-threatening if untreated.

Initial Management
  • Prophylaxis may fail.
  • Resuscitation: Begins with crystalloids and early use of balanced blood products.
  • Coagulopathy Correction: FFP or platelet transfusions are needed for coagulopathy or antiplatelet drug use.
  • Nasogastric Tube: Key for lavage and decompression in hemorrhagic stress gastritis.
  • Antisecretory Agents: IV PPIs are preferred over H2 antagonists for bleeding control.
  • Endoscopy: First-line for GI bleeding, effective despite high rebleed risk.
  • Angiography: For failed endoscopy, involves embolization or vasopressin infusion.

Surgical Indications
  • For unresponsive, recurrent bleeding or perforations.

Surgical Approach
  • A staged approach starting with bleeding control is safer.
  • Initial Surgery: Long midline incision for exploration; anterior gastrotomy.
  • Stable Patients: Vagotomy and pyloroplasty after bleeding control; abdominal closure.
  • Unstable Patients: Leave the abdomen open for resuscitation; second surgery for vagotomy and pyloroplasty when stable.
  • Rare Procedures: Due to the high risks, gastric resection, subtotal or total gastrectomy, and gastric devascularization are rarely performed.

question: A 55-year-old male with a history of a recent traumatic brain injury presents with sudden epigastric pain, vomiting of blood, and black stools. He is diagnosed with a Cushing ulcer. Despite initial management with IV fluids and proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), the patient continues to bleed. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

explanationHtml:
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF BURNS

Local responses:

Skin Damage
  • Burns cause cell membrane disruption and necrosis due to rapid temperature changes.
  • The depth of injury depends on temperature, exposure duration, and thermal conductivity (e.g., oil burns are deeper than water burns).

Jackson Levels
  • Zone of Coagulation: Irreversible tissue damage with cell destruction. (Statement B)
  • Zone of Stasis: Moderate damage with reduced perfusion; survival depends on timely intervention.
  • Zone of Hyperemia: Vasodilation around the wound; generally remains viable and aids healing.

Systemic Responses:

Inflammation & Edema
  • Burns trigger widespread inflammation, increasing vascular permeability, leading to fluid loss, edema, and decreased plasma volume. (Statement E)

Cardiopulmonary Effects
  • Microvascular changes reduce cardiac output, potentially leading to ventricular dysfunction despite fluid resuscitation. (Statement C)

Renal System
  • Decreased blood volume affects renal blood flow, risking acute tubular necrosis if not managed promptly.

Immune Suppression
  • Burns impair immune function, increasing infection risk due to compromised neutrophils, macrophages, and T lymphocytes. (Statement D)

Hypermetabolism
  • Burns induce a hypermetabolic state, leading to increased oxygen consumption, protein/fat breakdown, and muscle wasting.
  • The liver plays a key role in gluconeogenesis and fatty acid processing. (Statement A)

Ebb and Flow Phases
  • Post-injury, the body undergoes an initial low metabolic rate (ebb phase) followed by a hypermetabolic state (flow phase).

Complications:
  • Infection: Early excision and grafting of burns are crucial to prevent infections.
  • Organ Failure: Severe burns can lead to multiple organ failure due to a systemic inflammatory response.



Reference:
  1. Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 665, 666.
  2. Sabiston surgery, 21st Edition, Pages 485-490.

Rhabdomyosarcoma histotype:

  • Rhabdomyosarcoma is one of the few soft tissue sarcomas with a predilection for lymphatic spread, making this histotype particularly important when considering lymph node involvement.

Spread of Sarcomas:

  • Soft tissue sarcomas typically spread hematogenously to distant organs such as the lungs.
  • However, lymphatic spread, although uncommon, is seen more frequently in certain sarcoma subtypes and under specific conditions.

Sarcomas which are known to potentially spread through the lymphatic system:

  • Rhabdomyosarcoma
  • Synovial Sarcoma
  • Undifferentiated Pleomorphic Liposarcoma (MFH)
  • Angiosarcoma
  • Epithelioid Sarcoma
  • Clear Cell Sarcoma
  • Liposarcoma

Tumor Size >5 cm (Option A): While large size increases the overall risk of metastasis, it does not specifically predispose to lymph node involvement.


High-grade histology (Option B): Similar to tumor size, high-grade tumors are more likely to metastasize, but this typically occurs via the bloodstream.


Deep location relative to fascia (Option D): This factor primarily influences the potential for local invasion and hematogenous spread rather than lymphatic dissemination.

  • During the imbibition phase, which occurs within the first 24-48 hours, the graft survives through the diffusion of nutrients and plasma from the recipient bed.
  • The process of skin graft healing is called “Skin graft Take.”
  • The phases of graft take involve a series of 3 steps critical for the successful integration of a graft into the recipient site. These phases are
    1. Serum Imbibition (Plasmatic Circulation):
      • In the first 48 hours, the graft is sustained by plasma exudate from the capillaries in the host bed.
    2. Revascularization (Option C ruled out):
      • After 48 hours, two key processes commence.
      • Neovascularization, where new blood vessels grow from the recipient site into the graft, and inosculation, where graft and host vessels form direct connections.
    3. Organization:
      • This phase begins immediately after grafting, with a fibrin layer forming at the graft-bed interface to stabilize the graft.
      • By day 7, this layer is replaced by fibroblasts, and by days 10 to 14, the graft is typically well-adhered to the underlying bed.

  • A meshed split-thickness skin graft (STSG) is particularly advantageous in cases of extensive burns because it allows for the expansion of the graft over a larger surface area with limited donor skin.

  • The ideal meshing ratio typically ranges from 1:1.5 to 1:6, depending on the area that needs coverage.

question: A 30-year-old patient with extensive third-degree burns requires skin grafting. The surgical team opts for a meshed split-thickness skin graft (STSG). Which of the following is a key benefit of using a meshed skin graft in this scenario?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In this scenario, the accumulation of fluid beneath the graft is indicative of hematoma or seroma formation.
  • This complication can prevent proper adherence of the graft to the wound bed, leading to graft failure if not addressed promptly.
  • Hematomas are collections of blood, while seromas are accumulations of clear fluid. Both can occur when there is inadequate hemostasis or when there is excessive movement or pressure on the graft site post-operatively.

Complications of Skin Grafting:

  1. Graft Failure (Option A ruled out):
    • This occurs when the graft does not survive or integrate with the recipient site, due to poor vascularization or improper placement.
    • It is not characterized by fluid accumulation beneath the graft.
    • It can be prevented by ensuring good contact between the graft and the wound bed and avoiding movement or pressure on the graft.
  2. Infection (Option C ruled out):
    • Infection typically presents with redness, warmth, and pus rather than just fluid accumulation.
    • Strict sterile techniques during surgery and the use of prophylactic antibiotics can help prevent infections.
  3. Hematoma or Seroma Formation (Option B):
    • Occur when blood or fluid collects under the graft.
    • Proper hemostasis during surgery and the use of drains can prevent this issue.
  4. Poor Cosmetic Outcome (Option D ruled out):
    • If the graft does not match the recipient site's skin texture or thickness, or if it is not placed correctly, the cosmetic result may be unsatisfactory.
    • Careful selection of graft thickness and meticulous placement can help achieve a better aesthetic outcome.


Reference:

Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page 1917

  • Inflammatory phase: Neutrophils and macrophages infiltrate the wound, removing debris and bacteria.
  • Proliferative phase: This phase is characterized by collagen deposition, angiogenesis (formation of new blood vessels), and granulation tissue formation.
  • Remodeling phase: The final phase involves collagen reorganization and wound contraction.

The surgical classification of wounds includes four categories:

  • Class I (Option A)- Clean: Uninfected operative wounds without inflammation. Respiratory, alimentary, genital, or urinary tracts are not entered. Examples: Inguinal hernia operation, mastectomy, thyroidectomy.

  • Class II (Option B)- Clean-contaminated: Operative wounds in which the respiratory tract, gastrointestinal tract, or genitourinary tract are entered under controlled conditions without unusual contamination. Examples: Cholecystectomy, elective GI surgery.

  • Class III (Option C)- Contaminated: Open, fresh accidental wounds, operations with major breaks in sterile techniques or gross spillage from the GIT, and incisions with acute, non-purulent inflammation. Examples: Appendicular perforation, gastric perforation.

  • Class IV (Option D)- Dirty: Old traumatic wounds with retained devitalized tissue, wounds with clinical infection, or perforated viscera. Examples: Perforated diverticulitis, fecal peritonitis.

Class II: Clean-Contaminated 10% – 15% 3% – 5%
Class III: Contaminated 15% – 30% 10% – 15%

Surgical site infections (SSIs) are a significant cause of postoperative morbidity. Prevention strategies include:

  • Preoperative measures: Chlorhexidine showers, proper hair removal (clipping instead of shaving), and optimizing patient factors (e.g., glycemic control).
  • Intraoperative measures: Proper hand hygiene and surgical scrubbing, appropriate skin preparation, maintaining normothermia, and proper surgical technique.
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis: Administering appropriate antibiotics within 60 minutes before incision and redosing for long procedures.
  • Postoperative care: Early removal of urinary catheters and proper wound care.

Several specific measures that can help prevent surgical site infections:

  • Staff should follow hand washing between patients (Option B)
  • Length of hospital stay should be kept minimum (Option A) (to prevent hospital-acquired infections)
  • Preoperative shaving should be avoided if possible to minimize minor cuts
  • Antibiotic skin preparation should be standardized
  • Bowel preparation for intra-abdominal surgery should be followed
  • Best time to give preoperative antibiotics (Option D): At the time of induction via IV route or 1 hour before surgery
  • Attention to theater technique & discipline
  • Avoid hypothermia pre-operatively
  • Monofilament sutures should be preferred over polyfilament sutures (Increased risk of infection in polyfilament)
  • Proper apposition of the wound during suturing
  • Prevention of dead space & hematoma.

The Role of ERAS:

ERAS is a multimodal perioperative care pathway designed to achieve early recovery after major surgery. Regarding infection control, ERAS emphasizes:

  • Antimicrobial Prophylaxis: Strict adherence to timing (at induction) and stopping antibiotics within 24 hours post-op.

  • Normothermia: Keeping the patient warm, as hypothermia causes vasoconstriction and impairs immune response.

  • Glycemic Control: Maintaining stable blood glucose levels (even in non-diabetics) to prevent impaired wound healing.

  • Drains and Tubes: Minimizing the use of urinary catheters and wound drains to prevent ascending infections.

Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page 224

Avulsion due to shearing force strips off the superficial tissues exposing the neurovascular bundle, muscles, tendons, and bone.

Explanation:

The management of pressure sores depends on the stage and severity of the wound.

For a stage III pressure sore, conservative management is typically the initial approach, with surgery reserved for more advanced cases or when conservative measures fail.

Conservative management includes:

1. Pressure relief: Repositioning the patient every 2-3 hours

2. Wound care: Cleaning and dressing the wound

3. Nutritional support: Ensuring adequate protein and calorie intake

Surgical management is considered for:

1. Stage III and IV pressure sores that fail to heal with conservative measures

2. Exposed bone, tendon, or joint

3. Undermining, tunneling, or sinus tract formation

Surgical options include:

Immediate surgical debridement (Option A) is incorrect as it's too aggressive for initial management.

Negative pressure wound therapy (Option C) is typically used after debridement and is not the first-line treatment.

Basal cell carcinoma
  • Also known as Rodent Ulcer.
  • Locally invasive, meaning it destroys surrounding tissues.
  • Referred to as Tear Cancer, it occurs typically above a line drawn from the ear lobule to the corner of the mouth.
  • Originates from the basal layer of the epidermis.
  • The most common site is the nose, with the inner canthus being another frequent location.

Types
  • Nodular:
    • The most common type.
    • Appears as small, slow-growing pearly nodules.
    • Characterised by telangiectatic vessels on the surface.
    • Notable for a central depression called umbilication
    • It can also be pigmented.
  • Cystic
  • Superficial

Management
  • For non-aggressive tumours on the trunk or extremities, wide local excision with a 2 cm margin is usually sufficient.
  • For large, aggressive tumours affecting vital or cosmetic areas or recurrent tumours, Mohs micrographic surgery is recommended.

Melanoma (Option B) is a malignant skin tumour that arises from melanocytes, the pigment-producing cells of the skin. Melanoma appears as a dark, irregularly shaped nodule or lesion and is less likely to present as a small nodule of 0.3 cm in size, especially on the nasolabial fold.

Squamous cell carcinoma (Option C) is another type of skin cancer but is less common than BCC. SCC typically presents as a firm, scaly nodule or plaque with a tendency to become ulcerated. SCC has a higher likelihood of metastasising compared to BCC.

Nevus (Option D) is a benign growth of melanocytes, typically presenting as a small, well-circumscribed brown or black lesion. While nevi can appear anywhere on the skin, including the face, they are usually flat or slightly elevated and not typically a firm, pearly nodule like a BCC.

Angular Dermoid

Presentation

It commonly occurs as a smooth, non-tender, soft swelling at the fronto-zygomatic suture.

Location

They are most often located near the lateral canthus, which is the outer corner of the eye where the upper and lower eyelids meet. They may also occur near suture lines of the skull.

Symptoms

They are usually asymptomatic unless they become large enough to cause pressure effects on adjacent structures or become infected.

Diagnosis

Ultrasound or CT scans may be used to evaluate the extent of the cyst, especially if deep or orbital involvement is suspected.

Management

(Option A)

Surgical Excision: Complete surgical excision is the treatment of choice, especially if the cyst is causing cosmetic concerns or other symptoms.

  • Careful dissection is required to ensure the cyst is fully removed and avoid recurrence.
  • If left untreated, angular dermoids sometimes undergo resorption or indentation of the underlying base. CT is done to rule out dural attachments.

Radiotherapy (Option B) is not a standard treatment for dermoid cysts. It is typically used for malignant tumours or conditions such as cancer and is not indicated for benign lesions like dermoid cysts.

Antibiotics (Option C) are used for bacterial infections. They are not the treatment of choice for an uncomplicated dermoid cyst as it is non-infectious. They are only needed if the cyst becomes infected.

Intralesional steroids (Option D) are typically used for conditions like keloids or hypertrophic scars and are not effective in treating dermoid cysts. The goal for dermoid cysts is to remove the cyst hence, surgical excision is the appropriate approach.

explanationHtml:
• Third-degree burns affect the full thickness of the skin and can cause damage to underlying tissue, while fourth-degree burns extend into the muscle, bone, or internal organs. Both types of burns require prompt and aggressive treatment to prevent complications such as infection, hypovolemia, and shock.
  • The most appropriate order of sequence in the management of a woman who has sustained third and fourth-degree burns on her back is as follows:
  • Resuscitation: The first step in the management of severe burns is resuscitation. This involves assessing and stabilizing the patient's airway, breathing, and circulation. Intravenous fluids and electrolytes are administered to prevent hypovolemia and maintain hemodynamic stability.
  • Debridement: Once the patient is stabilized, the next step is debridement. Debridement involves removing all necrotic tissue and debris from the wound to prevent infection and promote healing. Surgical or non-surgical methods can do debridement.
  • Allograft or autograft: After debridement, the wound is covered with either an allograft or autograft. Allografts are skin grafts taken from another person, while autografts are skin grafts taken from the patient's own body. Both types of grafts can provide temporary coverage to the wound and promote wound healing.
  • Therefore, the correct option would be Resuscitation – Debridement – Allograft or Autograft.

Incorrect Choices:

  • Option a. Resuscitation – reconstruction – debridement is incorrect because Ressuscitation – Debridement – Allograft or Autograft is the correct sequence.
  • Option c: Debridement – resuscitation – autograft is incorrect because Resuscitation – Debridement – Allograft or Autograft is the correct sequence.
  • Option d: Reconstruction is not an appropriate step in the initial management of third and fourth-degree burns, as the focus should be on stabilizing the patient and preventing complications. Reconstruction is typically done later in the treatment process once the wound has healed. Thus, Resuscitation – Debridement – Allograft or Autograft is the correct sequence.

  • Skin grafts regenerate because of adult stem cells present in the basal layer of the epidermis (and hair follicle bulge).
  • These cells can differentiate into multiple cell types of the skin (keratinocytes, etc.) but not into cells of other germ layers.
  • Hence, they are Multipotent → multiple related cell types within the same tissue.

Pluripotent (Option B): Pluripotent stem cells, although capable of differentiating into derivatives of all three germ layers, are seen in embryonic or induced stem cell settings and are not involved in routine tissue repair of adult skin.

Totipotent (Option C): Totipotent stem cells are present only in the very early stages of embryonic development and have the capacity to form the entire organism along with extra-embryonic tissues; such cells are not found in adult skin and therefore cannot be responsible for skin graft regeneration.

Tru-cut biopsy

Aspect

Details

Purpose

A minimally invasive procedure to obtain a tissue sample from a suspicious mass or tumour for histopathological examination is often used to diagnose soft tissue sarcomas.

Procedure

A needle is inserted into the mass under imaging guidance (e.g., ultrasound, CT) to retrieve a core of tissue for microscopic analysis to determine the nature and characteristics of the tumour.

Advantages
  • Minimally invasive compared to surgical biopsy.
  • Provides sufficient tissue for accurate histological diagnosis.
  • Outpatient procedure with minimal recovery time.

Limitations
  • The sample size is relatively small, potentially not representing the entire tumour if it is heterogeneous.
  • Risk of sampling error leading to potential misdiagnosis.

  • It typically presents as a painless, rapidly growing mass, often in the head and neck region.

  • Immunohistochemistry confirms the diagnosis with positive for muscle markers like desmin, myogenin, and MyoD1.

  • Histology reveals small, round blue cells with Homer Wright rosettes and neurite-like processes, positive for synaptophysin and chromogranin.

Lymphoma (Option D) typically shows monomorphic lymphoid cells and is identified by markers like CD20, CD3, or CD45.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The given clinical scenario suggests an oncological emergency known as Tumor lysis syndrome, in which bisphosphonates are not used for management.

Tumor Lysis Syndrome

  • An oncological emergency which results when the release of intracellular metabolites overwhelms the kidney’s excretory capacity during cancer treatment.
  • Due to tumour cell lysis, there is the release of uric acid, potassium and phosphorus, leading to hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia and hyperphosphatemia, respectively, which in turn leads to hypocalcemia and acute renal failure.
  • This condition is commonly seen in poorly differentiated lymphomas (high-grade lymphoma, Burkitt’s lymphoma) and leukaemias (chronic leukaemia, ALL-acute lymphoblastic leukaemia).
  • Management includes,
    • Aggressive hydration to correct plasma volume (Option A)
    • Correction of lactic acidosis by Sodium bicarbonate)
    • Correction of hyperuricemia by Allopurinol, Rasburicase, etc. (Option B)
    • Hemodialysis is also done in case of renal failure. (Option D)

    • Some other features, such as nasal stuffiness, epistaxis, and tongue swelling, may also be seen.

  • The investigation of choice is CT scan (Option D).

  • Management of this syndrome depends on the cause.

question: Which of the following statements regarding desmoid tumours is NOT true?

correctAnswer: A. Superficial spreading and Acral lentiginous
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Superficial spreading melanoma is the most common histological subtype worldwide, accounting for about 70% of melanomas, and is seen predominantly in fair-skinned individuals.
  • Acral lentiginous melanoma is the most common melanoma subtype in individuals with darker skin tones (non-white populations). It arises on the palms, soles, and nail beds and is not related to chronic sun exposure.

Types of Malignant Melanoma

Superficial spreading
  • Most common subtype (≈70%)
  • Initial radial growth phase followed by vertical growth
  • Commonly occurs on the trunk in men and lower limbs in women.

Nodular
  • Second most common and most aggressive subtype
  • Predominantly vertical growth from the outset, resulting in early invasion.

Lentigo maligna melanoma
  • Develops from lentigo maligna on chronically sun-exposed skin, especially the face of elderly individuals
  • Has a prolonged radial growth phase and relatively slow progression.

Acral lentiginous
  • Least common overall, but most common subtype in non-white populations
  • Occurs on the palms, soles, and nail beds (especially beneath the great toenail).

  1. Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 656, 657.

question: A 48-year-old woman is referred from a dermatology clinic after an excision biopsy of a pigmented lesion on her left forearm. Histopathology confirms cutaneous melanoma with a Breslow thickness of 2.3 mm & no palpable regional lymphadenopathy. What is the most appropriate definitive surgical management for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The correct order of melanoma from best to worst prognosis is:

Lentigo maligna melanoma → Superficial spreading melanoma → Acral lentiginous melanoma

Types of Malignant Melanoma:

  • Superficial Spreading:
    • Most prevalent type, commonly found on the torso
    • Intermediate prognosis
  • Nodular:
    • The second most common type & the most aggressive form
    • Exhibits only vertical growth
    • Typically occurs on the head and neck
  • Lentigo Maligna:
    • Least malignant form
    • Common in elderly individuals
    • Primarily found on the face (sun-exposed areas)
  • Acral Lentiginous:
    • Least frequent type
    • Has a poor prognosis
    • Most often located on the sole (under the great toenail)

Breslow Thickness

Measures depth of invasion in mm from granular layer of epidermis:

  • < 1 mm → excellent prognosis
  • 1-2 mm → intermediate risk
  • 2-4 mm → high risk
  • > 4 mm → poor prognosis

Greater Breslow thickness = ↑ risk of metastasis & ↓ survival



Reference:

Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Pages 709-711

Anatomical site of the lesion (Option A): Site has some prognostic influence, but is far less important than tumour thickness in early melanoma.

Clinical stage (Option B): Staging incorporates tumour thickness and nodal status, but in localised disease, thickness is the key determinant.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given image depicts the Hutchinson sign.

  • Hutchinson sign: This is the extension of brown or black hyperpigmentation from the nail bed and nail matrix onto the surrounding cuticle and proximal/lateral nail folds.
  • Subungual melanoma is primarily associated with SSM rather than ALM when involving the fingernails. A definitive diagnosis requires a biopsy of the nail matrix, as sampling the nail plate pigment alone is insufficient.

Differential Diagnosis: The primary differential is benign racial melanonychia, common in dark-skinned individuals.

Auspitz sign (Option A) refers to pinpoint bleeding after a psoriasis scale is removed.

Darier sign (Option C) refers to the formation of a wheal (hive) after rubbing a lesion of cutaneous mastocytosis.

Nikolsky sign (Option D) refers to the shearing of the epidermis from the dermis with gentle lateral pressure, seen in blistering diseases like Pemphigus Vulgaris.

question: A 58-year-old patient presents with the nail lesion shown in the image. The clinician notes that the pigment is not confined to the nail plate but has extended to involve the proximal nail fold. What is the name of this specific clinical finding?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The presence of keratin pearls and atypical squamous cells is characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma.

  • Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) is a malignant tumour of epidermal keratinocytes.
  • Risk Factors:
    • UV exposure (chronic sun damage)
    • Immunosuppression (HIV, post-renal transplant)
    • Xeroderma pigmentosum, albinism, LP, DLE
  • Histopathological examination reveals characteristic keratin pearls.
  • SCC is the most common skin tumour in immunocompromised individuals.

Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) (Option A) typically presents as a pearly, translucent nodule with telangiectasia rather than a scaly lesion. Its histological hallmark is peripheral palisading of basaloid nests, not keratinisation.

Melanoma (Option C) presents as an asymmetric, pigmented lesion following the ABCDE criteria. Histology reveals atypical melanocytes and is staged based on the depth of invasion (Breslow thickness) rather than keratin formation.

Actinic Keratosis (Option D) is a pre-malignant, sandpaper-like scaly patch where dysplasia is confined to the epidermis. It lacks the invasive nodular growth and dermal keratin pearls characteristic of Squamous Cell Carcinoma.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 142.26, 142.27

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation and image suggest a diagnosis of Rodent Ulcer, a classical term for Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC).

  • Slow-growing, locally invasive, rarely metastasises; arises from basal epidermal or follicular cells.
  • Sites: Face, around eyes, nose.
  • Features: Scaly plaque → noduloulcerative lesion with rolled margin, telangiectasia, bleeds easily.

Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) (Option A): While SCC can ulcerate, it typically presents with more significant scaling, crusting, and everted (turned outward) margins rather than the translucent, pearly, rolled-in margins seen here.

Marjolin’s Ulcer (Option B) is a specific type of SCC that arises in areas of chronic injury, such as old burn scars or non-healing chronic wounds. There is no history of a pre-existing chronic scar in this case.

Healing Ulcer (Option D) would show signs of granulation tissue and shrinking size, rather than the progressive, "rodent-like" destruction of local tissue seen in this malignancy.

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 141.8, 141.9.

Explanation:

Keratoacanthoma is a low-grade squamous cell cancer. It presents as a proliferating dome-shaped keratin-filled crater. Patients usually give a prior history of minor trauma.

  • M/C Site - Face > hands
  • Phases of growth: Growth, Maturation, Resolution phase
  • Considered self-healing SCC

The treatment of choice is an excisional procedure with 4mm margins.

Cutaneous horn (Option A): Usually a hard, conical projection of keratin without a distinct dome-shaped fleshy base.

Bowen’s disease (Option B) presents as a slow-growing, scaly, red plaque (SCC in situ) rather than a rapidly growing nodule.

Actinic keratosis (Option D) typically manifests as a small, rough, sandpaper-like patch on sun-exposed skin, not a large nodule.

correctAnswer: D. Broders’ grading is used to grade SCC histologically
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Broders’ grading classifies SCC based on the proportion of differentiated vs dedifferentiated tumour cells and is a histological grading system.

  • Grade I → Well-differentiated (>75% keratinisation)
  • Grade II → Moderately differentiated (50–75%)
  • Grade III → Poorly differentiated (25–50%)
  • Grade IV → Undifferentiated (<25%)

Tumour depth (Breslow thickness/depth of invasion) significantly affects the risk of metastasis (Option A). Deeper and poorly differentiated lesions → higher metastatic potential, especially in high-risk sites like the lip and ear.

SCC of the lip has a worse prognosis (Option B) due to higher metastatic risk (rich lymphatic drainage), whereas trunk lesions are usually less aggressive.

Squamous cell carcinoma is the second most common skin cancer (Option C) (≈ 1 SCC: 4 BCCs)



Reference:

Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 654, 655.

question: A 70-year-old man presents with a slowly enlarging ulcer on the lower lip. It has raised, everted margins and a firm base. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Option B - Rasburicase:

  • Rasburicase is the preferred treatment for reducing uric acid levels to prevent kidney damage in tumor lysis syndrome (TLS). TLS is a dangerous complication of cancer treatment where cancer cells release their contents into the bloodstream, causing a buildup of uric acid that can harm the kidneys. Rasburicase, an enzyme, converts uric acid into a less harmful compound, reducing the risk of kidney damage.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Furosemide: Rasburicase is a loop diuretic used to treat fluid retention and edema caused by various medical conditions such as heart failure, liver cirrhosis, and kidney disease.

Option C - Corticosteroids: This is incorrect, as corticosteroids have no renal protective role in tumor lysis syndrome.

Option D - Febuxostat: Febuxostat is another xanthine oxidase inhibitor used to lower uric acid levels in patients with gout. It is similar to allopurinol in its mechanism of action and is not the preferred drug for preventing renal damage in tumor lysis syndrome.



Reference:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Based on the information provided, the most likely diagnosis for the lesion over the left ear in the 40-year-old chronic smoker with histopathologic evaluation showing keratin pearls is Squamous Cell Carcinoma.

Squamous cell carcinoma

Definition

It is a type of skin cancer that arises from the squamous cells, which are the flat cells found in the epidermis, mucous membranes & tissues lining your organs. It is the second most common type of skin cancer after basal cell carcinoma.

Risk factors
  • High sunlight exposure
  • Arsenic exposure.
  • Immunosuppression (organ transplant, HIV)
  • Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
  • Human papilloma virus.

Presentation

It commonly presents as papules, nodules, or plaques with induration and signs of photodamage like crusting and scaling.

Diagnosis

It involves physical examination and biopsy

Histopathology

Reveals characteristic keratin pearls.

Treatment
  • Primary treatment involves wide surgical excision with margins.
  • Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS) aids in intraoperative histopathological examination.
  • Advanced cases may require radiation or chemotherapy.

Nodular melanoma (Option A) is a type of melanoma that is a malignant skin cancer originating from melanocytes. It typically appears as a darkly pigmented, elevated nodule with irregular borders. It often has a different histopathological appearance, with atypical melanocytes rather than keratinisation.

Basal cell carcinoma (Option B) is the most common type of skin cancer, which commonly presents with non-healing ulcers, pearly or translucent papules or nodules with rolled borders, often associated with telangiectasias. Histologically, BCC arises from basal cells of the epidermis.

Malignant melanoma (Option D) is a malignant tumour arising from melanocytes at the epidermal-dermal junction. It presents as a pigmented lesion that enlarges, ulcerates, or bleeds. They generally have abnormal melanocytes and lack keratinisation.



Reference:

Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Page 142.10
question: A 40-year-old man presents with a lesion over his left ear. It slowly grew in size over the past 3 months, and he is a chronic smoker with 20 pack years. Vitals are within normal limits, and his physical examination is otherwise unremarkable. The histopathologic evaluation shows keratin pearls. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Given the rapid growth, pigmentation, and associated itching, the most likely diagnosis is Malignant melanoma.

Malignant melanoma

Definition

Melanoma is a malignant tumour arising from melanocytes at the epidermal-dermal junction. Though it is a rare skin cancer, it has a high mortality rate. It presents as a pigmented lesion that enlarges, ulcerates, or bleeds.

Risk factors
  • Positive family history.
  • Fair skin.
  • Genetics: CDKN2A (chromosome 9p21), MC1R, and TYR genes.
  • Nevus:
    • Congenital melanocytic nevi.
    • Junctional nevi.
    • Atypical nevi.
    • Dysplastic nevi.

Diagnostic criteria

(Pneumonic: ABCDE)

  • Asymmetry: Irregular shapes.
  • Border: Irregular.
  • Colour: Various colours present or uneven distribution.
  • Diameter: > 6 mm.
  • Evolution: Changes in lesion over time (size, shape, itching, or bleeding)

Investigations
  • Clinical examination.
  • Dermoscopy.
  • Biopsy.
  • Immunohistochemistry: The markers are S-100, HMB-45 (the most specific), Melan-A (MART-1), and MITF.
  • CT scan.

Management
  • Wide local excision (with margins measured before excision and determined by Breslow depth, sentinel lymph node biopsy indicated for tumours with a depth of >1.0 mm).
  • If the tumour is aggressive:
    • Immunotherapy.
    • Chemotherapy.
    • Targeted therapy.
  • Interferon-𝛼 is the only adjuvant treatment that has documented beneficial effects on overall survival.


Dysplastic nevus (Option A), also called as atypical moles, are abnormal moles that have irregular borders, varied pigmentation, and larger size and are at higher risk of developing into melanoma. However, they typically grow slowly and don’t cause rapid enlargement or significant itching.

Congenital melanocytic nevus (Option B) are present at birth and are usually large, pigmented moles. They generally grow slowly over time. They don't usually grow rapidly in adulthood or cause itching, unlike the lesion described in this case. They also have a higher risk of developing melanoma.

Acquired melanocytic nevus (Option C), also commonly called moles, is a benign, small, symmetrical, and well-defined lesions that develop during childhood or adolescence. They grow slowly and do not typically cause rapid changes or itching. This is in contrast to the features described in the patient’s presentation.



Reference:
  • Rook’s Textbook of Dermatology, 9th Edition, Pages 143.7 - 143.28
  • Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Pages 587

  • This high prevalence is due to the vascular nature of the brain and the tendency of lung cancer cells to spread hematogenous
  • Ca lung is the most common primary for metastasis to: (Pneumonic- KEPABS)
    • K– Kidney
    • E– Esophagus
    • P– Pancreas
    • A– Adrenal
    • B– Brain
    • S– Skin

Thyroid (Option A) can metastasise to the brain, but it is not as common compared to lung cancer. Thyroid cancer more commonly spreads to the bones and lungs.

Liver (Option C) cancer, particularly hepatocellular carcinoma, does not commonly metastasise to the brain. It usually spreads to the lungs and other abdominal organs.

Breast (Option D) cancer is also a common cause of brain metastases, but it is not as common as lung cancer. However, it remains a significant cause, particularly in cases of advanced-stage breast cancer.

question: Most common primary source of metastasis to the brain is:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient's occupation, history of weight loss, abdominal pain, and hepatomegaly, coupled with the imaging findings of extensive haemorrhage and necrosis, strongly point to Angiosarcoma of the liver as the likely diagnosis.

Hepatic Angiosarcoma

Definition
  • It is a high-grade vascular malignancy that arises from the endothelial cells lining blood vessels or lymphatic channels.
  • It is the most common sarcoma arising in the liver, especially in those with significant exposure to Vinyl chloride.

Common in

Men and elderly

Risk Factors
  • Arsenic,
  • Radiation,
  • Thorium dioxide (Thorotrast)

Metastasis
  • It can spread through lymphatic and hematogenous routes, but due to the tumour's vascular nature, hematogenous spread (via blood vessels) is more common.
  • The liver and lungs are common sites of metastasis, reflecting the tumour's aggressive nature

Clinical presentation

It presents as a red-brown, indurated, and ulcerated skin lesion.

Cavernous hemangioma (Option A) is the most common benign liver tumour. It appears as a discrete red-blue, soft nodule less than 2 cm in diameter, commonly located in a subcapsular location. It does not explain the severe symptoms or the findings of tumour necrosis and haemorrhage in this case.

Metastatic carcinoma of the liver (Option B) refers to the spread of cancer from other sites to the liver. While it can cause hepatomegaly and liver involvement, the description of extensive necrosis and hemorrhage is more suggestive of a primary malignant tumour.

Primary hepatocellular carcinoma (Option D) is the most common primary malignancy of the liver. It typically presents with symptoms like hepatomegaly, weight loss, and abdominal pain. However, the extensive necrosis and hemorrhage described in this case are more characteristic of angiosarcoma rather than HCC.



Reference:
  • Robbins and Cotran’s Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page 522
  • Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, pages 661, 662

    • Well-differentiated: chromosome 12 amplification, including p53 inhibitor MDM2.

Rhabdomyosarcoma (Option B) is a malignant tumour arising from skeletal muscle progenitors. It is the most common soft tissue sarcoma in children and adolescents, and it commonly presents in the extremities, not the retroperitoneum.

Synovial sarcoma (Option C) is a rare, slow-growing cancer that affects the soft tissues. It is commonly found in the arm, leg, or foot, and joints such as the wrist or ankle but it is not very common in retroperitoneum.

Neurofibroma (Option D) is a benign nerve sheath tumour often associated with neurofibromatosis. While it can occur in the retroperitoneum, it is not as common as liposarcoma in that region.

correctAnswer: C. Chemotherapy is given before radical surgery to reduce the bulk of the tumour.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Neoadjuvant chemotherapy refers to chemotherapy given before surgery to reduce the tumor size, making the surgery more effective and improving outcomes.
  • Neoadjuvant Systemic Therapy (NAST) refers to treatments like neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT), targeted therapy, or hormonal therapy administered before surgery.
  • The goal is to shrink the tumour and assess its in vivo response to therapy.

Indications for Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy (NACT):

  • Locally advanced breast cancer (T3, T4, N2, N3): To reduce tumor size.
  • Select cases of early breast cancer:
    • To downsize the tumour for breast conservation surgery (BCS).
    • HER2/neu-positive tumors.
    • Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC).
    • Premenopausal women (age <50 years).
    • Patients with axillary node metastasis.

Neoadjuvant Targeted Therapy: Administered for HER2/neu-positive tumours>5 mm in size, using trastuzumab and pertuzumab.

Neoadjuvant Hormonal Therapy: Offered to elderly or frail women with ER and/or PR-positive advanced tumours who are unfit for chemotherapy.

  • This therapy takes longer (3-6 months) for a clinical response to become evident.

Other options:

Option A: Chemotherapy is given along with radiation - This describes concurrent chemoradiation, not neoadjuvant therapy. It is the standard of care for stage IIB–IVA disease.

Option B: Chemotherapy is given during surgery - There is no intra-operative chemotherapy used in cervical cancer (HIPEC is for peritoneal cancers—unrelated here).

Option D: Chemotherapy is given after radical surgery for micrometastases - This defines adjuvant chemotherapy, not neoadjuvant.



Reference:

Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 933

Explanation:

  • Prostate cancer commonly metastasizes to bones, especially the lumbar vertebrae.
  • Batson’s venous plexus (valveless vertebral venous system) connects the prostatic venous plexus to the vertebral column, providing a direct route for metastasis.
  • This system allows retrograde venous flow, especially in conditions of increased intra-abdominal pressure, facilitating spread to the lumbar spine.

Spread of Prostate Cancer

Route

Mechanism & Common Sites

Local spread

Direct extension into the seminal vesicles, bladder, or rectum

Lymphatic spread

Obturator, internal & external iliac nodes are commonly involved

Hematogenous spread

Via Batson’s venous plexus → lumbar vertebrae, pelvis, femur, ribs

Arterial spread

Rare, usually occurs late in disease progression

Arterial spread (Option A): Incorrect because arterial dissemination is rare in early prostate cancer and occurs mainly in advanced cases.

Local spread (Option B): Incorrect because local invasion affects seminal vesicles, bladder, and rectum, but does not explain vertebral metastasis.

Lymphatic spread (Option C): Incorrect because lymphatic metastasis affects pelvic nodes first (obturator, iliac) before distant sites.

  • Role in Follow-Up:

    • During androgen deprivation therapy (ADT): Persistent or rising PSA indicates treatment resistance.
    • Post-radiotherapy: A gradual PSA rise may suggest local or metastatic progression.

question: In a follow-up case of prostate cancer, what do we need to check?

explanationHtml:
Answer: A) Phyllodes Tumor

Explanation:

  • Phyllodes tumors are fibroepithelial breast tumors that exhibit stromal overgrowth and a leaf-like architecture on histology.
  • They often present as large, bosselated (lobulated) masses with rapid growth.
  • Ulceration of overlying skin suggests an aggressive nature, which is common in borderline or malignant phyllodes tumors.
  • Histopathology confirms the diagnosis by showing stromal hypercellularity and cleft-like spaces resembling leaf-like structures.

Phyllodes Tumor

Feature

Description

Age Group

30-50 years

Growth

Surface

Uneven, bosselated

Histology

Treatment

Wide local excision / mastectomy

Galactocele (Option B): Incorrect because it occurs in lactating women due to ductal obstruction, presenting as a smooth, cystic mass without ulceration.

Fibroadenoma (Option C): Incorrect because it is a well-defined, mobile mass with smooth surface, lacking ulceration and stromal overgrowth.

Paget’s Disease (Option D): Incorrect because it involves the nipple-areolar complex, with eczematous changes, and is associated with underlying ductal carcinoma.



Reference:

Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No.1062-63.
question: A 30-year-old female presents to the OPD with a 3 cm breast lump in the upper medial quadrant. The lump has an uneven, bosselated surface, and the overlying skin is mildly ulcerated. Microscopic examination reveals the given findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: A. Paget disease of the breast
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Persistent eczema-like changes of the nipple–areola complex that do not respond to topical therapy are characteristic of Paget disease of the breast. Histopathology shows large malignant cells with pale cytoplasm and prominent nuclei (Paget cells) within the epidermis.

Paget disease represents intraepidermal spread of underlying ductal carcinoma, most commonly DCIS or invasive ductal carcinoma.

Invasive ductal carcinoma (Option B): Presents as a breast lump; does not primarily cause eczematous nipple lesions.

Ductal carcinoma in situ (Option C): Confined to ducts and usually detected on imaging; nipple skin involvement occurs only when associated with Paget disease.

Phyllodes tumor (Option D): A fibroepithelial tumor presenting as a rapidly enlarging breast mass, not nipple eczema.



Reference:

Bailey and Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 924

question: A 43-year-old patient presents with a 4.6 cm breast lump with ipsilateral mobile axillary lymph node involvement. There is no evidence of distant metastasis. What is the clinical stage of the disease?

correctAnswer: C. Trauma and Injury Severity Score (TRISS)
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

TRISS (Trauma and Injury Severity Score) is designed to predict the probability of survival in trauma patients by combining the physiological aspects of trauma (Revised trauma score/RTS), anatomical aspects (Injury severity score/ISS), and patient age. It is widely used in trauma settings for patients with multiple injuries, as in this scenario. TRISS is calculated using a logistic regression formula and has been validated as one of the most accurate predictors of survival in trauma patients.

The ISS (Injury Severity Score)(Option A) quantifies the overall injury burden by summing up the square of the highest Abbreviated Injury Scale (AIS) scores in different body regions. It is useful in determining the severity of the injury but does not take into account physiological responses like the TRISS score does, making it less useful for predicting survival.

RTS (Revised Trauma Score) (Option B) focuses on the physiological status of the patient, assessing respiratory rate, systolic blood pressure, and Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS). While it helps in triaging trauma patients, RTS alone is less comprehensive than TRISS, as it does not account for anatomical injury severity.

The MESS (Mangled Extremity Severity Score)(Option D) is specific to assessing the severity of limb injuries and predicting the need for amputation. While useful for patients with severe extremity trauma, it is not appropriate for assessing the overall survival probability in patients with multiple systemic injuries.

Score

Application

question: A 35-year-old male arrives in the emergency department after a motor vehicle collision with unstable vitals and multiple injuries. Which trauma severity score is most appropriate for predicting his likelihood of survival?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Shock

Explanation:

The lethal triad includes:

  • Hypothermia
  • Acidosis
  • Progressive coagulopathy.

These three factors worsen each other in a vicious cycle during major trauma.

Shock (usually hemorrhagic) is the precipitating cause but is not part of the triad itself.



Reference:

SRB’s manual of surgery, 6th Edition, Page. 114
question: In the context of severely injured trauma patients, which of the following is not classically included in the “lethal triad” that worsens outcomes?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Allowing permissive hypotension

Explanation

  • Balanced resuscitation
    • Avoids excessive crystalloids.
    • Uses blood products in a balanced ratio (PRBC:FFP: Platelets ≈ 1:1:1).
    • Includes permissive hypotension (target SBP 80–90 mmHg until bleeding controlled) to prevent clot dislodgement and worsening hemorrhage.
  • ABC (Option A): Initial trauma assessment, not balanced resuscitation.
  • pH correction (Option C) Supportive care, not the definition of balanced resuscitation.
  • Colloids and crystalloids (Option D). Old approach: excessive fluids worsen coagulopathy, acidosis, and hypothermia (lethal triad).


Reference:

Balanced Resuscitation in Trauma Management - PubMed

question: A 28-year-old man with head trauma is on mechanical ventilation. On examination, he opens his eyes spontaneously and shows purposeful movements in all four limbs. What is his GCS?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - 1, 2, and 3

Explanation:

  • Oculocephalic reflex (Doll’s eye reflex): True brainstem reflex; its presence indicates an intact brainstem.
  • Babinski reflex: Spinal reflex, does not require the brainstem, and can persist after brainstem death.
  • Decorticate/decerebrate posturing: Generated at the subcortical or spinal level, not proof of intact brainstem.
  • Tachycardia / BP >100 mmHg: Due to circulating catecholamines, not reliable for brainstem activity.

Therefore, 1 (Babinski), 2 (Posturing), and 3 (Tachycardia) may be misinterpreted, but do not indicate normal brainstem function.



Reference:
  • Sabiston’s principles of surgery, 21st Edition, Page. 1885
  • Guidelines for the Diagnosis of Brain Death

Explanation:

  • Neurogenic (nerve) injury is not a component of the Mangled Extremity Severity Score (MESS).

MESS includes four parameters:

  • Age - Younger patients score lower.
  • Ischemia - Duration and severity of limb ischemia.
  • Energy of injury - High-energy injuries (e.g., crush, blast) score higher.

A score of 7 or higher consistently predicted the need for amputation, whereas all limbs with initial scores of 6 or less remained viable in the long term.

The surgeon plans to calculate the Mangled Extremity Severity Score (MESS) to guide the decision on amputation versus salvage. Which one of the following factors is not a component of the MESS scoring system?

Correct Option D - 1, 2, and 4

Explanation

The Revised Trauma Score (RTS) is calculated using:

  • Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) - assesses neurological status
  • Respiratory Rate (RR) - reflects respiratory function

It does not include pulse rate or mechanism of injury.

question: Which of the following does not typically rise as part of the acute neuroendocrine response to surgical stress or trauma?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Prothrombin complex concentrate

Explanation:

  • Prothrombin Complex Concentrates (PCC) are purified products derived from pooled plasma, containing coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X. They are primarily used for the urgent reversal of warfarin therapy in patients with uncontrolled bleeding.

Incorrect Options:

Cryoprecipitate (Option A): Used primarily for fibrinogen replacement and is not effective in reversing warfarin anticoagulation.

Fresh-frozen plasma (Option C) is an alternative but takes longer to infuse and has more volume load, making it less preferable for rapid reversal.

Platelets (Option D) are used for thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction, not for warfarin reversal.



Reference:

Bailey & Love Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page. 21
question: A 60-year-old man taking medication to prevent blood clots suddenly suffers severe bleeding after an accident. Which treatment option is most effective for quickly reversing the blood-thinning effects and controlling the bleeding?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option D - 8 g/dL

Explanation:

A restrictive transfusion strategy targeting a hemoglobin level of 7–8 g/dL (70-80 g/L) is recommended in cases of significant internal bleeding.

  • Levels >8 g/dL → increase the risk of rebleeding
  • Levels <7 g/dL → lead to hypoperfusion and ischemia.


Reference:

Schwartz's Principles of Surgery, 11th Edition, Page. 144

Based on current best practices, which of the following target values is considered appropriate for restoring blood levels in such a situation?

Correct Option D - Platelets

question: With respect to the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocol, which of the following statements is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient is in the Flow phase or catabolic phase, typically occurring 2–7 days post-trauma, characterized by increased metabolic rate, higher oxygen consumption, and tissue catabolism. Catecholamines, such as adrenaline, drive this hypermetabolic response as the body uses energy substrates for repair and organ function maintenance.

Phases of Metabolic Response to Trauma

Phase

Timing

Key Features

Ebb Phase (Option A)

First 24–48 hours
  • ↓ Metabolic rate,
  • ↓ Energy expenditure,
  • ↓ Nitrogen excretion, Hemodynamic stability

Flow Phase or Catabolic phase

2–7 days post-trauma
  • ↑ Metabolic rate,
  • ↑ Oxygen consumption, Catabolism,
  • ↑ Catecholamines

Anabolic Phase (Option C)

Weeks post-trauma
  • Positive nitrogen balance,
  • Protein synthesis,
  • Restoration of tissue mass

The Recovery phase (Option D)refers to the period when the metabolic response returns to normal, with stabilization of energy requirements and cessation of catabolism, which happens after the Anabolic phase has run its course.

question: A 40-year-old male is admitted to the hospital after a major traumatic injury. On the third day post-trauma, his oxygen consumption and metabolic rate have increased significantly, and he exhibits elevated catecholamine levels. Which phase of the metabolic response is this patient most likely in?

correctAnswer: D. Transport immediately and delay interventions
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The initial critical intervention is done, and the patient is transported. Initial life-saving critical interventions are not delayed and are immediately done at the site; only then is the patient transferred.

Initial approach to an injured patient in the prehospital setting include 4 key priorities:

  1. Evaluates the scene
  2. Perform an initial assessment
  3. Make triage-transport decision
  4. Initial critical interventions and transport the patient

Initial assessment:

  • It is done rapidly and includes the identification of life-threatening situations that need immediate intervention.
  • The airway, breathing, and circulation are assessed.
  • Once the spine is secured, the airway is secured, and assisted ventilation can be given as necessary.
  • External bleeding is identified and immediately controlled, and resuscitation is initiated.

Triage-transport decision:

  • Rapid critical intervention is essential, but triaging and quick transport are equally important for optimal outcomes.
  • The goal is to minimize the time from injury to definitive care, ideally keeping on-scene time under 15 minutes.
  • The “load-and-go” approach enables critical interventions during transport, saving valuable time and improving hospital outcomes.
  • Trauma patients with prehospital hypotension (<90 mm Hg), GCS ≤8, or non-extremity firearm injuries have higher mortality with prolonged prehospital time.
  • Any previous comorbidities should be identified and communicated to the hospital for effective treatment and expedited care.


Reference:

Sabiston’s principles of surgery, 21st edition, pg: 389, 391.

question: A road traffic accident has occurred, and the first response team has arrived at the scene. Which of the following is not a key priority in prehospital care?

correctAnswer: C. Nasogastric tube in a patient with mid-facial fractures
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Insertion of a nasogastric tube is contraindicated in patients with mid-facial fractures due to the risk of intracranial placement. Instead, an orogastric tube should be used if necessary.

Steps of Secondary Survey in Trauma Management

Step

Description

Prerequisites
  • Primary survey must be completed.
  • Resuscitation initiated.
  • All life-threatening conditions identified and addressed.
  • Normalization of vital signs should have begun.

Obtain AMPLE History

(Option A)

A focused history covering: Allergies, Medications, Previous medical history/illness or Pregnancy, Last meal, Events/environment related to the injury. This guides ongoing care and anticipates complications.

Complete Physical Examination
  • Systematic head-to-toe exam including front, back, sides, and hidden areas (scalp, axillae, perineum).
  • Reassess airway and lung function.

Vital Signs Assessment
  • Monitor vital signs regularly.
  • Narrow pulse pressure and tachycardia suggest hypovolemic shock.
  • Be cautious with delayed hemodynamic changes in the elderly.

Head and Face Examination
  • Check for scalp hematomas, skull depression, facial fractures, septal hematomas, raccoon eyes, or Battle’s sign.
  • Avoid nasogastric tube insertion if facial trauma is present.

Neck Examination
  • Immobilize and palpate the neck.
  • Rule out cervical spine injury with imaging or clinical criteria..

Chest Examination
  • Palpate for tenderness, crepitus, and fractures.
  • Inspect for seatbelt bruising and assess respiratory and heart sounds.

Abdomen Examination
  • Look for distension, bruising, tenderness, and marks.
  • Assess for peritoneal injury.

Pelvic and Rectal Examination

  • Check for pelvic instability and perineal injury.
  • Perform digital rectal exam if there is suspicion of rectal or urethral injury, especially in spinal cord injury, pelvic fractures or gunshot wounds to the pelvis.

Genital Examination
  • Vaginal examination in women with pelvic fractures or lacerations.
  • Assess for signs of vaginal trauma or pregnancy-related complications.

Extremities Examination

Evaluate for fractures, tenderness, deformities, neurovascular status, and signs of compartment syndrome.

Neurological Examination
  • Reassess Glasgow Coma Scale
  • Evaluate sensory and motor functions, pupillary response, and signs of head injury.

FAST

Use Focused Abdominal Sonography for Trauma (FAST) to check for internal bleeding in abdominal injury or unexplained blood loss.

Special Considerations
  • Update tetanus status.
  • Assess urine output.
  • Remove dressings to reassess injuries.
  • Remove cervical collar briefly to evaluate the neck while maintaining immobilization.

Diagnostic Tests and Consultations

Obtain additional imaging or lab tests as needed and request specialist consultations.

Tertiary Survey

Conducted within 24 hours for multisystem trauma patients to identify missed injuries from primary and secondary surveys.

  1. Schwartz Textbook of Surgery, Edition 11, Page 195.

question: A 30-year-old woman with mid-facial trauma from a car accident is stabilized and the secondary survey begins. Which of the following is not an appropriate step in the secondary survey?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Identifying and controlling external hemorrhage is a step in the primary survey, not the secondary survey. During the primary survey, life-threatening conditions such as external hemorrhage are identified and managed immediately as part of the "C" (Circulation) in the ABCDE approach of trauma care

Secondary Survey:

  • Obtain AMPLE history of presenting complaint:
    • A: Allergies
    • M: Medication - about anticoagulant and antiplatelet therapies, corticosteroid use, and any possible immunosuppressive treatment
    • P: Past medical and surgical history - about anesthetic in the past, and were there any complications
    • L: Last time - something to eat or drink
    • E: Events - events that led to the injury
  • Top-to-toe examination by a systemic approach to the injured extremity:
    • Look
    • Feel
    • Move (active and passive)
    • Special tests
    • Special investigations
  • Neurovascular examination

A full neurological examination (Option B), including the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), pupil response, and motor function, is crucial in the secondary survey. While GCS is assessed in the primary survey, the secondary survey provides a more detailed evaluation of non-life-threatening but significant injuries.


A complete head-to-toe physical examination (Option C) is essential in the secondary survey to identify injuries not obvious during the primary survey, such as soft tissue injuries, fractures, or subtle internal injuries.


Obtaining a detailed patient history (Option D) is also part of the secondary survey. The AMPLE mnemonic (Allergies, Medications, Past medical history, Last meal, Events leading to injury) offers key information quickly.



Reference:
  1. Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Pages 416, 417.,418
  2. Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page 395.

question: A 25-year-old male involved in a high-speed motor vehicle accident is brought to the emergency department. After completing the primary survey and stabilizing the patient, the trauma team begins the secondary survey. Which of the following steps is not a part of the secondary survey?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is a tool used to assess a patient’s level of consciousness based on three parameters: eye-opening, verbal response, and motor response. Each parameter is scored, and the total GCS score ranges from 3 (deep coma) to 15 (fully awake).

  • Eye response: The patient's eyes do not open, even in response to pain, corresponding to a score of 1.
  • Verbal response: The patient makes incomprehensible sounds, corresponding to a score of 2.
  • Motor response: The patient exhibits abnormal flexion (decorticate posturing) in response to pain, corresponding to a score of 3.

Thus, the GCS score for this patient is: 1 (Eye) + 2 (Verbal) + 3 (Motor) = 6

correctAnswer: B. TXA reduced all-cause mortality versus placebo.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

According to the CRASH-2 trial, tranexamic acid reduced all-cause mortality in hemorrhagic patients compared with a placebo.

Tranexamic acid is a synthetic analogue of the amino acid lysine and an effective antifibrinolytic agent that competitively inhibits plasminogen activation to plasmin.

It prevents the breakdown of fibrin that forms blood clots, thereby helping to form clots.

The Clinical Randomization of an Antifibrinolytic in Significant Hemorrhage (CRASH-2) Trial:

  • This is a multicenter randomized controlled civilian trial of 20,211 patients.
  • It showed that tranexamic acid (TXA) reduced all-cause mortality versus placebo (14.5% vs. 16%). The risk of death caused by bleeding was also reduced (4.9% vs. 5.7%).
  • The study found that administering tranexamic acid within 3 hours of injury improved survival rates. A dose of 1 gram is usually given over 10 minutes in the field, followed by another 1 gram given over 8 hours.
  • CRASH-2 suggested that TXA was less effective and could even be harmful if treatment was delayed more than 3 hours after admission (Option A).
  • The PED-TRAX study also suggests that TXA administration was associated with decreased mortality and improved neurologic and pulmonary outcomes (Option C).
  • The drug is inexpensive and easy to use with minimal side effects. The key is dosing, timing, and patient selection.

CRASH-3 trial is currently being done to assess the effect of TXA on the risk of death or disability in patients with TBI.

question: A 35-year-old male is brought in after a fall from height and is found to be in hypovolemic shock. According to ATLS protocol, which of the following investigations is not recommended during the primary survey to identify the cause of the life-threatening bleed?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The symptoms here point to the diagnosis of shock, which is a part of the assessment of circulation.

Shock refers clinically to evidence of end-organ hypoperfusion present on physical examination.

The major reason for shock in trauma patients is hypovolemia due to hemorrhage.

Even though there are no major external injuries, hypovolemic shock can still be caused due to internal hemorrhages that may not be identified at first.

The primary goal of cardiovascular assessment is to determine the presence or absence of shock.

Clinical features of shock:

  • Agitation or confusion
  • Tachycardia
  • Tachypnoea
  • Diaphoresis
  • Cool, mottled extremities
  • Weak distal pulses
  • Decreased pulse pressure
  • Decreased urine output
  • Hypotension

As soon as shock is recognized, the following procedures are to be followed as per ATLS:

  • IV access should be established with two large-bore peripheral catheters or an interosseous needle or central venous catheter.
  • Initial resuscitation should involve 1L of warm crystalloid solution.
  • Product-based resuscitation should be administered if fluid resuscitation fails.
  • >1.5 L of crystalloids should be avoided as it increases the risk of death.
  • Rapid screening should be conducted to identify the cause of life-threatening blood loss.
  • Urine output is the best indicator of tissue perfusion, and central venous pressure is the best indicator of resuscitation needs.
  • Patients are monitored for the progress of shock or its resolution. If it resolves, a comprehensive evaluation for all injuries is done. If not, then,
    • Blood and blood product transfusions,
    • Emergency laparotomy(abdominal bleed),
    • Pelvic binder or sheet followed by surgery or angiographic treatment for embolization of artery (for pelvic fracture and increases pelvic volume),
    • Thoracotomy (continued bleeding after chest tube placement) might be needed.

The major locations that lead to extensive blood loss are:

  • Chest
  • Abdomen
  • Retroperitoneum
  • Pelvis / long bone fractures

During this initial assessment, the cause of blood loss and any fracture is identified and immediately managed with

  • Immediate direct pressure
  • Fracture splinting

Airway (Option A) issues are assessed by a simple verbal response and any difficulty is identified immediately and presents with different clinical signs.

Neurological (Option C) deficits present with low GCS score and issues with mobility of extremities.

Hypothermia (Option D) is evaluated and presents with a low core body temperature, and immediate measures to increase the same are done.



Reference:

Sabiston’s Principles of Surgery, 21st edition, pg: 394, 395.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The detailed history is part of the secondary assessment according to the ATLS protocol.

ATLS protocol/ Advanced Trauma Life Support protocol:

Primary survey:

  • It includes the airway, breathing, circulation, disability or neurologic condition, and exposure and environmental control, which is known by the mnemonic ABCDE.
  • The airway is assessed (Option B) immediately by a verbal response, and if it is not clear, needful intervention is carried out.
  • Breathing is evaluated by chest movements, breath sounds and saturation and assisted ventilation is provided if needed.
  • Circulation assessment includes ruling out shock (Option C). IV access and immediate fluid resuscitation are recommended according to the ATLS in case of shock.
  • Neurological assessment (Option D) is done to assess any traumatic brain or spinal injury and neurogenic shock. The GCS score is evaluated.
  • Environmental control: The patient's clothes should be removed for a thorough examination, and hypothermia should be prevented (warm IV fluids, raised room temperature, body warmers).

Secondary survey:

  • This includes a complete patient history and a thorough head-to-toe assessment. It is done almost immediately in stable patients and includes radiological investigations.
  • The AMPLE history mnemonic is used to gather key details (Allergies, Medications, Past medical history, Last meal, Events/Environment related to the injury).
  • Face deformities, posterior neck injuries, the torso, a per rectal examination for GI bleed, and prostate location are all included in this step.
  • A thorough neurological examination and evaluation of superficial injuries are done.
  • The complete physical examination and use of imaging are now included in the tertiary survey.

  • A preexisting anemia is a contraindication for BPD-DS.

Biliopancreatic diversion:

  • It begins with a distal subtotal gastrectomy with a residual 200mL gastric pouch.
  • The terminal ileum is divided 250 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve.
  • The distal end is then divided and anastomosed to the stomach.
  • A 2 to 3-cm stoma is created.
  • Proximal end of the ileum is anastomosed side-to-side to the terminal ileum.
  • Cholecystectomy is done prophylactically due to the high incidence of gallstone formation with malabsorption of bile salts.

Duodenal switch:

  • The only difference is that instead of a distal gastrectomy, resection of all the stomach except for a narrow lesser curvature of the stomach is performed.
  • The duodenum is then divided in its first portion.
  • The end of the duodenum is anastomosed to the distal 250 cm of ileum.
  • Distal bowel configuration and cholecystectomy are similar to BPD.

Indications:

  • Higher BMIs ( (BMI >50 kg/m ²) (Option A).
  • Failed another operation for weight loss or metabolic control (Option B & C).
  • Type 2 DM with poor metabolic control.
  • Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH).

Contraindications:

  • Geographic distance from the surgeon.
  • Lack of financial means to afford supplements.
  • Preexisting calcium, iron or other nutrient deficiencies (Option D).
  • Severe esophageal reflux (GERD).
  • Preexisting severe malabsorption (IBS/Crohn’s).
  • Inability to comply with lifelong vitamin/mineral supplementation.
  • Patients with high surgical risk (ASA IV).

This overcomes the fulcrum effect of standard laparoscopy where tools are restricted to 4 degrees of freedom, allowing for precise suturing and dissection in confined spaces.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Air Embolism
  • Occurs when air enters accidentally into the vascular system.

  • The external jugular vein (EJV) is a superficial, thin-walled vein without valves in its terminal part.

  • When it is injured, negative intrathoracic pressure during inspiration can suck air into the venous system.

  • Even a small volume of air entering the central circulation can obstruct right heart outflow → air embolism → sudden cardiac arrest and death.

  • Commonly iatrogenic via interventional procedures, but also from trauma, diving, childbirth, and other circumstances.

Treatment

  • Positioning:
  1. Trendelenburg position: Keeps air bubbles away from coronary arteries.(Option C)
  2. Left lateral decubitus position: Helps trap air in the non-dependent segment of the right ventricle, preventing it from entering the pulmonary artery.
  • Hyperbaric oxygen therapy: Useful in both venous and arterial air embolism as it reduces ischemia, bubble size; in arterial embolism it removes nitrogen from bubbles to improve perfusion and oxygenation.
  • Aspiration: Air should be aspirated from the right ventricle with a needle.
  • Open Thoracotomy: Life-saving procedure required to aspirate excess air causing the block.

question: Which of the following correctly matches the zone in an OT (Operating Theatre) complex with its primary function?

correctAnswer: A. Administering prophylactic antibiotics before the first incision and maintaining positive pressure in the operating room (OR).
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Administering prophylactic antibiotics before the first incision ensures that maximal antibiotic levels are present in the tissues when the incision is made, reducing the risk of bacterial contamination during surgery.
  • Maintaining a positive pressure differential in the OR helps keep outside air from entering the sterile environment, which is crucial for preventing airborne contamination and thus reducing SSIs. (Option A)

Prophylactic Considerations

Details

Prophylactic Antibiotics
  • Administered before the first incision to ensure maximal antibiotic levels are present in tissues at the time of incision, reducing the risk of bacterial contamination. (Option C)

Operating Room (OR) Air Pressure
  • Positive pressure differential in the OR is essential to keep outside air from entering, preventing airborne contamination and reducing the risk of Surgical Site Infections (SSIs). (Option C)

Antisepsis Application Technique
  • Concentric circles are often used, but WHO guidelines state that the specific pattern (concentric circles, horizontal or vertical) does not significantly impact SSI prevention. (Option B)

Operating Room Temperature
  • Recommended OR temperature is 21 ± 3°C. A temperature of 18°C is too low, potentially causing hypothermia in patients, negatively affecting wound healing and outcomes. (Option B)

Skin Antisepsis Solution
  • Alcohol-based solutions like chlorhexidine alcohol are recommended for skin antisepsis because of their effectiveness in reducing transient organisms and preventing SSIs. (Option D)

Antibiotic Selection
  • Antibiotics with a short half-life might not maintain adequate tissue levels throughout surgery.
  • Long-acting antibiotics or those that can be re-dosed during long surgeries are preferred. (Option D)

Glucose Control

  • Tight perioperative glycemic control (target <180 mg/dL) significantly reduces SSI risk; hyperglycemia impairs neutrophil function and wound healing.

Feature

Typhoid (Enteric Fever)

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

5th intercostal space in the anterior axillary line is the safest and most common site for chest drain insertion. It lies within the “triangle of safety,” minimizing the risk of injury to vital structures.

Safe Insertion Site:

  • Triangle of Safety
    • Anterior to mid-axillary line
    • Above nipple level
    • Below and lateral to pectoralis major
  • Typically at the 5th intercostal space.

Technique:

  • Local Anaesthesia: Adequate to include pleura.
  • Dissection:
    • Sharp dissection: Skin only.
    • Blunt dissection: Use artery forceps through muscle layers, particularly the serratus anterior, creating a short tunnel to reduce air entry.
  • Drain Direction:
    • Pneumothorax/Haemothorax: Towards lung apex.
    • Pleural Effusion/Empyema: Near lung base.
  • Avoid Neurovascular Bundle: Pass drain over the upper edge of the lower rib.
  • Stitches:
    • Secure retaining stitch, but don’t obstruct the drain.
    • Vertical mattress suture: For pneumothorax

Post-Insertion:

  • Connect to an underwater seal device (one-way valve).
  • Verify with a chest radiograph.

  • Suction is not always necessary and can worsen air leaks in fragile lungs or shift the mediastinum.
